There’s a fork still lying on the placemat from dinner, and some sauce smeared on the edge of my thumb. I should go wash it off but instead I keep staring at it, listening to the fridge make that hum. Today was just one thing after another—up early to get Mom her breakfast, then the usual scramble to prep for class, forgot my own lunch again. When I finally got home this afternoon, I could feel the tension already, that edge when Mom’s been alone too long and everything irritates her. I tried talking about something light (the daffodils coming up in the yard, the neighbor’s new puppy) but she was sharp with me, barely looked up from her puzzle book. I know she’s lonely and scared but sometimes I just want to be able to sit down and breathe without feeling like I’m messing everything up.

This morning before school, she got annoyed because I couldn’t find her slippers, and then I snapped back, ugh, I hate how fast my patience runs out. I apologized before leaving but it didn’t seem to go in. I’m still replaying it hours later, wondering if I could have handled it better, if she’ll remember it tomorrow. I keep telling myself I’m doing my best, but my best feels so thin lately. The students were sweet today, someone drew me a silly little cartoon and left it on my desk, which made me smile for the first time in hours. I wish I could bring that warmth home, but the moment I walk in I feel like all my energy gets zapped, like there’s no room left for optimism. Maybe tomorrow will be easier. For now, I just need to get up, clean the table, and remind myself that small things count, even if it’s just a clean fork and a little less mess.

This afternoon I kept thinking about that moment in the supply closet, when I dropped the entire box of gauze and it made such a loud thud. I remember the look on my coworker's face, just a flicker of annoyance, but of course I read so much into it. Now, standing in the kitchen before sunrise, kettle hissing and the fridge humming, I keep replaying that stupid look in my mind. I wonder if I come off as careless at work sometimes, even though I try so hard to keep it together. The floor tiles are cold under my feet and the light from the stove clock says 5:18, which feels way too early to be awake, but I couldn't sleep after tossing for hours.

Thinking about my partner too, how we argued yesterday about who was supposed to pick up groceries. It wasn't even a big thing, just a misunderstanding, but then it spiraled into something else—me getting defensive, them shutting down. We're supposed to be working on communicating better, but I keep falling into the same habits: over-explaining, apologizing too much, then getting frustrated when I don't feel heard. It makes me anxious for the rest of the day, like I'm walking on eggshells and can't relax. I know it's not all my fault but sometimes it feels like I make everything harder than it has to be.

I keep meaning to write things down, thinking if I get it all onto paper (or my phone, whatever), maybe it won't feel so jumbled in my head. The tea bag is steeping and I'm watching the steam curl up, trying to focus on that instead of the million little things I could have done differently today. I want to text my partner something nice before they wake up, but I'm scared it will come off as needy. Maybe I'll just wait and see how things feel in a few hours. For now, I'm just going to stand here and let the quiet soak in, hoping I can carry some of this calm into whatever comes next.

In our neighborhood we host a fair number of wild turkeys. We are rather proud that we have them living so happily with us. But I am afraid our turkeys are losing touch with reality. They are coming perilously close to disgracing wild turkeydom by their goofy behavior.
The other day when my friend and I were out on our morning walk, three turkeys came charging out of the church yard, jostling each other in a big hurry to get across the road. They looked for all the world like three old ladies completely unaware of their surroundings, flapping their arms and talking to each other not looking where they were going.
Of course the commuters leaving the neighborhood (going way to fast around the corner) were not exactly mentally or emotionally prepared to encounter gesticulating turkeys on the road at 7:45 in the morning.
There were a few exciting moments when all parties became abruptly
aware of each other. Traffic halted, turkey feathers flew and tragedy was narrowly avoided. The old turkey ladies bounced their way across the road and into the field beyond looking all around in feigned confusion as if they didn’t know quite which direction to go now that the crisis was over. They moved off rearranging their wings and harumphing to each other at the shocking state of traffic these days.
I don’t think they would be so bold if they were aware that in a very short time their domestic counterparts are going to be roasting away in our suburban ovens, to be devoured in great pomp and circumstance accompanied by the soothing sounds of football games in the background.
Or it’s possible they know FULL WELL what is going on and were winging their wattles at us all….(Well they don’t have noses or thumbs, so what else can I say ?)
These suburban wild turkeys do not face the usual pressures of country wild turkeys and perhaps have become a bit arrogant. Hunters are not allowed in the church yard. Or anywhere else near us for that matter. The dogs don’t get a chance to chase them because of the leash laws, and really all that ever happens to them is people point at them like a tourist attraction commenting that it is amazing that they live so close to our homes. So they think they live in complete immunity.
A couple of flocks of turkeys roaming around hearing nothing but, “Oh look, there go the wild turkeys!” May have convinced them they are celebrities and are now supposed to get special treatment. Like dressing trailers filled with corn cobs and all the acorns they can eat wrapped in Canadian maple leaves and imported Wild Turkey whiskey on Perrier ice.
(You KNOW how those divas can get!)
I am thinking about disabusing them of this delusion. I am keeping my eyes peeled for the next few days. I might be able to save a considerable sum by chasing down one of those soft, complacent and dare we say snooty turkeys, and inviting him or her over for dinner. Suburban style !
Happy Thanksgiving !

It’s weird how everyone assumes I have my life together because I’m a therapist, but all I feel lately is overwhelmed and kind of lost. I kept thinking about my clients and whether I’m actually helping anyone or just pretending to know what I’m doing. On the walk, I noticed some new graffiti on the side of the old bakery and wondered if I’ll ever do anything that leaves a mark, even if it’s small and messy. Honestly, I’m starting to question if I really fit into this role or if I just ended up here because it was expected. I wish I had more space to figure things out without everyone watching or commenting. The air was chilly but it helped clear my head a little, at least for a few minutes. When I got home, my sister asked where I’d gone like I’d disappeared or something. It’s exhausting always having to justify taking a break. I wish I could just be, without having to explain myself every second. Maybe tomorrow will feel less heavy, but right now I just want some peace and quiet, even if it’s just in my own thoughts.

I don't know why I'm feeling a little restless right now.
My siblings and I ended a game session more than an hour ago. I know I should be sleeping, but here I am—still wide awake, feeling uneasy. Why exactly? I'm not even sure what's causing it.
There aren't many thoughts in my head at the moment. I just feel like I need some kind of catharsis, like I'm trying to wring whatever this feeling is out of my body.
Yeah, this probably doesn't make much sense.
All I know is that I feel the urge to watch something. The past few days, it feels like I've only been doing two things: playing games with my siblings or writing. Not that those aren't fun—they are. But it also feels like I'm not doing anything else.
Maybe I'll watch something later on Netflix. Something light. Or I could start Pluribus. I have a feeling that show will make me think a lot—in a good way.
I'm honestly just trying to squeeze out this emotional bloatedness. It's uncomfortable. Fuzzy. I can't quite name what I'm feeling or thinking, but I want it out of me, somehow.
Whatever. I was thinking of writing a new story today, but I'll probably just force myself to sleep instead.

I just closed the shared calendar app after another round of adjustments. Trying to fit the kids' doctor appointments, school pick-ups, and my own errands into what feels like a shrinking amount of free time is more complicated than I remember. Somehow, the dance class has shifted to Thursday afternoons, but that was already packed with my ex's work meetings so I had to push our grocery run to Friday morning. I keep making lists, but they seem to grow instead of shrink.

I haven’t even tackled the emails from the temp agency yet—half of them about jobs that start too early or last far too late considering the kids. I want to be patient about the job hunt, but coordinating childcare and my own schedule is wearing me down. There's a pile of laundry I meant to fold last night and the floor in the kitchen still has crumbs because I was distracted trying to map out the upcoming week. Somehow I feel both behind and busy at the same time. Maybe tomorrow I’ll finally sort out the paperwork and confirm which weekend the kids are with me, but for now, I’m just crossing my fingers that I don’t forget something important overnight.

The hum of the refrigerator was louder than usual in the kitchen as I got a glass of water around midnight. The streetlights leaked in through the blinds, giving everything a washed-out look. I was too wired to sleep right away, even though my eyes felt gritty. I kept thinking about the dinner I had with her earlier—nice enough, but I left feeling unsure. She laughed at my joke about the office printer jamming, but then there was this awkward pause neither of us filled. 

I’m not sure if I’m overthinking things or if the vibe really was off. Maybe I’m tired and reading too much into it. I know I have a tendency to be direct, and maybe I should have just asked her what she was thinking, but I held back. Part of me is optimistic—she texted me a smiley face before bed. Still, I can’t shake the feeling that we’re not quite on the same page. I’ll try to get some actual sleep now; tomorrow’s going to be a busy one at work, and I can’t afford to drift through it.

The bus engine is louder than usual this morning, and there’s a flicker of sunlight through the dirty window. I keep checking my phone, scrolling through emails that I don’t want to answer yet. My mind is foggy. Last night I was up late debugging a client’s code and now I can’t focus on anything for more than a few seconds. The bus bumps over a pothole and I almost drop my laptop bag. There’s a crumpled receipt under my shoe that I can’t remember getting.

Freelance income is a mess right now. I have three clients, but only one paid me on time this month. I keep thinking I should find something more stable, maybe a part-time contract, but I like being on my own schedule. Still, the uncertainty is making it hard to concentrate on the actual work. Deadlines are stacking up. I tried making a list of priorities, but everything feels equally urgent. I need to send two invoices, finish a bug fix, and somehow plan my week before noon. The bus is almost at my stop, but I’m not sure if I’m ready to face another day of endless small tasks. It’s hard to keep track of what matters when every job feels like it might be the last.

I was asleep when my cell phone rang. I have my phone set up to announce calls, and it said Jackie Paul was calling me. Okay, I answered it and no one was talking to me on the other end. I was not incredibly happy. If Jackie were calling me to talk about something with work, that would have been acceptable. Do I have to put on my ‘do not disturb’ on my phone from 8 PM to 7 AM?! I should.

The hum of the refrigerator is louder than usual in the kitchen at lunch. Sunlight is coming through the blinds, catching on the pile of invoices I still haven’t sorted. It’s quiet enough that I can hear my own chewing, which makes me oddly self-conscious.

This morning, I called Mom to check in, like I do most days. She sounded tired, but insisted she was fine. There’s a strain in her voice lately that she tries to hide. I can tell she’s still struggling after Dad’s funeral, even though we don’t talk about it directly. I wanted to say something comforting, but the words stuck. Instead, I just asked if she needed groceries, and she said no, as usual. It’s frustrating not knowing how to help, or if I’m even helping at all.

Remote work makes it too easy to stay in my own head. I keep thinking I should drive over to see her, but the days blur together, and by evening I’m too drained. I keep replaying that last conversation I had with Dad in the hospital, wondering if I missed something important. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try again with Mom, just sit and listen. That feels like the only thing I can do right now.

I made a genuine attempt to kitten-proof the apartment last night, but I was tired, and the kitten is in need of Ritalin. I left my watch on the bathroom sink counter and found it this morning in the middle of the living room. The newspapers, awaiting recycling, were scattered across the floor. A small pile of change by my computer was apparenly redistributed to the needy. Things that she never bothered with before are now fair game, as I remove other things from her reach.
Some days it's funny, but this morning it just makes me weary. It's a good thing I never had kids. They'd have spent the bulk of their formative years locked in the bathroom, which is where the Kitten is now.
Kitten? Hah! She's got to be over nine pounds now. I'v seen full grown cats smaller than this kitten. She has a ways to go to catch up to WP and CW, but she's going to get there, if I don't kill her first.
Her last bit of defiance before getting locked into the bathroom was to blast the door to the bedroom open. The door is warped, and does not close properly. It can be jammed shut, and that's good enough for CW and WP. But kitten has learned that if she runs full speed at the door and hurls herself into it, the door will open for her. If not the first time, then the second or third. I was occupied at the computer, and did not realize that KfH had blown her way into the bedroom until I heard "Thunk! Thunk! THUD!" and the bedroom door slam shut. The Professor apparently had three unwanted guests - the one who opened the door and the other two who followed (cats are nothing if not opportunists). I doubt he's going to be in a good mood when he gets up.
I stepped up the regimen a bit at the gym. I can handle the cardiovascular pretty well - even when my heart rate goes above the suggested limits I don't feel I'm working too hard, so keeping the HR withing acceptable levels is a piece of cake. The leg strengthening, on the other hand....
I had no idea how my right leg had gotten until I started some of the quad strengthing exercises. Depending on the exercise, my left leg (which is NOT my dominent side) can handle twice the weight of my right leg. Things I can do ten reps with on my left side I can barely manage five on my right. My left side has been doing a lot more compensating then I was aware of. I'm never going to get the hunk of muscle back on my right side, but the other muscles should be compensating better than this. I have my work cut out for me.
Today: cut hair, refill prescriptions, run over to IKEA and price out furniture, try not to kill KfH. Hopefully all items are accomplished.

I wonder if I’m actually helping anyone or just treading water. Too tired to figure it out tonight.

The blanket feels scratchy against my legs and the lamp is casting this weird yellow light over the coffee table, which is still cluttered with receipts and my old planner from last year. I meant to go to bed earlier, but I kept going over the budget spreadsheet, double-checking whether I really needed to buy those vitamins or if I could have just made do. It's funny, I spend all day listening to others and helping them untangle their thoughts, and then I come home and my own head is still full of lists—groceries, bills, what to say to the landlord if the rent goes up. Even with all that, I feel... not exactly stressed, just aware, maybe. I can see the progress, even if it's slower than I'd like. I caught myself smiling when I realized I actually managed to put a little into savings this month, even if it was barely enough for a pizza. The air in here is dry, and my shoulders ache from sitting at my desk for so long, but I think I'm learning how to notice the good things, even when they're small. Tomorrow will be packed with clients, paperwork, and probably another evening spent tracking expenses, but for now, I feel a kind of calm settling in. There's hope in that, and I want to hold onto it for a little while longer before sleep finally wins out.

Just sent a text trying to clear the air, but I’m not sure if it helped or made things worse. He hasn’t replied yet, and the silence is louder than I expected. I sat at my bedroom desk with my laptop open, staring at the screen but not really working. The lines between job hunting and personal stuff are so blurry today that nothing feels focused. I made a list of possible jobs but kept getting distracted thinking about how we ended the last conversation. I wish I could rewind and say something different, less defensive maybe. The tension is just hanging there, and it's wearing on me more than I thought it would. I brewed a second cup of tea but didn’t finish it—just left it there, like how I’m leaving things unsaid. I want to find a way to fix this without overstepping or seeming needy. Maybe I should wait till he initiates next time. Or maybe I’m already overthinking again. Guess I’ll try to get back to my applications soon, but this restless feeling won’t quit. Maybe a walk later will help clear my head.

Feeling restless but focused this morning, like my brain is racing ahead but my hands haven’t caught up. The kitchen is quiet except for the faint hum of the fridge and the soft clicking of the kettle heating water. I keep glancing at the clock—5:42 am—because somehow I woke up before my alarm again, mind buzzing with plans for the day. I keep thinking about the regulars at work and wonder if they notice how new I still feel, even though I act like I’ve got everything under control. I keep replaying little moments from yesterday: the customer who asked about local hiking trails, the way my coworker laughed about my attempt to stack cups too quickly, my own awkwardness when someone tried to invite me out after closing. I probably came off as uninterested, but really, I just got overwhelmed and froze up.

I wish I had someone here to talk to without feeling like I have to make a good impression every time. The smell of toast is comforting, and I’m glad for the simple routine of making breakfast. My brain keeps jumping from thoughts of work to what I need at the grocery store, to whether I should text that new friend or not. It’s so hard to stop overthinking every interaction, but maybe that’s just how I process things in a new place. I keep telling myself to be more spontaneous, but then I worry about all the things that could go wrong. The sun is barely rising and already my mind is full. Maybe today I’ll try saying yes instead of hesitating so much.

Laptop charger snaking across the coffee table, I finally let myself exhale after a day that felt like a constant shuffle. It's almost midnight, and the only sound is the hum of the fridge in the kitchen. This afternoon was just a blur of calls and Slack pings, squeezing in meetings while calculating whether I could make it to the dry cleaners before they closed (I didn’t). I’m grateful for the flexibility of running my own company, but sometimes the sheer volume of decisions – big and tiny – is so much. I had to rearrange my co-founder’s pitch prep for tomorrow because our roommate suddenly needed the living room for a video interview. That meant shifting my own prep to after dinner, which now feels like a mistake because my brain is fried. Still, I caught myself smiling when I noticed how we’ve all started labeling our leftovers in the fridge – a weird sign that we’re making this chaotic living situation work. I know I tend to overthink these scheduling issues, but I want everyone to feel considered. Maybe tomorrow I’ll actually get to cross something off my personal to-do list, instead of just moving things around. For now, I just want to close my eyes and hope my brain slows down enough to sleep.

I feel the festering of nausea, that nicotine-whirling frenzy of falling from the city's stary skies, plumating into the depths of nostalgia. Books cannot satiate the solitary sediments of my being. I've become a fragmented mirror, staring into a million fractured eyes lost to silenced dreams. Dreams filled with infinite bounds, luminescent abysms, water-wells wrought over with rusty words. Books enfold.
Trying to scrap the ligaments of profligacy, salvage the thoughts I've brushed aside; it only leaves trails of empty space where a saterated memory should subside.
Androide love has befallen my fate, always washed astray from eyes of sentious allure: bold, brilliant yet frail and gaunt. I play a passive child, always fleeing from their taint caress, a great trepidation of ominous compassion. I always love the lonly men, lost in their shattered relation.
Always do I flee from the palapable self, circumvolute through the shadows of grappling hands, everything a phosphorescent illusion to keep me from the wanton self.
We all need a kind of rebellion to return to the threshold of mankind - the primative man, the story based man, the religious man, the docile man, 'the refined-defined man.' It's always the ones who live by order, that play the label game. It's the artists and dreamers who shift through tangent realms, feed upon their vices to encumber a rebellion, a rebellion like no other --- the universal against order.
Sometimes I wonder how it is I don't fuck in saddness, or drink wine by moon-light, or simply get wasted at the bars, where man battles with the many facetes of his disallusioned artistry, hopless romantics, dwellers of the dreams or vice to disarrange and partion the effigies of man and woman.
"Brim me a glass of your most poignant ether, and I'll weave you a tapestry of the most effusive disorder!"
These allusions I play in thought. Someday these racing explosions of randomly fired projections, in mind and nerve, shall subside and bring stabble ground. The hour has reached it's time of closure. -fin-

Just finished texting Jen about the pickup fiasco for this afternoon and now I’m sitting in my car with my phone buzzing every two seconds. I really thought we had this week mapped out, but somehow soccer practice got rescheduled and now it’s colliding with my second interview at that tech place downtown. The car is still warming up and I’m staring at my calendar app, trying to figure out how to not let anyone down. It’s weird how hyperfocused I can get on these little logistical puzzles, like if I just stare at the time slots long enough, some magic solution will appear. I keep flipping between work emails, the coparenting calendar, and job applications, wondering if normal people use sticky notes or if it’s all digital now. Jen suggested switching to a shared app, but honestly, every new system just adds another layer of confusion for me. On the bright side, at least I remembered to pack the lunchbox this morning, so I’m counting that as a win. Part of me gets skeptical that any of this juggling will ever feel normal, but I guess I’m also a little bit excited every time a plan actually works out. I need to remember to call my mom back too. She left a message about some family dinner, but I can’t even think about next weekend yet. Maybe if I land this job, I’ll finally have one less ball to keep in the air. Or maybe I’ll just get better at juggling. Either way, I’m curious how other people make this look so easy.

Just closed my laptop after answering a few late emails. The room is quiet except for the hum from the old fan next to my desk. My head feels heavy and I keep replaying parts of the day, trying to remember if I forgot something at work. The stack of sticky notes in front of me keeps growing, even when I think I'm on top of things. There’s a pile of laundry on the chair that I keep ignoring, and I noticed I’m running out of clean socks again.

I ate dinner at the same time as usual, just microwaved leftovers while scrolling on my phone. Sometimes I wonder if I should try to change things up, but I don’t know where I’d even start. My phone keeps buzzing but I’m too tired to check most of the messages. It’s late, but I don’t feel ready to sleep. I keep thinking about the long list for tomorrow and how it always feels like I’m barely keeping up. Maybe things will feel lighter in the morning. For now, I’ll just sit here a bit longer and listen to the fan.

She definitely had a short fuse. I know she didn't have an easy life and maybe that is why she was so angry most of the time. I don't really know for sure. She treated my mom like she was her personal servant and rarely thanked her for anything. I believe that because my mom was the only daughter, it was what was expected from her. Her job was to do whatever she was told. Grandma and Grandpa stepped in big when my bio-dad left. My mom very unexpectedly became a single mom and of course entered into a major breakdown. If not for my grandparents I don't know what we would have done. I appreciate all they did for us and how they tried to give us a good childhood despite my mom's issues. I guess it's not a surprise that I wasn't close to her, but my brother was. I hadn't really thought about it much until my brother got to talking about her and then like a slide show it all flashed through and then it made sense. I was always Grandpa's sidekick! He was very often the target of Grandma's anger and she would scream the most hateful things at him. It's no wonder he drank. 😕 Just like my mom, apologizing was never something she did. After a year of not speaking to me, one day she just did and everything went back to normal. We never talked about it and just like that it never happened. Like mother like daughter. This is one of the biggest reasons I decided not to have children. I never had a good mothering role model and because I saw my mom turn out to be just like her mother I was terrified I would do the same. I never wanted to take the chance of putting my own child through what I experienced. It's funny that just a week ago I was talking with my mom about some of the books I have read and I told her about the Fredrik Backman book "My Grandmother Asked Me To Tell You She's Sorry". I picked it up years ago in an airport as soon as I saw it because the title made me laugh because MY grandmother would NEVER do that! I like the theory some of you have about her apologizing. It would be just like her to wait until she's been dead for decades. P.S. In my book haul are FIVE books by Fredrik Backman. So I will definitely be getting more familiar with his style. Ciao!

Myth #2
"He had a previous partner who mistreated him terribly, and now he has a problem with women as a result. Hes a wonderful man, and that bitch made him get like this."
An abusers bitter tales of emotional destruction by a past wife or girlfriend can have a powerful impact on his current partner. In the most common version of this story, the man recounts how his ex partner broke his heart by cheating on him, perhaps with several different men.
He may describe other wounds he received from a previous partner: She tried to control him, she wouldnt let him have any freedom, she expected him to wait on her hand and foot, she turned their children against him, she even had him "arrested" out of vindictiveness. What he is describing usually are his own behaviors, but he attributes them to the woman so he is the victim. He can gain sympathy from his new partner in this fashion, especially because so many women know what its like to be abused, unfortunately, so they can connect with his distress.
The abusive or controlling man can draw a rich set of excuses from his past relationships. For controlling his currents partners friendships and or accusing her of cheating on him "Its because my ex partner hurt me so badly by cheating on me so many times, and that's why I'm so jealous and cant trust you" He may also throwing temper tantrums or use this as an excuse for having affairs. He can craft an excuse to fit any of his controlling behaviors.
I recommend applying the following principle to assertions that an angry or controlling man makes about past women in his life:
IF ITS AN EXCUSE FOR MISTREATING YOU, ITS A DISTORTION.
A man who was genuinely mistreated in a relationship with a woman would not be using that experience to get away with hurting someone else.
When a client of mine blames a past relationship for his cruel or controlling behavior int he present, I jump in with several questions "Did your ex partner ever say that she felt controlled or intimidated by you?" What was her side of the story? Did you ever put your hands on her in anger? or did she ever get a restraining order?" By the time he has finished providing his answers, I usually can tell what happened. He abused that woman too.
It is fine to commiserate with a man about his bad experience with a previous partner, but the instant he uses her as an excuse to mistreat you, stop believing ANYTHING he tells you about that relationship and instead recognize it as a sign that he has problems relating to women. Track down his ex partner and talk with her as soon as possible, even if you hate her. An abuser can mistreat partner after partner in relationships, each time believing that the problems are all the woman fault and that he is the real victim.
Whether he presents himself as the victim of an ex partner, or of his parents, the abusers aim, though perhaps unconscious, IS TO PLAY ON YOUR COMPASSION, so that HE can avoid dealing with HIS problem.
From "Why Does He Do That?" by Lundy Bancroft

Feeling a little out of it today, but not in a bad way—just a bit cloudy around the edges. The day started with my alarm buzzing at 7:15, but I hit snooze twice before dragging myself to the desk across from my bed. I stared at the blinking cursor in my inbox for way longer than I’d like to admit, trying to make sense of the long thread about supply orders that popped up overnight.

Most of the day blurred together with back-to-back Zoom meetings, answering messages, and sorting through spreadsheets. I kept my water bottle close and tried to remember to stretch, but somehow my shoulders still ended up stiff. There’s something so tiring about always being 'on,' even when I’m technically home. I paused around two for a quick walk to the kitchen, where I ate a handful of almonds and scrolled on my phone, just to clear my head. The cat jumped onto my keyboard during a meeting, which got a laugh out of my team, so that was a small bright spot.

Now, as I sit here in the dim light from my desk lamp, I’m reflecting on how I managed to get through everything on my list, even if it took a bit longer than I hoped. I appreciate that my curiosity kept me engaged, even as my brain felt foggy. There’s satisfaction in checking off tasks, but I wish I could draw a clearer line between work and rest. Maybe tomorrow I’ll set a firmer boundary and actually shut my laptop before dinner. For now, I’m just glad the day is done. 💤

Oh my goodness gracious. Today was not the greatest day for a neighbor and her name in Cathy. She was an emotional wreck and didn’t want to be here anymore. When a friend or neighbor feels suicide is the answer to their problems, never do I take it lightly and it’s NOT A JOKE, either! Jackie, my caregiver is Cathy’s go to person whrn Cathy has a ’bad‘ day. My heart aches when someone threatens or does commit suicide. All I can do is pray for the person and talk calmly with them as they talk. I find living in a building a community within itself, and this building at Garden Court has enough people in this one building, and everyone has a bit of history that plagues us apparently. I wish and pray for the best for Cathy nonetheless than anything else because whrn she’s happy, she’s helping others. Now why did Cathy have a ’bad’ day today,, let me tell you why, ok?
Why the Bad Day?
There are tenants, including myself, that have a history that has followed each and everyone here. Even Cathy, and there’s no need to tell what happened to her a few years ago. There are tenants who live in here who have caused some trouble while living here and have been evicted and booted out of here yet there is still some troublesome tenants. I thought I may get better about writing more often, but that hasn't happened yet. I started my own business several months back. I don't think I wrote about it. Anyway, it is an educational services business that helps new homeschool families navigate the ins and outs of homeschooling and offers both tutoring and developmental therapy. I have about 10 clients right now, which is actually all that I want. I am working on phasing out of my current position with Early Steps and transitioning fully over to my business. Early Steps has seen a lot of changes over the past 2 years and the implementation of those changes is terribly organized, and I truly believe will crash and burn in the end. I am honestly concerned for them at this point, as they have lost almost all of their providers in our area over their new training and how it is being handled. I won't bore you with the details. I have known for a long time that this was coming down the line and started building my business earlier this year so that I could prepare for leaving. I am still only working 2 days a week, but at this point it is two VERY long days per week. I am honestly ready for a break and ready to see less clients. Eric and I started occasionally going to a very small church last year around Christmas-time and this year something in his heart changed and God truly started working on him. Our family ended up all getting saved and Baptized over the summer and Eric has become an active member of our church. Our church family has been such a big part of our lives over the last year and I am so thankful for the change it has brought to our family. Eric and I have truly never been happier, which is hard to imagine. Eric offered to drive the van and pick up the elderly and the kids for church on Sunday mornings, so now him and one of the elders of the church do that every Sunday....I just cannot believe this is the same man as I married. Hah. I feel like every time I write I'm having surgical consultations for one thing or another. I'll get to that in just a sec. A little background first. Emily needed a palate expander several months back and has had that for a bit now. She now also has braces on her top teeth. Well, her orthodontist (one of the best in our area) specializes in working with surgeons for people who need jaw surgery. Well, I am sure no one here remembers, but way back in 2016 I was referred for double jaw surgery due to my overbite. Anyway, I ended up going to a not-so-great orthodontist and got denied for the surgery. I ended up asking this orthodontist about it, and he encouraged me to schedule a consultation and said those are his favorite clients because it is literally life changing. So, long story short, my airway is significantly compromised due to my overbite, so he referred me to a surgeon to correct this. I had that consultation today and got the go ahead to start the process with the orthodontist for the surgery. It is a really long process because insurance doesn't love to approve this surgery because it is expensive and complex. My surgeon, Dr. Ricalde, is one of the best in the whole country and she doesn't think we will have insurance issues. So, I'll do a year (ish) of braces, surgery, and then another year of braces. I am pretty excited to start this process, as it should fix my sleep apnea and could potentially fix my migraines, too, since both doctors believe my migraines are caused by tension from my jaw. Anyway, that is the incredibly short version of that story. What else??? I think that is about it. The kids are doing great. They all seem to be getting more of an appreciation for homeschooling. I think from hearing about public school from other kids. Haha. Oh! We got a new kitten. His name is Mac (like mac and cheese). We have had him for like 6 weeks now. He is honestly the cutest little thing and is the perfect companion for Daisy. I think that is about it. I'll try to update more regularly!

Most of the time money makes me want to puke.
I just finished balancing my checkbook. Thank goodness it is over and I won’t have to deal with it for another month. Can one EVER have enough money? And if you do, will you ever stop wanting to puke ?
I want to have enough money to stop puking !
I mean listen, I know people who have plenty of money, but they still worry about it. What is UP with that ? Seems like if you have more than enough money to cover your basic needs, then you should at least get a frigging break from wanting to puke over it !
Is frigging a word? I hear people saying it, but should it be written ? Why do we use swear words anyway? What is their REAL purpose ?
Dictionary time.
Swear - profane or blasphemous curse
Profane – pro (before) fanum (temple) (outside the temple) , secular
Blaspheme – irreverent
Curse – call down wrath upon
I’ve been pretty down on swearing over the years. Railed at people for having such a limited vocabulary. I mean if f ____ is the only expressive word you know, I am sorry for you.
BUT, I am honest enough to admit there are times in one’s conversation and even thoughts sometimes, when regular words just don’t cut it. But when you use swear words in every other sentence, they definitely lose their power. It’s like they are diluted by overuse. So when you REALLY need one, all you have are watered down, worn out words that don’t come near expressing your frustration or outrage. Then there you are fuming with nothing at hand but limp, wimpy, frayed at the edges words that you wasted on the cranky toaster that burned your bread this morning. Tsk, Tsk. Poor baby.
I remember when I was about 13 or 14 my girlfriend and I used to practice swearing while walking home from school. (Other kids tried out smoking, we tried out swearing) We tried on swear words for size like we were trying on clothes. At first the words seemed like they had power and were highly charged forces, and perhaps something outrageous would happen if we uttered them. But after a few days of this we decided we just sounded silly. So we stopped.
You know when God cursed for the first time, it MEANT something. “Cursed be the ground because of you” is one that sort of STUCK ya know ?
But F _ _ _ you ! coming out of the mouth of a 14 year old just doesn’t
quite produce the same effect. It just sounds silly. Just as silly as we sounded in 1963. Although I have to tell you, at that point in our lives we had never heard the f word. Amazing as that sounds, it’s true.
How did I get HERE ? All I really wanted to say was that money makes me want to puke ! Must come from reading too many stream of consciousness essays late at night. My brains are addled. Forgive me ? :-)

A friend once said to me: “Count your days by smiles, not by tears that fall...this is how to live”…
Just wondering, what’s the proportion of those would be in life, if there would be possible to count? What one could do to protect self from “needless loss” of valuable days?
Build the walls. A Castle to uphold. A personal place for No One to ever enter.
Or - live out in the open space and religiously believe in fairness of fate, when whatever happened – happened for the best…
But the Castle might turn out to be made of sand. And fate is never famous of her fairness. Constantly ppl find themselves on the ruins of their hopes. Or – trying in vain to keep the walls up, when the bricks they collected with such a confidence, simply began to fall, one by one under the pressure of events happening…Do we need to fight it? Do we need to summon our strength and stand to the end, whatever it’ll be? Or – give up and make surrender “quicker and less painful”?
For me first reaction to any pushing always has been – to take a firm stand...behind my wall, to gain time to assess the situation. In most cases nothing would follow, as eventually I would feel much more comfortable being behind, then out in the open and would just let things to dry up…
Fear originates not from personal experience, but rather from fictitious assumptions. From indecisiveness and diffidence. Every time I’m trying to grow that belief that I could be more then I think of myself. Every time confronted with another challenge, I’d retreat back behind my beloved wall, where feels safer. I’m not a warrior. You're either part of the steam roller or part of the road. I don’t roll that road...[sigh]
The funny part of this is that I’m always confronted with somethings. As if it is my karma – to work on gaining self confidence. I’m getting there. Slowly but steadily. And I hope one day I will pull down that Wall Of My Refuge, brick by brick...Although it is so comfortable to be behind.
One who knows does not speak.
One who speaks does not know.
Close your holes, shut your doors,
Soften your sharpness, loosen your knots.
Soften your glare and merge with the everyday.
This is called mysteriously attaining oneness.
[~Tao Te Ching]

I was reading about what psychology has to say about happiness and found some very interesting tidbits. The following is what I think was the best parts. It's a bit wordy and long, but I think it's worth it.
Which life circumstances change our happiness level and which don’t?
Here is some important research we need to know:
Relationships--a close, lasting, caring love relationship is for many a wellspring of happiness. Having good friends also gives most people continuing pleasure, too. A quarrelsome relationship can be the cause of much lasting unhappiness. Being lonesome continues to be unpleasant year after year. Maintaining a loving partnership is one of the surest way to happiness—40% of married people say they are “very happy” (that is a little higher than the usual estimates). Only 25% of unmarried, divorced, separated and widowed say they are “very happy.” Remember they have suffered a significant loss.
Religion--religious people tend to be a little happier and more satisfied with life. And why not, since they have a relationship with God, maybe a special sense of purpose, the promise of a wonderful life after death, and a facilitated social life? The more fundamentalist the religion, the more optimistic the believers tend to be, and the higher level of hope they tend to have.
Money—while, in general, people living in a wealthy, free country are clearly happier than people in a poor country, making a lot of money is usually an ineffective way to achieve happiness. In fact, once we get into a materialistic mode of acquiring “things,” the result is often less happiness, maybe even compulsiveness, competitiveness, boredom, or meaninglessness in the long haul.
Negative feelings--one might think that avoiding negative emotions and situations might make our lives happier, i.e., filled with more joy, but that is not necessarily true. Some people don’t have many feelings, positive or negative. Other people have lots of negative feelings and lots of positive feelings. Indeed, women have about twice as much depression as men…and they have about twice as much joy. So, holding down or escaping unpleasant feelings might help a little to be happy but it isn’t a sure-fire powerful tool.
Most other situations in life have relatively little to do with happiness. That includes age, health, degree of education, climate you live in, race, and gender. You can’t change most of these things anyway. Thus, it is easy to see that gaining happiness by changing your circumstances is a hard way to go. Only 25% or so of us achieve a really good, lasting, loving relationship. Perhaps only 10% or 15% of us worldwide can arrange to live in a wealthy democracy. Getting religion if you don’t have it is hard, it can’t be forced. Likewise, reducing negative feelings requires psychological skills and methods.
A
little summary: According to Seligman the role of circumstances in happiness is quite limited: education, income, and climate don't influence happiness very much; feeling healthy, avoiding trauma, and developing hope through religion only contribute moderately to happiness; however, important life conditions include achieving a good marriage and living in a wealthy democracy. OK, but what about other life circumstances, such as raising a healthy, happy family? Having a successful career one is very proud of? Living an altruistic life devoted to helping others? What about being the best mechanic or a loved teacher in your town for 50 years?
More promising routes to happiness
Seligman obviously doesn’t think “trying to change your circumstances” is the best way to become happy. Instead, developing new personality traits, different outlooks, and more positive attitudes offer more hope because they may be more under your voluntary control.
Starting from the great virtues identified by philosophers over the last 5000 years, such as wisdom, courage, love, justice, temperance and transcendence, Seligman tries to help each person discover their own unique strengths or virtues. He calls these individual traits your “signature strengths.” Much of his book focuses on teaching you to nurture your positive natural traits or virtues, so you can live “the good life” and experience authentic happiness in work, love, and child rearing. To his credit, he has also developed a Web site (http://www.authentichappiness.org) which supplements his book. The site offers rating scales which are automatically scored, explained, and stored in your personal test folder. The ratings measure and provide norms for several of your traits or characteristics, such as your Signature Strengths (listed later), happiness, positive and negative feelings, optimism, close relationships, and so on.
The Interaction of Happiness and Depression
It is commonly thought that happiness is the positive end of the depression scale. Of course, in the extremes, great happiness and deep depression are mutually exclusive; you can hardly be in the depths of suicidal depression and be considered happy at the same time. But in the less extreme ranges, happiness and depression appear to be rather independent of each other. It is very interesting that psychologists consistently find women in general are more depressed than men, but psychological tests also show men and women are equally happy. This clearly shows that happiness is not just the opposite of depression (Myers, 1992). This also fits with common sense about happiness. That is, people know they can go out and have a good time at a party, then come home to be lonely and miserable again. Another example: you can handle some situation that is causing you to be very unhappy, but that accomplishment may not produce much happiness, just relief from the pain. You can be unhappy about some things and happy about others at the same time, much like you can both love and hate a person at the same time (Swanbrow, 1989; Diener, Sandvik, & Pavot, 1990). In contrast, you can't be both relaxed and anxious at the same time.
We are learning more about happiness. One interesting point is that happy people tend to be decisive, healthy, creative, motivated, social, trusting, and caring, compared to unhappy people. Another is that they feel "in control" and/or have a sense of well being. As you might expect, happy people have more faith in a "higher power" than unhappy people. Among atheists and non-religious, only about 15%-30% claim to be "very happy." Among religious folks, 25% to 40% say they are "very happy." A religion helps us handle great losses (probably due to the concept of eternal life), but religious people sometimes feel less in personal control (Myers, 1992)
In some cases, however, religion reinforces feelings of guilt and the person becomes a martyr who feels he/she deserves punishment or needs to endure unhappiness. They may feel so unworthy that life only has meaning if they suffer great hardship and pain. Others think they do not deserve to feel good; thus, if life is going well for them, they quickly find a problem to feel badly about (see later discussion of shame and guilt). Such people focus on the seriousness of life. Overall, however, to most people religion probably gives more satisfaction than grief.

The bus jolted over another pothole, making the numbers on my spreadsheet blur on my phone screen. I must be the only person on this route reviewing invoices at 6:30 PM, but deadlines have a way of following me home. There’s a low hum from the engine and someone’s earbuds leaking tinny pop music a few seats back. I caught myself thinking about Laura again—she texted a meme about accountants being boring, which, fair enough, but it stung a bit more than I let on. It’s strange to be in this limbo where things feel new but undefined, like waiting for a meeting agenda that never arrives. Work is relentless this week, quarter-end always is, and I’m already dreading tomorrow’s stack of reconciliations. Still, I keep wondering if I should say something to her about where this is going or just let it develop, assuming it’s developing at all. The bus turns sharply and I almost drop my phone; maybe that’s a sign to stop working for the day, but shutting off isn’t exactly my strong suit. There’s comfort in numbers—they add up or they don’t, no ambiguity. Relationships are a whole different ledger. I’m trying to keep calm, focus on what’s in front of me, but it’s easier to balance accounts than emotions. At least the ride’s almost over. Maybe tonight I’ll actually cook instead of microwaving leftovers again.

The dishwasher is humming and plates are stacked beside me, some still wet. The kitchen lights feel too bright, but it’s better than bumping into things. Dinner wasn’t quiet tonight. Everyone kept talking over each other, and I barely got a word in. I wanted to ask for help with the groceries but ended up doing most by myself, again. 

My husband seemed distant, barely looking up from his phone. I wanted to ask if we’re okay but chickened out, not the right time with the kids around. I’m tired and my brain keeps skipping around, forgetting what I was about to do. I wish I had a room to myself just for an hour. I told myself I’d fold the laundry after dinner, but I might just leave it for tomorrow. I need to breathe and not think for a bit.

This afternoon I caught a glimpse of my kid laughing with their dad while looking at the calendar app on our phones. It was one of those rare moments when the calendar chaos seemed to slow down, and they just shared a normal laugh. I usually keep my distance from these exchanges because scheduling feels like a battleground, but today it hit me how much these little moments matter.

Now, after dinner, my shoulders are still tense from the endless coordination. I’m restless, knowing tomorrow’s shift will be just as demanding. The clutter of dates and drop-offs swirls in my head. I want to be straightforward about what works and what doesn’t, but I worry that being too blunt might backfire. Maybe I just need to take a breath and focus on the small wins, like that laugh I saw earlier. It’s not much, but it’s enough for tonight. ☕

The quiet hum of the heater fills the living room while the street outside feels totally still, almost like the city is holding its breath. I was just on the couch, trying to unwind after the late shift, but my mind keeps flipping back to Mom. I didn’t call today like I promised myself because I didn’t want to break down while everyone was around. It’s hard being so far away now, and I keep wondering if I’m doing enough to keep her memory alive. She would have loved this little apartment, I think, even with its crooked shelves and the tired couch I’m sinking into. Sometimes I catch myself talking to her in my head when I’m walking to work or stacking boxes, and it’s like she’s there telling me to keep going. I know I’m still figuring out how to live here, making friends feels like a slow drip, but tonight I realized how much I need to make this place home, not just a stopgap. I might try that community group next week, even if it makes me nervous. It’s weird how grief makes your chest feel full but empty at the same time. I miss her so much I can almost hear her voice when I’m alone. I guess that’s why I’m jittery now—half hopeful, half scared about building something new without her. But I also know she wanted me to be happy, wherever I ended up. So, maybe tomorrow, I’ll call her old friends here and see how they’re doing. It’s like I’m walking a tightrope between holding on and letting go, and some nights it’s harder to find my balance.

In typical fashion I wanted to redo my nails shortly after I took the photos. And that's what I did. I had bought a few new polishes a couple of weeks ago. One of those was "Blue-tiful" which I tried out. The result is a blue with orange shimmer, and whilst it's mostly blue there are some orange undertones/accents. It's a very interesting colour, and one I would definitely buy again! I did my nails on Christmas Eve. L had done shopping a few days before that and it was nice to have someone else stress over it for once. Now I usually enjoy shopping, it's one of the few outings I truly do enjoy, and it's been the same since I was a kid. However, the closer you get to public holidays, the more crowded the stores get, and Christmas time is extra busy. There's more people, some are stressed and rude, others are in the way, or indecisive. Some snatch items from under your nose that you were about to grab. The queues are lengthy. L did say that the shop where we usually get our food was really busy, so I definitely think it's a good thing I stayed home. Then Christmas was of course much like any other day, albeit a bit more lazy. However, what we did do was eating leftover Chinese food from the day before and watching a Lord of the Rings marathon. We watched The Fellowship of the Ring, then we started The Two Towers, but stopped after an hour because it was getting late. So the last parts of Two Towers as well as the entire The Return of the King will have to wait until next time. It was my first time seeing The Fellowship of the Ring on the big screen, by that I mean, non-cinema TV. No doubt I've mentioned before that LotR used to be one of my favourite fantasy series. I watched the movies a bunch of times, and sometimes back to back on the same day. However it has been years now since I last saw them. Sometimes I wished I could watch them again, but mostly I haven't felt I had the energy or time. But I'm happy we watched them, and I discovered that the movies were far more enjoyable than I'd thought they'd be now that I'm much older. It's not the same as when I was young, where I could watch the same movies several times over the course of a couple of months without ever getting bored. Now I just enjoyed them for what they were. And as an adult watching them I can appreciate details in the scenery, cinematography, costumes, props, acting, and the music, much more than I could as a kid or a teenager. The movies, especially the extended versions, are lengthy. But they didn't drag on, though there were a few scenes that I felt could have been cut shorter without any great loss. Tomorrow I'll be having another lazy day. Not necessarily by choice though, because the weather forecast is looking grim. Heavy rains and thunder. Sounds lovely in one way, but also it means my mood will be affected. But I'll try to make the most of it. Maybe we will finish the LotR marathon. I also need to catch up with my friend L.A and tell her about my new hobby (which is writing, but in another language).

Earlier today, I caught myself rereading an email to the product manager for the third time before sending it. I wanted every word to sound precise, but even then I wasn’t sure if I was being too blunt or too vague. Now, during this quiet lunch break, I’m just sitting at my desk, sandwich in hand, trying to let my mind slow down. My code review backlog keeps popping into my head, and I know it’s not healthy to think about work constantly, but the boundaries are so blurry with remote work that I don’t even notice the switch flipping anymore.

I keep wondering if I’m doing enough or if my teammates think I’m slacking. The optimistic part of me says I’m learning fast, but I can’t shake the feeling that I miss things others catch easily. I’ve started doubting the value of our current project, which probably isn’t helping my focus or motivation. There’s a meeting later that I’m already overthinking. I am trying to catch up to my son's level of computer literacy.
This will take me the rest of my life. But true geekdome lures me ever onward.
While putting my personal folder on my desktop the other evening, I asked my son, "On a scale of one to ten, ten being staying up all night, how much tweaking would it take to change this icon on my folder?"
He said, "Oh, well, there you have about a four tweak project on your hands."
"Sure, I said, but what if you had two geeks working on it?"
We then began to think of other computer projects and how many geeks and tweaks would be required for each one and this is what we came up with.
Changing the appearance of your desktop :
1 geek, 1 tweak job.
Very straightforward, but remember to click on the APPLY button or you have to start over.
Reconfiguring your internet software :
2 geeks, 4 tweaks .
This will include calling tech support at least three times, ( be nice to the person, they have a hard life) and don't forget to save your password !
Learning to save your work on a floppy for the first time:
You and one remote geek, 5 tweaks.
The high tweak level comes from opening the floppy 3 or 4 times to make sure that the stuff is really on that little plastic thingy. (Excuse me for a moment, I am going to check my floppys right now.)
Opening a file that someone has attached to your e-mail for the first time.
3 geeks, 3 tweaks.
By the way, if you get more than 3 geeks working on the same project, the tweak level goes up due to arguing.
(And then you find out it is the Dancing Baby you have just worked so hard to open. Oy)
Setting up a computer for the first time and installing Windows:
3 geeks, 9 tweaks plus munchies and long distance consultant geek from Alabama, (our friend Tom who sent us the computer)
Remote geeks do not count as added tweaks because you can hang up on them and the prefered munchies of my resident geeks are chocolate and Doritos.
Added note : be prepared, my son tells me that installing windows requires that you re-start your computer 50 times, allow extra munchies for this.
Changing the icons on your desktop:
2 geeks,4 tweaks.
Plus some program called....what else?, Tweak UI which needs to be downloaded from the internet, this adds one tweak.
Learning to use your word processor :
You and 3 geeks. Tweak level off the scale.
Hopefully, one geek will be remote. Hitting the computer does not count as a tweak, and watch out for those default settings !
These of course are only rough guesses. Depending on the arrogance or argumentitiveness of your geeks, and the speed of your computer, the amount of it’s RAM , ROM and RUM… (rum ?) all of which are among the mysteries of the universe. You may come up with different results.
Happy Tweaking !
Better go to the store right now for emergency munchies, just in case I decide to reconfigure anything in my device manager. See ya in cyberspace !

I had the day off because I worked on New Year's Day. I should've had a quiet, easy morning. Instead I got up and went to the hospital to get an MRI. I know what you're thinking: an MRI on Sunday? That's weird. Yeah, I thought it was weird, too. I imagine they just have so many people needing to get tests that they just schedule through the weekends. I have a new primary care provider. She's an internist and a DO. I casually mentioned that I've been having problems with facial numbness and trouble swallowing. I got scolded for not going to the ER every time it happens, but honestly it happens A LOT. She mentioned sending me to get a brain MRI to rule out any tumors or lesions but emphasized that she didn't think it was likely an issue. I low-key thought, "yeah, I'll decide later whether or not I follow up on that…" But here's the thing: she also offered me HRT therapy for my perimenopause symptoms… which means I could maybe start sleeping better at night. Score! But, wait: you can't take hormones if you have a tumor. So she told me she wouldn't prescribe the HRT until we got the results of the MRI. So this was the dilemma: how bad did I want the HRT? Bad enough to schedule the MRI, it turns out. I knew it was going to be rough, and it was. I mentally prepared myself as much as possible for being stuck in a tube, not able to move, with very loud noises going on all around me… but I don't know how much it helped. They gave me headphones and put on some "easy listening" soft rock, but I could barely hear it because the machine was so loud. I can't breathe! Yes, you can. That's just your tongue sliding back into your throat. Push it forward. I can't breathe! Yes, you can. This is just your brain trying to panic. Ground yourself and take deep breaths. I need out now! No, you don't. You're fine. And if you move you're going to have to start over. I was eventually able to cope by counting and gently tapping with one finger. It worked against me once, though, when I tapped a little too hard and got a blurry image and had to repeat a scan. I kept track of time by counting songs. The scan only took 30 minutes, but it felt like an eternity. Halfway through they pulled me out and injected the contrast. I was shaking so they gave me another warm blanket. "Are you okay?" "Yup." Lies. I got through it, though. I should get results in the next 24-36 hours. I'm sure they will be clear, which is ultimately a good thing. It doesn't feel like a good thing at this moment. The hum of the bus engine almost drowns out everything else, and the glow from the streetlights through the window keeps flickering on my notebook. I'm trying to make sense of what still needs to be done today, but my head feels stuffed with cotton. Work was nonstop, especially since it's month-end again, and every little error seems to stick to me. Still, the bigger worry is figuring out how to juggle the bills and appointments for Mom. I keep thinking I’ll get ahead if I just organize everything better, but I never do.

There’s a pharmacy run I skipped last week, and now I need to remember to call her doctor before Friday. Groceries are running low, but I’m not sure when I’ll have time to get to the store. I also need to finish up with next week’s payroll reports, but I know I’ll just end up doing them when I’m already tired. I wish I could stop thinking about all this for even ten minutes, but the lists keep looping in my brain. Maybe I’ll try setting reminders on my phone tonight and see if that helps, though I doubt I’ll get through half of it tomorrow.

The early sun glare is bouncing off the neighbor’s window right onto my desk, lighting up the clutter in a way that makes it all look even more chaotic. I’m running on maybe four hours of sleep and my brain feels like it’s moving through syrup, but I keep replaying that conversation with Josh from this morning. He stopped by before work, apparently just to “check in,” but the way he kept glancing at my empty wallet on the desk, I could tell he wanted to say something about my situation. I tried to keep things light, tossed out a sarcastic comment about my new minimalist lifestyle, but I’m not sure he picked up on it. Sometimes I wonder if my dry humor just flies right over people’s heads or if I’m unconsciously using it to keep things at arm’s length.

I know he means well, and maybe I’m reading into things because I’m tired and stressed, but it felt like he was judging me a little. Or maybe I was the one judging myself and projecting it onto him. Either way, the whole thing left me feeling a bit raw. I don’t like talking about money, especially when things are tight. Part of me wants to reach out later and clarify, but the other part just wants to let it go and hope it didn’t come off as awkward as it felt. Social stuff always feels trickier when I’m running on empty. I need to remember that not every interaction is a referendum on my life decisions, but it’s hard not to get defensive when things are this precarious. At least in here, behind the closed door, I can just breathe and be irritated in peace.

We had a few days of cooling off weather. The trees have just barely started turning color. They haven't even lost their leaves yet. It's getting toward the end of October, but................
Winter came roaring in early this morning (Tuesday). Horizontal rain. Winds up to 58 mph at the airport. Snow in the mountains. Boreal expects to open at least one lift by this weekend. Mud slides in the areas already devastated by fire. Parts of Highway 50 closed because of mudslides. Almost an inch of rain in Sacramento. About 1-1/4 inch in Stockton, just down the road. Wow!
I had a doctor's appointment this morning, and debated whether to go by freeway or surface street. My doctor's office is about 20 miles away, and I can get there pretty fast by surface street, but I elected the freeway because I thought that some low parts of the surface street might be flooded. They weren't, as it turned out.
Maniacs on the freeway. I was driving in the far right lane at 50 mph. I set my cruise control because my foot gets a little heavy sometimes, and I didn't want to take any chance on hydroplane speed. Too many others on the road apparently don't care, think it can't happen to them, or simply don't know. I'm really surprised that a couple cars didn't go flying off the freeway when they hit the curves. Now, admittedly the curves aren't all that sharp, but at excessive speed in high wind and heavy rain, hydroplaning can mean disaster on even a gentle curve.
No such accidents were reported on the evening news, but there were cars crushed by falling trees or heavy limbs. Happens every year. So far, no trees have smashed into homes, but it'll happen. Power lines knocked down by falling tree limbs. Earlier about 30,000 homes, it was reported, were without power, but most of them have been rescued by now.
The storm covered pretty much all the Pacific Coast, and there's more churning out there on the Ocean, just waiting to slam into us. It was a doozy! Kind of invigorating, though. As long as the snow stays up there.
Shalom

This morning I dropped my calculator in the kitchen while rushing to get out, and the batteries rolled under the fridge so I had to crouch on the cold tile, reaching around for them with a pen. Now it’s almost midnight and I’m sitting at my desk, staring at spreadsheets and half-finished notes for my ethics class. The stack of receipts on the left keeps sliding down, and it’s making me irrationally irritated. I keep glancing at the clock and feeling like I’m running out of time, but I’m not sure for what exactly. I finished a big project at work today but I couldn’t really enjoy it because my mind kept circling back to an offhand comment my professor made about "finding balance." I don’t know if I’m supposed to feel proud or just tired—probably both. There’s a half-eaten apple next to my laptop, and the skin’s started to wrinkle already. I replayed a conversation with a classmate in my head at least three times, picking apart what I said, worrying I sounded cold or distracted. I’m anxious about the exam next week, but more than that I’m anxious about what I’m even doing right now. Am I just checking boxes, or is there actually something I want out of all this? The hum of my laptop fan is loud tonight, or maybe the apartment is just too quiet. I keep thinking if I could just get one thing perfectly right, maybe the rest would feel easier. Instead, everything feels like it’s at the edge of slipping away, and I can’t seem to decide if I’m doing enough or just pretending. I wish I could shut off the second-guessing for an hour. I’m tired but not really sleepy. I’ll probably read through my notes one more time before bed, even though I know I won’t remember much in the morning.

Tired and my head’s all over the place. I’m in the kitchen, it’s way too early and the light from the fridge is the only thing on. There’s a pile of boxes in the corner I haven’t unpacked, and I keep tripping over the same suitcase every morning. Nothing is where it should be, and I can’t even find the stupid toaster, so I just ate dry bread before my shift. I keep making lists of things to do (change address, buy hangers, call the bank) but I never really finish anything, just add more. My work uniform is wrinkled and I don’t know where the iron is, so whatever. I hate how every little thing feels like a big deal lately, like I can’t just relax for one second. The clock says 6:17 and I already feel behind. Maybe tonight I’ll try to tackle the dishes and set up my bed frame, but honestly, it could all wait. I just want one day where I don’t have to think about all this stuff, but it keeps piling up.

It’s nice to have found Prosebox. It’s a journaling community where you can share diaries—or whatever you write—with other people. I know some folks immediately go, “Shouldn’t diaries or journals be private? Why would you want to share that?”

First of all, it’s anonymous. Whether you choose to put your name on your writing or not, sometimes it’s just nice to talk to the void and hear it answer back.

Second, it’s nice to connect with people in a more raw, unfiltered way—nothing like what social media has turned into over the years.

I’m really late to this whole journaling‑community thing. Reading through people’s entries on Prosebox, a lot of them came from Open Diary, which ran from the ’90s up until just a couple of years ago. Open Diary is officially closing in January 2026, so many users have migrated over to Prosebox—although Prosebox has been around for almost as long, as far as I know. Someone from OD created PB for… well, I’m not entirely sure why. Regardless, I’m just happy I found this place.

This is one of those thoughts that’s constantly sitting at the back of my mind lately. I don’t actively think about it all the time—but when I notice it, I really start thinking about it. You know what I mean?

It feels regrettable, in a quiet, lingering way, that I never discovered any journaling communities back then. When I think about when they started—late ’90s, early 2000s—I was in high school or college. Sure, I wrote in planners, notebooks, whatever I could get my hands on. But lately I keep thinking, “God, imagine if I had written and saved all my journals since then. What an incredible time capsule.”

Being able to look back and reference something properly. To point at an entry and say, “See? I wasn’t entirely terrible. This proves it.” To keep memories from completely fading into obscurity. Now I mostly just have vague recollections of things, and sometimes I can’t tell whether they’re real memories slowly dissolving—or something I’ve unintentionally fabricated along the way.

I think I’m also in this liminal stage of being single—not really alone (something I’d like to try eventually)—and enjoying it, while also feeling lonely and wanting to be witnessed by someone. I’m not much of a hoarder to begin with, so memory hoarding wouldn’t really be on brand for me either. But I think what I’m grieving isn’t the lack of archives—it’s the lack of being witnessed.

If I had years of journals, especially within a community, then I would have been witnessed. And I would have been witnessing myself, too. I think that’s what most of us want anyway, no? To be witnessed. Proof of existence. To be felt. To matter.

All that said, I really wish I’d known about a community like this earlier. But hey—I came late to this journaling community… at least I’m starting. I may not be a hoarder, but I guess I’m becoming a memory hoarder now.

Prosebox feels warm and welcoming, yet quiet. Quiet in a good way—the kind of quiet you expect from a void. It listens, but it doesn’t judge. I don’t know if that makes sense, but it feels right.

In a way, this community feels like a different—and better—flavor of social media. You share your life, you connect with people, but it doesn’t feel performative or judgmental. You feel safe being your true self, warts and all.

I hope this site doesn’t shut down for a very long time. I hope it continues to flourish, continues to be a safe space, and continues to give people that gentle feeling of the void finally answering back. I really, deeply appreciate it.

And on this note, I'm slowly tapping out of writing my diaries here on Reddit. It's been nice. But if I'm being honest, I just enjoy hearing the void respond back more.

For a while there, going to the grocery was the highlight of Eugenia Mae’s day. She tackled it in a unique way, quite unlike anyone I have ever met. She never bought anything that was not on her list. She roamed the aisles like she was visiting a museum, slowly and appreciatively. Items were poked, prodded, hefted and squeezed. Prices were compared meticulously and the cheaper item always chosen. Now I admit, this is all pretty normal shopping behavior. However when it came to her choices in produce, I was completely stymied.
She selected the wilted lettuce, the ugliest avocado, the peach with the bruise, the broken carrot, and the pithy radishes. Once I tried to point out some better choices, but she stuck to her guns, so I didn’t argue. This behavior puzzled me for the longest time. But eventually, as I got to know her better I came to understand this idiosyncrasy.
She had grown up in a very poor family and had lived frugally all her life. I came to believe that she was taking pity on the ‘rejects’ in the produce department. Having been passed over so many times in her own life, she had developed the keenest sense of compassion. And this compassion extended even as far as the shriveled zucchinis and less than perfect apples that everyone else had left in the display case.
She appreciated the barely functioning, the flawed and undesirable things in life. She could take the most pitiful bits and pieces and make a little arrangement for her kitchen table and find joy in it. Out in her yard, she would mark off with string and a few sticks the most scraggly clump of flowering weeds and make them look special.
In the end, I learned a valuable lesson from Eugenia Mae. She showed me that beauty bloomed in even the most rank and desolate places. In her world everything was precious. She never ran short of things that gave her pleasure. From the ancient cardboard Santa , complete with sleigh and reindeer, that she carefully displayed on a table in her house each year, to the tattered tablecloths that came out at the change of each season, she was declaring her determination to find joy in small things. Even small, worn out and tattered things.
Though she had very little, Eugenia Mae was the richest person I have ever known.

This morning, I woke up to the sound of my phone buzzing on the nightstand again—another group text from the lab team, already arguing about who’s taking the lead on the new sample protocols. Half awake, I scrolled through the messages, rolling my eyes at how quickly it turned into a passive-aggressive mess. I made a mental note to avoid replying until after breakfast, otherwise I’d get sucked into the drama before even brushing my teeth. Now it’s about 10:15 AM and I’m on the couch, laptop open, receipts and a spreadsheet spread out in front of me. The numbers don’t lie—groceries are up, rent is due in four days, and I can’t ignore the fact that I’m barely scraping by this month. I keep thinking about how easily the lab team gets into arguments over the smallest things, like who cleans the glassware or who left unlabeled tubes in the fridge. I try to stay organized and keep my head down, but it’s getting harder to ignore the tension. It’s not that I expect everyone to get along, but the constant sniping is exhausting, especially when I have to double-check everyone’s data because I’m skeptical about their shortcuts. I’m nervous about bringing up my concerns in the next meeting; I know I’ll probably sound blunt, but someone has to say something if we want to publish anything decent. The couch cushions are lumpy, my back aches, and my coffee’s gone cold, but I can’t seem to get up. I keep rereading the last email from my supervisor, trying to figure out if there’s a hidden message about my performance. Part of me wonders if I’m just overthinking it, but the other part knows I’m probably right. I wish I could just focus on my own work without getting dragged into everyone else’s drama. At least I’ve got my color-coded expense tracker—small victories where I can find them. Maybe after lunch, I’ll finally reply to those texts and try to steer things back on track. Or maybe not. Either way, I’m tired of feeling like I’m the only one paying attention to the details that actually matter.

The unfamiliar hum of the fridge keeps catching my attention, pulling me away from the half-formed sentences in my head. I keep telling myself that once I settle in, the stories will flow again, but right now, I feel unanchored and a little lost. The pressure to deliver something good is real, but my thoughts feel slippery, hard to pin down. I know I’ve been through transitions before, but this one feels different—maybe because I’m older, or maybe because I expected it to be easier. I want to believe the creative spark is still there, just hiding under the surface, but doubt keeps creeping in. Even so, there’s a small part of me that holds onto hope, imagining that tomorrow will be lighter. For now, I’ll just sip my tea and try to coax a few words onto the page, even if they’re not the right ones yet.
