I’ve been doing some thinking lately, and I’m not happy with where my thoughts have taken me. What started all this was a conversation I had with my sister or my daughter, I can’t remember which. My sister, I think. Anyway, she had caught a talk show on which the interviewee was, I don’t remember, a petroleum engineer (?).
The show host asked the interviewee how much oil reserves do we have. After much hemming and hawing, he finally answered: 50 years. It’s been a couple weeks since the conversation, so if I seem vague about the source, well, my attention span is sometimes limited.
But it got me to thinking. Without petroleum, where are we going to get power for our automobiles? Solar power, maybe. Automakers are working on electric motors. But, still, even with a power source, what are we going to use to keep the wheels and cogs oiled? Surely not butterfat. If solar or electric doesn’t work, then we go back to horse and buggy, but the problem of lubrication still exists. Buggy wheels don't self-lubricate.
I don’t think engines powerful enough for airplanes can be engineered with solar or electrical sources. Oh, yes, there’s nuclear power. Well, that source is probably limited, too. At least as far as our scientific knowledge goes today. Science fiction, notwithstanding!
Then it occurs to me that our huge cities are in trouble. Without petroleum products, no taxis, no inter-urbans, no local buses. No commutes.
And our large cities have skyscrapers with elevators to take us to the 200th floor. How do we keep the elevators running? They need lubrication, too. And, I know for sure, that NObody is going to walk up and back down 200 floors just to get to and from work. Hmmm. Looks like our cities are endangered. And the industries incorporated into those cities.
So now what do we do with all those six million or so people in Los Angeles? How do we get food to them? Food is hauled into cities by truck or train. And those conveyances need lubrication to operate. Farm machinery need lubrication to operate. We could go back to the mule and the plow, I suppose, but I hardly think that’s efficient on 1,000 acre plots. And that’s what it takes to feed large populations.
Aha! say the Luddites among us. And there are some. This is what we’ve been warning about all along. Too much mechanization. Too much dependence on “progress.” But the fact is, that’s where we are. So what do we do about it now?
As for the production of lubricants, suppose we could start raising cattle specifically for their rendered fat?
Is it possible, with billions of people on this planet for families to raise their own food? Somebody better start thinking about it.
Now, if that wasn’t enough to give me a headache, I just got the latest National Geographic. The main article was about global warming. Glaciers are melting. Large chucks of ice shelves are falling off into the oceans, north and south hemispheres. Climate is changing. Ocean water is changing in temperature and salinity, and these factors have a huge influence on climate. Ocean levels have risen to the point that some islands in the Pacific are in danger of being inundated within the next few years.
People make jokes about California falling off into the Pacific because of our earthquakes. It’s more likely that Nevada will end up with a seacoast more because of ocean levels rather than earthquakes. As a matter of fact, taking it another step, if the coastline of California disappears, wouldn’t that include Oregon and Washington, too?
Well, of course, we have the coastal mountain ranges that might, possibly, stop the incursion of the ocean that far into what is presently inland. Small comfort, that.
One conclusion of the National Geographic article was that we might well be going into another interglacial era. It has happened before. We have an ice age. Then the ice retreats and we have seasonal weather, then we have unusually hot weather, and the cycle is repeated. Fortunately, perhaps, for us, these interglacial periods take thousands of years.
Even so, I don’t think I’ll cling to the idea of living till I’m 120 years old. Another 10 maybe, and that’s it.
Shalom

There are days, those days, you know the days, just before my monthly cycle, when I feel disconnected from my body
There are days, those days, you know the days, just before my monthly cycle,(sorry for the indelicate subject, but I am trying to talk about real life stuff in this diary) when I feel disconnected from my body. My mind is one place, thinking things that only suicidal people think. But my body is busy doing stuff to keep me occupied until the madness passes.
(Keep her moving, get that dust under the refrigerator. Rake those leaves. Prune the bushes. Let’s make her bake something. Something
CHOCOLATE !
And for heavens’ sake, don’t let her look at the bills.)
I know the madness WILL pass. It has passed many times before. What I can’t figure out is why I have to come down this fruitless road again. Every single atom of my life could be in place, and in a good place, but my hormone crazed brain will try to convince me otherwise. The good me and the evil me are having a stare down and the good me is about to blink.
It’s ridiculous to be fully aware that you are having a ‘hormone event’ (sounds cosmic eh ?) yet being equally as aware that you can’t get OFF the train. The train that is headed straight for the black tunnel where not only is it dark, but you are not sure there IS a light at the end.
What makes this trip particularly difficult is that I am an optimistic person most of the time. (In an introverted kind of way) I am
never
bored. There is always something interesting to do around here. So this strange, depressed way of living in the world hits me pretty hard.
These alien thoughts run through my head that seem to come from some bizarre movie like "Brazil". You know, scary thoughts like,
This is the REAL you Alice. That woman that’s here the rest of the time is fake !
But Miss Jabberwocky ends up overplaying her hand and says something SO outlandish that even the depressed me has to laugh.
Statements like, ‘What YOU need to do is sell everything you own and live in a cabin somewhere with no electricity.’
A few minutes contemplating this scenario and the good me realizes that this would mean not being able to play SNOOD anymore and I snap out of the spell, just like that!
Screeeeeeech…… Train arrives at the station. Whew !
It’s NOT platform 9 ¾ either. Dang.
I will tell you what, Menopause is starting to look REAL good to me.

I just finished a slow walk around the block, trying to shake off the tension from this morning. It’s strange how even a short outing can feel like stepping into a minefield when you’re anxious about what people think. I ran into a neighbor briefly, enough to exchange awkward pleasantries, but it left me more unsettled than before. I think it’s the constant awareness of who might overhear or judge that keeps me on edge. At home, there’s barely any privacy. Every room has ears. Trying to hold space for my own thoughts feels impossible sometimes, especially when the family conversation shifts to topics I’d rather avoid. I’m supposed to be the one helping others manage their issues, yet I’m struggling to handle the friction close to me. Maybe it’s the mismatch of wanting to stay grounded and intense emotions bubbling under the surface. No one sees that part, or if they do, they don’t mention it. I ended up pacing by the streetlight, feeling like I was caught between wanting to say something and just keeping quiet. The air was cool, and that helped a little. I thought about grabbing coffee on the walk but decided against it—too much chance of running into someone I wasn’t ready for. Tomorrow, I want to try being less hard on myself, even if it means small steps. It’s just hard when you live in a house where every sound feels magnified and every expression gets dissected. I’m hoping for some calm, or at least less noise in my head. ☁️

I spent most of today trying to keep my head above water with grading and lesson planning, but my mind kept drifting back to that awkward moment after dinner. He asked me if I saw this going somewhere, and I laughed it off like I always do when I’m caught off guard. Honestly, I have no idea what I want to say or how I even feel sometimes. It’s like there’s this office meeting in my head where all the conflicting thoughts are running late and no one has the agenda. I feel restless, like the usual tiredness after a long day is mixed with this weird anticipation, but I can’t tell if it’s excitement or anxiety. Work is stressful enough without trying to decode new feelings that don’t fit any neat category. I keep turning over his words in my mind, dissecting the tone, the timing, trying to find a clue I probably missed. It’s exhausting and I’m not even sure it’s worth that kind of mental energy yet. On the bright side, the dry humor we share is a good reminder not to take myself too seriously, even if I feel a bit like a character in a play who forgot her lines. Maybe tomorrow, I’ll have a clearer picture. Or at least a better plan for how to deal with this guessing game. For now, I’ll just sit with the uncertainty and hope it doesn’t spill into my classroom tomorrow. Coffee might be my only reliable friend at this point.

The rumble of the bus tires on wet pavement is strangely calming, even though my mind won’t stop racing. I replay the conversation with my co-parent from earlier—something about the schedule just felt off, like we were talking past each other. I thought we agreed on the pickup times, but by the end, it was clear we had different versions of the plan. I guess after juggling work shifts and the kids’ activities, it’s easy to miss details or assume the other is on the same page. The tension in our voices caught me off guard though; it wasn’t what I expected from something so routine. Makes me wonder if the stress we’re all under seeps into these small talks, turning them into bigger deals than they need to be. I’m tired, no doubt about it, and maybe that’s why I’m reading too much into it. Still, wrapping my head around how to keep things running smoothly while grieving and not snapping is exhausting. The late-night quiet on this bus contrasts sharply with the chaos in my head. I want to be more present, less reactive, but sometimes it feels like I’m just surviving the day. Tomorrow’s calendar looks packed again, so I’ll have to find a way to reset without breaking down. I’m holding onto the hope that clarity will come by morning, or at least some peace. For now, I’ll watch the blurry streetlights flicker past and try to breathe through it all.

I made a quick salad from the fridge and sat at my tiny kitchen table, phone buzzing every few minutes with work emails I’m trying to ignore for now. It’s weird how I can feel both accomplished and frazzled at the same time, going through the motions of balancing accounts while my mind jumps to tonight’s plans. I told myself I’d finally organize the closet after dinner, but I keep thinking about all the little things piling up—laundry, bills, overdue texts to friends. The apartment is quiet, almost too quiet, except for the hum of the fridge and the occasional car passing outside. I know I’m lucky to have this steady routine and my own space, but sometimes I wish I could just switch my brain off for an hour or two. My planner is already out on the table, with tomorrow’s to-do list half filled in, and I keep glancing at it even though I promised myself a real break. Maybe tonight I’ll actually put my phone down and just watch a show, but I doubt I’ll stick to that. I want to feel more in control, but right now I’m just trying to keep all the pieces moving.

This morning, I remembered how my son used to run ahead of me on these same sidewalks, giggling and yelling for me to catch up, and it hit me again how different things feel now. The air was colder than I expected for June, and every step I took felt a little heavier, maybe because I didn’t sleep well last night. My mind kept jumping between client deadlines and that weird ache in my side, and I can’t decide if it’s just stress or something I should get checked out. I passed the neighbor’s garden and noticed the lilies are blooming, orange and stubborn, and for a second I wished I could just sit and watch them instead of circling the block to clear my head. I keep thinking about how much time I spend worrying about money since I started freelancing, and how some months I feel confident and others I can barely look at my bank account. Walking usually helps me sort things out, but today it just felt like my thoughts were tangled up, one minute remembering Dad’s laugh, the next worrying about this week’s invoices. Sometimes I wonder how much of who I am is just reacting to what’s happening, rather than actually deciding anything. I heard birds but couldn’t really focus on their songs, kept checking my phone for no reason, almost hoping for a distraction. It’s like I’m waiting for something to just click into place, some moment where I know what I’m doing again, but it hasn’t come yet. I guess I’m still figuring out how to move forward with all these old memories and new uncertainties mixed together. Might try to do some sketches later, see if that helps. For now, I’m just circling back to the house, trying to breathe a little deeper and not overthink every little thing.

There’s a low hum from the fridge and the streetlight is throwing a weird yellow glow across the kitchen floor. It’s quiet, finally, after a day that felt like chasing a hundred timers set to different speeds. This morning started with a scramble, both kids needing different breakfasts at the same time—oatmeal for one, toast with no crust for the other—and me burning my own toast because I was checking the school calendar on my phone. I have a new respect for the phrase "organized chaos." 

Work was packed, as usual. I spent more time overseeing deliveries and double-checking prep lists than actually cooking. There’s something satisfying about seeing everything in its place, but the mental gymnastics of swapping shifts and remembering which parent pick-up is today almost broke me. My ex and I texted back and forth about baseball practice and dentist appointments so many times, I scrolled back tonight and laughed—our thread looks like a logistics spreadsheet with the occasional sarcastic meme. Tired doesn’t really cover it, but I’m not unhappy. It’s busy, and sometimes I wish for a clone, but I got through today and everyone got fed (mostly on time). That counts for something, right?

The leftover plate from dinner still sits on the table, crusts of bread and some wilted salad forgotten in the dim kitchen light. I washed a few dishes but left the rest for tomorrow. The quiet of the house feels heavier tonight, maybe because I’m trying not to think too hard about the text he sent earlier. It was vague, something about not knowing where this is going, and I just folded into that uncertainty again. I keep flipping through the conversation in my head, wondering if I missed a signal or if I’m just overanalyzing because that’s my default when things aren’t clear.

I tried organizing my desk earlier to distract myself but ended up moving papers from one pile to another without really sorting anything. My mind races, wanting clarity but also fearing an answer that might make things more complicated. I wish I could be more spontaneous with this new relationship like I am in coding — just trying stuff and seeing what works. Instead, I’m stuck waiting for signals I’m not even sure I want. I should sleep, but anxiety keeps the thoughts circling around. Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel less tangled up in this.

The remote is wedged awkwardly between the cushions and I can’t decide if I want to fish it out or just leave the TV off. The apartment feels too quiet but also too full at the same time, if that makes sense. Earlier, Jess and I tried to talk about her mom again and I could tell I was getting impatient, even though I know I shouldn’t. She gets quiet and I end up filling the silence with questions that don’t really help. I wish I was better at just letting things sit instead of trying to fix everything right away.

Work was slow today, and that didn’t help my mood. My hands still smell faintly like oil. Every time I think about family stuff, I get this restless feeling, like I should be doing something instead of just thinking. I keep remembering how my dad used to deal with things by just working late in the garage. Maybe that’s where I get it from. Jess says it’s okay to just be sad or upset sometimes, but I honestly don’t know how to do that without wanting to change something immediately. I guess I’m still figuring out what being supportive actually looks like. Wish there was a manual for this kind of thing.

I just finished dinner and I’m still thinking about that call with my brother earlier. He asked if I could help him organize some stuff for Mom’s birthday, which honestly sounded doable, but then he kept adding on more things. I kept nodding along even though my mind was all over the place, and now I’m not sure what I actually agreed to or if I missed some important details. It’s so hard to pay attention lately, especially when I’ve been staring at a screen all day for school and work. There’s no real line between when I’m supposed to be working or relaxing, and I think I let that spill into my conversation with him. I want to be helpful, but I also feel annoyed that I can’t just say no or set boundaries. Was I being too passive? Or maybe he just assumes I have more time because I’m home so much. I can’t tell if I’m making this into a bigger deal than it is. Either way, I need to sort out what I actually need to do for this birthday plan, or I’m going to forget something important. My brain feels like it’s packed with half-finished lists.

This morning I left my apartment a little later than usual because I couldn’t decide what to wear. My closet is overflowing but nothing felt right. Ended up grabbing the gray sweater again, the one that has started to pill at the elbows. The train was more crowded than normal and I spent most of the ride replaying last night’s conversation in my head. He asked where I see things going and I just sort of shrugged, which didn’t feel great, but I honestly don’t know. There are moments I feel certain, and then suddenly I’m not. 

Now I’m at my desk eating a turkey sandwich during my lunch break. The office is so quiet you can hear people typing, which makes me hyper-aware of every crinkle of my sandwich wrapper. I keep glancing at my phone, half-hoping he’ll text something light or funny. Work is piling up, and I keep making lists but never quite finishing them. My mind jumps between code issues and worries about whether I’m being distant or just protective. This new relationship is good in so many ways but the uncertainty is distracting. I wish I could just know how I really feel instead of analyzing every small thing. Sometimes I think I’m overcomplicating it all, but then I also want to be sure. Maybe I just need more time. For now, I’ll try to finish this sandwich and get back to debugging. I’m hopeful things will make more sense soon.

Walked around the block this afternoon to try and clear my head. It was supposed to help but honestly I just kept replaying the argument from earlier with my partner. The sidewalk was uneven and I almost tripped twice, which felt about right for the day I’m having. My phone buzzed in my pocket and I ignored it, not ready to see another message about picking up groceries or being late again. The air smelled like cut grass and car exhaust.

I keep wondering if I’m the one making things worse by snapping when I’m tired. School deadlines are piling up, and I keep missing details at work. Parenting is another layer on top of all that. I know we both have too much on our plates but I don’t know what to cut. I wish I could just stop overthinking it all for a minute and actually be present when I get home.

Earlier this morning, I dropped my phone under the couch and then somehow managed to lose my socks in the process of retrieving it. That pretty much set the tone for today. Now it’s lunchtime and I’m holed up in my favorite corner of the apartment, eating a slightly stale cheese sandwich and contemplating whether I should panic about my next freelance payment or just eat some chips and pretend it’ll all work out. The sunlight is kind of nice despite the mess on the table—empty mug, half-open notebook, receipts from god-knows-when. I keep telling myself I should feel more in control at this point in my life, but honestly, I just feel tired and a little floaty, like I’m watching someone else try to assemble a jigsaw puzzle with half the pieces missing. Sometimes I think about how everyone else seems to have these clear paths and labels for themselves, and I can’t even decide what to put down for my occupation on forms. I wish I could just be content floating for a while, but the uncertainty is a bit much today. I keep scrolling through job boards, half-interested, half-terrified of actually committing to something. Maybe I’ll take a nap instead and call this lunch break a win. At least the sandwich was edible.

Just finished washing the dishes and wiped down the table, which is about as much cleaning as I can handle tonight. It’s late—the clock on the microwave says 11:43—and there’s a weird hum from the fridge that I keep meaning to look at, but I just don’t have it in me right now. My mind’s still racing from class earlier, trying to keep all these formulas and torque specs straight, and I’m honestly surprised how much of it I remember when I’m this tired. I caught myself replaying a conversation with the instructor about diagnosing electrical issues, thinking through each step and where I might mess up if I missed something small. 

Balancing work at the garage with school is a lot, but I feel sharper these days, like my brain’s finally firing on all cylinders. Still, it’s hard not to get skeptical about just how long I can keep this pace up without something giving. I notice more details lately—the sound of an engine that’s off by a fraction, the way a classmate hesitates before answering—and I kind of like that. I know this hyperfocus won’t last forever, but for now it’s making the grind feel worthwhile. I’ll probably crash as soon as my head hits the pillow, but at least I can end the day feeling like I’m not wasting my time.

The couch cushions are a bit too firm tonight, digging into my back as I try to unwind and sort through the conversation replaying in my head. Earlier, my partner mentioned something about needing more space, which hit me harder than expected because I don’t even know if I’m giving too much or too little. Their tone was calm but the way their words hung in the air made me question if I’m misreading everything—as usual, caught between wanting to clarify and not wanting to seem defensive or clingy. We’ve been working on communication, right? But moments like this make me wonder if it’s just a series of small missteps accumulating silently. I keep turning over the phrase "more space" like it’s some kind of riddle, trying to determine whether it’s about physical distance, emotional breathing room, or just a pause from all my anxious over-explanations. Did I miss a sign earlier? Was my last comment too dry, too blunt? I know my humor doesn’t always land the way I intend, especially when anxiety clouds my filter. Yet I’m not sure if bringing it up again tonight would help or just open another round of uncomfortable probing. I want to be direct but not destructive. I guess it’s okay to admit that I don’t have all the answers yet, even if the silence afterward makes me feel like I’m walking a tightrope without a net. For now, I’ll let the quiet settle and remind myself that understanding probably takes more than just good intentions and awkward jokes. Tomorrow is another chance to try again, maybe with less tension and a little more patience from both of us. Maybe that’s the hopeful part I need to hold on to before sleep takes over. ☕

The house is quiet except for the humming of the fridge and the distant sound of someone moving upstairs—probably Mom, awake earlier than usual. The sunlight is just starting to filter in through the blinds, making everything look a bit softer. I made some toast and tea, just something quick, because I know the afternoon will be packed. I keep thinking about the customer returns I have to process today, and whether I’ll have time to drop off Mom’s prescription on my lunch break. Balancing work and caring for her is exhausting, but somehow I’m managing to keep up with it all. I keep going over my to-do list in my head, making sure I don’t forget anything. My mind keeps jumping from one task to the next, almost like I can’t stop planning every minute. I try to remember to breathe and eat, even when I feel like I can’t slow down. Being patient with myself is harder than being patient with customers, honestly. Still, I’m grateful for the small moments of quiet, like this one, where I can just stand still and listen. I know this afternoon will be busy, but I feel ready to handle it. As long as I keep focusing on one thing at a time, I think I can get through it all. I just wish there were more hours in the day. I’m hopeful, though—maybe I’ll even have a few minutes to read after work if Mom is feeling okay. For now, it’s just me, my tea, and the sunlight sneaking across the counter.

This morning felt heavier than usual, like a weight pressing on my chest that I couldn’t quite shake off. After breakfast, I found myself replaying the awkward dinner conversation from last night—everyone seemed on edge, and I’m still not sure if it was just the usual tension that simmered beneath the surface or something deeper. I’m grateful to be in this new city, but it’s isolating in a way I didn’t fully anticipate. My art is the one thing that keeps me grounded, though even that felt tenuous today. I tried to sketch a few things, but the lines were hesitant, and the colors felt muted. It’s frustrating because I want to connect with people here, but starting from scratch at this stage of life is exhausting and intimidating. I keep thinking about my family, the ones I left behind, and what they would say if they saw me now. Would they understand this slow unraveling? Or would they just tell me to toughen up? I miss them more than I’m willing to admit out loud. Maybe it’s the grief that makes every interaction feel like an uphill climb, every attempt at friendship a question I can’t answer. I know I need to be patient with myself, but some days, patience feels like a luxury I don’t have. Today, the silence after meals feels louder, and my thoughts are tangled. Still, there’s a small hope that this discomfort is temporary and that somewhere in the coming weeks there will be a moment of ease. For now, I’ll sit with the uncertainty and try not to judge my restlessness too harshly. It’s okay to feel lost sometimes, even if it’s uncomfortable.

I keep tapping my pen, thinking I missed something, but there’s nothing left to trim unless I want to live off beans and rice all month. My phone keeps buzzing with messages from work. Tomorrow’s shift schedule is a mess—two call-outs, and I keep replaying possible coverage scenarios in my head. I wish the warehouse would stick to the delivery times, so my team wouldn’t get caught off guard every week.

Feels like I’ve been running on edge since last week. There’s a stack of envelopes next to me—bills, mostly, unopened. I keep telling myself I’ll breathe easier after payday, but that’s still a week away. At work, everyone’s tired, small mistakes piling up. I end up smoothing things over, but it’s draining. I know I’m patient, but even patience wears thin when nothing feels under control. The clock says 11:42 p.m. My eyes are heavy, but my mind’s still looping through tasks and numbers. Maybe I’ll sleep after making one more list.

This morning, I dropped a tube of ultramarine blue paint on the floor and watched it roll under the couch. I left it there. Now, during this so-called lunch break, I’m staring at the half-eaten toast on my plate and trying to ignore the way my phone keeps buzzing with invoices and overdue reminders. The house is especially quiet; the only thing I can hear is the ticking of the wall clock and the distant rumble of a delivery truck outside. I should be sketching ideas for the commission I took last week, but my mind keeps flicking back and forth between unfinished projects and the uncertainty of next month’s rent. The sketchbook is open in front of me, but the page is still blank. There’s a list of tasks in my head—follow up with the gallery, price out new canvas, respond to the client who keeps changing her mind—but none of it feels urgent enough to overcome this weird inertia. Maybe I’m just tired from not sleeping well last night, but it feels like I’m moving through mud today. I keep telling myself to just start, to do anything, but the organizing part of my brain wants to make a plan first, and the skeptical part is already doubting whether any of it will pay off. Even eating feels inefficient, like I should be doing two things at once just to keep up. I’ve checked my email three times since I sat down, hoping for something decisive, but there’s nothing new. A shaft of sun is coming in through the blinds and making a bright stripe across the table, catching the crumbs left over from breakfast. If I don’t get moving soon, the rest of the afternoon will disappear, and I’ll be left with another day where nothing really got finished. I keep thinking there must be a way to get ahead of this, but right now, all I want is for the noise in my head to quiet down enough to draw one decent line.

My classes are piling up, deadlines are looming, and yet here I am, somehow managing to keep everything moving. I wish I could slow down, but rushing seems like the only way to keep everything afloat. Still, I’m grateful for these brief moments that feel like a pause, even if they’re just a quiet lunch break in the middle of a hectic day. Hopefully, tomorrow will bring a little more space to breathe.

I spent most of this morning double-checking some code I wrote yesterday, but my mind kept drifting back to the call I had with Mom before work. She sounded tired, and her voice was quieter than usual, which has been happening more often since Dad passed. I tried to ask about her doctor’s appointment without making her feel like I was prying. She said everything is "routine" but I could hear something else underneath, maybe just sadness, maybe more. It's hard to focus on technical details when the bigger questions about her health and how she's really coping keep sneaking in.

During my lunch break, I sat quietly at my kitchen table and replayed parts of our conversation. The fog in my head hasn't really lifted, and I keep wondering if I should visit soon, even though I know she always says she doesn’t want me to worry or rearrange my life. I wish I could do more than just call. I feel anxious but also hopeful that with time, both of us will find a new kind of normal. For now, I’ll keep checking in, even if it’s just to hear her talk about the weather or what she’s cooking for dinner.

No one ever tells you how hard it is being a parent. I mean they say its hard but no one ever talks
about how you truly lose yourself.
Now I dont know if this is mostly for mothers but when you have a child you lose your identity all together. You spend every waking moment doing something for someone else. Making sure your child is happy, fed, clean, safe, comfortable. You forget to do those things for yourself.
I dont regret having my child for even one second but there are times when I want to get into my car, drive away, and never come back. The postpartum after giving birth didnt help. Luckily that didnt last forever.
Sometimes I want to be selfish and just be alone. I want to be able to eat a meal without a small person crawling all over me. Or read a book without cartoons playing in the background. Or enjoy a coffee and run errands peacefully. I want to not always have a happy face plastered on so that my kid doesnt see a sad mommy.
I sometimes wonder if I was too young to have a kid. I wasnt ready mentally or emotionally but its not my childs fault. They deserve a better life than I had. I am far from a perfect mom. But I will do everything in my power to be the best mom I can be....

Dear lover,
I miss the old us. I miss being madly in love. I miss when you couldnt keep your hands or your eyes off me.
There was a time when you made me feel like I walk on air. We used to make love constantly. You took pictures of me. You put thought into your gifts. You took me on dates.
But we have hurt each other so much now. You slapped me. You cheated on me.
I lied about my sobriety.
I cheated to get back at you... you just dont know.
We hurt each other with words. We have no more passion. There are times when I hate you.
We have become the fighting parents to our child I always promised myself I would never become. We never make love anymore. You barely sleep in the same bed as me. We dont laugh or cuddle or touch each other anymore.
You drink and drink and drink. You dont care about the way you look anymore.
I love you. I miss you. But I miss the way it was. Im terribly terribly afraid we will never be in love the same again. It scares me to death.
I want to go through with this marriage but not like this.
What can I do?
Love,
Me

Just finished scrubbing down the kitchen and collapsed at the table with a lukewarm glass of water. My feet still ache from the dinner rush, but my mind is buzzing louder than the dishwasher. The new menu items went over well, and a couple of regulars actually complimented the plating, which gave me a little jolt of satisfaction. Still, I keep replaying that moment when I snapped at one of the line cooks for burning the risotto. Was I too harsh? Maybe I could have handled that differently, but it’s hard to switch gears in the middle of chaos.

It’s so strange being in a new city where I know barely anyone outside of the restaurant. Everyone else seems to have their own circles already, and I worry I come off as intense or closed off. Sometimes I wonder if I’m overthinking every small conversation or if I really am making things awkward. I want to be more relaxed, but I can’t help analyzing each interaction, especially when I’m tired. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try to invite someone for a drink after work, even if it feels risky. For now, I just want five minutes of quiet before I drag myself to bed and do this all again.

The pavement is still a little damp from the afternoon rain, and my shoes keep picking up bits of grit as I circle the block tonight. The air feels heavy but not cold, and there’s that smell of wet earth mixed with distant laundry from someone’s window. I needed to get outside, even though I’m pretty wiped after work—too many people, too many complicated orders, and way too much fake smiling. But walking helps, even if my thoughts are racing. I keep replaying the conversation I had with my partner earlier about my family. We’re trying so hard to be honest with each other about how hard things have been since my uncle got sick, but I always worry I’m saying the wrong thing or not enough. I want to be open but sometimes I feel like I’m talking in circles, or just shutting down completely. Maybe it’s just the exhaustion, or maybe it’s years of not really knowing how to talk about this kind of sadness. I keep wondering if I should be doing more to help my mom, but I’m scared I’ll mess things up or make her feel worse. The streetlights flicker a little as I pass under them, and I find myself focusing on the sound of my own footsteps just to quiet my brain. Part of me wishes I could call my partner right now and ask if I’m being weird, but I know they’re probably tired, too. I hope tomorrow feels a little lighter, or at least less tangled.

Earlier today I remembered dropping my keys somewhere stupid again, probably behind the microwave, and having to move a bunch of stuff to get at them. That’s been happening a lot lately, just small things going missing or being put in the wrong place. Now it’s my lunch break and I’m just sitting at the table with reheated leftovers, trying to make sense of all the tasks I wrote down last night. The list is ridiculous: supplier calls, invoice approvals, tracking two shipments, and I still haven’t finished the pitch deck edits. My phone keeps buzzing with notifications, but I just keep tapping ignore. My head feels heavy, not exactly tired, more like trying to see through fog. I know I’m missing some small but important detail, but I can’t put my finger on it. I keep telling myself I’ll sort out the schedule after lunch, then I end up scrolling or just staring out the window. There’s a stack of unopened mail on the counter, and I should probably go through it, but it feels like another thing to add to the pile. Even making decisions about what to eat has started to feel like work. I’m hoping the afternoon will be better, that I’ll get a burst of energy or at least some clarity, but right now it feels like I’m just spinning in place. I guess this is what happens when I let the logistics pile up instead of just handling them as they come. I need to get back to work but I keep putting it off, and the more stuff I ignore, the heavier it feels.

Sunlight is slanting across the kitchen table, catching the edge of my laptop. The hum from the fridge is the loudest thing in the room right now. It’s just after 1:00, and I have half a toasted sandwich on my plate because I’m not really hungry. Work pings have finally quieted, but my mind keeps circling back to the conversation with Mark this morning. We were both short with each other, nothing dramatic, just clipped. He asked if I was listening, and I nodded, but I was checking a work email. Now I feel guilty for splitting my attention when I keep insisting we need to make more space for each other.

Remote work is supposed to give more flexibility, but it just means I’m always half at work, even when I’m here. I catch myself glancing at the clock, counting minutes until my next meeting, instead of focusing on what he’s saying. I know he feels it, even if he doesn’t say much. We haven’t fought, but there’s a distance lately that feels heavy. I want to fix it, or at least acknowledge it, but it’s easier to just drift into the next task. Maybe I’ll message him later, suggest a walk after work. Simple, but I have to start somewhere. I don’t want us to keep missing each other, even when we’re in the same house.

I did it! I completed a full year of daily journaling here. My entry count is 368, because I also wrote New Year's Eve last year, and I wrote twice on a couple days. I wasn't planning to journal every day this year - I thought it would be helpful through a stressful time, and then I just never stopped. I wrote 121,674 words this year, an average of 330 words per day. I wrote them in bed, on planes and trains and buses, in friends' living rooms and my parents' kitchen, in parks and parking lots and airport bathrooms. I feel really proud of maintaining this habit and the self-knowledge it's brought me. I didn't share all the hard things I've been through this year, but this was a place for me to slow down and reflect on them, and that's helped me get through it. Not just the tough things, but it's helped me notice and appreciate the beautiful, joyful, lovely things that made this year so rich. I was worried I'd run out of things to say or get bored with writing here, but that hasn't been my experience at all. It's still one of my favorite parts of the day. Thanks for being here and reading along. All the best to you in the new year.

But my discontent started when they started sending 'breaking news' emails with the score of the football team, and then tried to appeal to the entire state instead of the metro area with their news, and then they made their news cut-off time 3pm and moved printing to IOWA(!), and had page after page of public notices, it was a worthless newspaper. I now get local news through the library edition or through an RSS feed using Feedly. And the comics from GoComics.com (because it's not a good day unless I can read the comics!). All free.
Speaking of reading, I calculated yesterday that I read or listened to at least 32 books this year. (I'm sure there were more, but I couldn't figure out which Kindle free ebooks I read this year.) Switching to digital audiobooks from the library has made a huge difference in how many books I can get through, as I have a hard time just sitting and reading a book, but I can take audiobooks along on my daily walks or when I drive to honey's (2 hrs roundtrip). I'm such a fan of libraries. I just don't understand people who buy books. Good authors I discovered this year are Ann Patchett and Alina Bronsky.
It appears we got about 6" or so snow, a far cry from the 7-12", but the wind is still howling this morning. I shoveled a path from the door to the backyard for dog a couple times yesterday. There is a layer of ice under the snow, so it will be slick the next couple of days since it will be too cold to melt. For the first time that I can remember, I-35 is/was CLOSED(!) for 125 miles across two states because so many cars were in the ditch. That ice I was talking of combined with blizzard winds. Too many people who didn't pay attention, thinking they could return home after the holiday on Sunday. Anyway, I have very nice neighbors (yes, plural) who come over with their snowblowers and do my driveway so I don't have to shovel the whole thing. That's one of many benefits of having moved to the city, having neighbors who look out for each other. I never had that in the suburbs and obviously not in the country at honey's.
Well, today's paper has posted, so that's it for today. Happy to be going back to work and having something to do.

I remembered this morning when Mom called me before work. She sounded tired, but she tried to make a joke about my cooking skills. I could tell she was covering up how she really felt. I went through the day with that stuck in my mind, just replaying her voice and feeling a bit helpless.

Now, after dinner, I’m just sitting at the table, not really wanting to move. It’s weird how grief comes in waves. I keep thinking about whether there’s anything actually helpful I can do from here. I sent her a text saying I love her, but it felt kind of small. I guess I’m wishing I could let go of the worry for just an evening. Still, I’m hopeful she’ll feel a little better tomorrow. For now, I’m just breathing and trying to stay present.

I just finished dinner and I'm still thinking about the text exchange with my sister earlier. She wanted to know if I could help her with some paperwork for her new apartment, but between my own assignments and remote work tasks piling up, I honestly don't know how I could fit it in. I tried to explain but I don't think I was very clear, and now I'm worried she thinks I'm just making excuses. The weirdest part is I want to help, but I feel like my brain is moving through sludge lately. I keep replaying our messages, wondering if I should have picked up the phone instead. Maybe this is just the stress talking, but it feels like every little thing is another item on a never-ending list. Is it selfish to put my own stuff first right now? I keep telling myself I'll have more clarity after the weekend, but who knows. I wish boundaries were easier to set, or that I could explain myself without sounding cold. For now, I just hope she understands, even if I barely do myself.

The hum of the fridge is the only thing breaking the quiet right now, and the glow from the TV screen makes everything look kind of blue. I haven’t bothered to turn on the main light because I like how the room gets softer at night. My mind keeps looping back to that weird conversation with my brother earlier. He called to check in, which was nice, but then we got on the topic of Dad and it got awkward fast. I don’t know if I misunderstood what he was asking or if he was fishing for something, but I felt like I was supposed to have some big insight about why Dad’s been distant lately. I just didn’t. Maybe he thinks I’m not paying attention, but honestly, I’m just tired of guessing what everyone wants from me.

I replayed the call after we hung up, trying to figure out if I’d sounded cold. I wanted to say, “I get how you feel,” but the words never came out right. Sometimes I wish I was better at these conversations, but I always end up hyperfocusing on little details, like the way he paused or changed the subject. Maybe I’m overcomplicating it. I know I care, but it’s easier to focus on work or my own routine than to dig into family stuff. Anyway, I’ll probably text him tomorrow, maybe ask if he wants to grab food this weekend. It feels like the right thing, even if I’m not sure what I want to say yet. For now, it’s just me, the fridge, and this weird blue light keeping me company.

My feet are tucked under the scratchy old blanket on the couch, and every time I shift, it bunches up in a weird way. The apartment is quiet for once, just the hum of the fridge and the soft traffic outside, but my mind is still racing. I tried to organize the shared calendar again tonight, but someone keeps adding things without telling me, and I’m starting to feel like I live in a puzzle where the pieces keep changing. I keep thinking about what I’m supposed to do next now that I’m not working. Part of me is hopeful that this is just a weird in-between moment, but I also feel kind of lost, like I’m waiting for a signal that probably isn’t coming. It’s exhausting to keep acting like everything is fine with my roommates when I don’t even know how to answer when people ask what I do all day. I did manage to cook dinner (spaghetti again, because it’s easy and nobody complains), and afterward, I sorted old receipts into neat piles, which made me feel a little more in control. I keep thinking about signing up for something new, maybe a class or volunteering, but I haven’t actually done it yet. The living room light is too bright and I should get up to turn it off, but I just keep sitting here, thinking that maybe tomorrow will feel less confusing. I know I can figure this out eventually, but tonight everything feels a bit too much. Still, I made it through today, and I guess that counts for something. 😊

After dinner tonight, I found myself replaying the brief moment at class when a group project partner dismissed my idea without much thought. It wasn’t just the rejection but how it added to the weight I've been carrying all day. Balancing work hours with studying is like juggling flaming torches, and every little social friction feels magnified. I want to push through, but the logistics of managing schedules, assignments, and job applications leaves me drained.

I'm trying to remind myself that feeling overwhelmed is temporary and that each small step matters. Maybe I need to break tasks down even more or reach out for help more often, though asking feels like admitting weakness. Still, hope lingers—hope that this overload will ease and that the right opportunity will come my way soon. For now, I’ll take a deep breath and try to get some rest before tomorrow’s chaos begins again.

Closed my laptop after yet another hour of scrolling job boards this morning, trying to decide if I’m actually looking for something stable or just torturing myself. There’s a persistent sense that I should be doing something more impressive or at least more secure, but I don’t even know what that would mean for me anymore. I thought freelancing would feel freeing, but lately it just feels like I’m drifting. The fog in my head isn’t helping, either. I keep rereading the same emails, overthinking every line before I send a response, and still worrying I sound unprofessional or unreliable. My savings are okay for now, but the anxiety about next month makes it hard to focus on the projects I do have. Sometimes I wonder if I’m cut out for this field or if there’s something fundamentally wrong with how I approach things. Other people seem to have a plan or at least some confidence, and I keep comparing myself, even though I know it’s pointless. I watched a webinar about building a personal brand and felt like I was watching someone describe an alien species. There was a moment today when I looked at the unfinished code on my screen and just felt completely detached from it, like it belonged to someone else. I know I’m supposed to push through, but the self-doubt feels heavier lately. Maybe if I broke things into smaller steps or stopped expecting everything to click instantly, I could get somewhere. For now, I just want to quiet the noise in my head long enough to get some actual work done.

I woke up late again today, which meant I had to rush through making breakfast for Mom and I barely had time to check her meds. The pill organizer is missing Wednesday and Thursday—did I forget to refill those or did she take them already? I can’t even remember what day it is half the time. The living room is a mess; there are magazines and blankets everywhere, and I keep tripping over her slippers near the couch. I swear, every time I get a moment to myself, there’s a new thing I realize I forgot—doctor’s appointments, groceries, laundry piling up. I started making a to-do list on my phone but then I misplaced the phone under a cushion and spent twenty minutes looking for it. I know I should ask for more help, but it feels like I’m the only one who knows how to keep things going. My partner tries, I know he does, but I get so frustrated when he leaves things half-finished or doesn’t listen to what I’m actually asking. We keep promising to talk more, to actually sit down and have a conversation, but it never seems to happen because there’s always something urgent. I snapped at him about the bills this morning, which I regret, but sometimes I don’t even realize how tense I am until I hear my own voice. The TV was blaring some morning show in the background, and I couldn’t even focus on what I was saying. I miss having just a few minutes of quiet, where I don’t have to think about anyone else’s needs. Maybe I’ll try to get out for a walk later, if I can sneak away for half an hour. Right now, I just want to sit here and not move for a bit, but there’s still so much to do. The sun is coming through the window, and for a second it actually felt peaceful, until the phone rang again. I wish I could keep that peaceful feeling for longer than a few seconds at a time.

I'm tired of being my neighbor's fact-checker.
The stuff that comes out of his mouth is astounding. Most of the time I have the knowledge to correct him, from 'massive' fraud to immigrants not paying taxes to immigration only taking the worst of the worst. And other times, what he says sounds fishy but I don't have the info at hand. Like yesterday. Last year he bought the new Toyota pickup, obviously cost mega-bucks. And he was complaining yesterday about how high the tab renewal fees were. He said the price it was based on wasn't changing and that it was the Democrat's fault because they changed how it was calculated last year. That didn't sound right to me, so I couldn't comment specifically, but I was able to counter that we used to all pay a flat fee, but it was the Republicans who changed it to a depreciation model and raised it 20 yrs ago. He brought up the fraud in MN again, I countered that there is fraud in every state, Brett Favre was even involved in a huge fraudulent scheme in Mississippi, and if neighbor really wanted to be concerned about fraud, he should be concerned about the $200 billion in tax fraud going uninvestigated because the investigators were slashed. He brought up how the workers from his wife's former employer (county agency) were going to strike which he thought was a good thing, so I reminded him that it was the Democrats who support the unions that allow them to strike, that Republicans do not. Back and forth it went. And this was my lunch break. I needed a mental break and that was no break. I finally said "well I guess my vote will cancel your vote." And went inside. I looked up the tab renewal thing, and he was wrong. Of course.
I wish I knew where he gets his information. His algorithm is probably feeding him what he wants to believe and he has no intention of seeking out answers and doing the hard work for truth. It is presented as believable so it must be true. I actually read the MN statutes on vehicle licensing to get my information. It's this simplistic thinking that has taken over so many people, the failure to even look further and dig deeper to see if something is true. They just take it at face value.
He keeps saying he's gotta move. I don't dissuade him. I just respond that he should do what he needs to do.
Ugh. I need a fence.

The kitchen clock ticked loud in the quiet after dinner, and I caught myself just staring at my empty plate for a while. The leftover warmth from the food was still lingering in the air, mixed with the faint scent of dish soap from earlier. It’s these small, ordinary moments that feel so strangely heavy lately.

I tried calling Mom after eating, but her phone went straight to voicemail again. It’s been weeks since Dad passed and some days I think I’m doing fine, sticking to my routine and keeping busy with work, but then I’m blindsided by these waves of restlessness and sadness. The house is too quiet at night. I find myself pacing between rooms, picking up books or half-finished projects, but nothing holds my attention for long. I’m supposed to be the practical one, the one who helps everyone else organize and move forward, but right now I just feel lost. Even remembering to eat feels like an accomplishment some days.

I keep telling myself I should reach out to my brother, but I don’t know what to say that doesn’t sound hollow. Grief is such a weird, unpredictable thing. Maybe tomorrow I’ll go for a walk after work, or finally try that recipe Dad used to love. For now, I just want to sit here in the quiet, trying to make sense of how everything changed so quickly. The clock keeps ticking, but I feel stuck somewhere in between.

Just finished scrolling through some tech news on my phone, trying to shake off that weird heaviness that settles in when the house is too quiet. It’s still early, so everyone else is either asleep or pretending to be, and I have the living room to myself. I keep thinking about how different mornings used to feel when grandma was around—her voice echoing from the kitchen, the smell of ginger tea wafting in. Now, there’s just this emptiness mixed with the hum of the fridge and the soft ticking of the wall clock. I tell myself I’m handling her passing well, but sometimes I catch myself looking for her slippers under the coffee table or expecting her to ask for help with her tablet. Maybe I’m being too hard on myself for not moving on faster, but it feels like life keeps piling on small reminders when I least expect them. My family doesn’t talk much about her, and maybe that’s why I feel restless, like I should be doing something more or being stronger for everyone. At least work keeps me occupied—debugging a new module today, which should be a good distraction. Still, I wish there was more space for privacy around here, somewhere I could just process things without worrying about someone overhearing. For now, I’ll just hang out on this couch, try to focus on the things I can control, and remind myself that missing her is okay. Maybe that’s what moving forward looks like, even if it’s messy.

Nasty places both.
Have a good day….

I tried to focus on the week ahead: pickup for Jamie on Tuesday, parent-teacher conference Thursday (is that at 3 or 4?), and prep for the new summer menu that’s not even half done. My phone kept buzzing with calendar reminders I must have set in a blind panic earlier, and I kept swiping them away, telling myself I’d remember everything. My mind was a jumble—one minute thinking about inventory orders, the next about whether I actually sent in that field trip form, or if I just dreamed about it. The more lists I make, the more I seem to lose track, like the act of writing them down scatters the thoughts instead of collecting them. Funny how I can run a kitchen with six people shouting orders, but I get tripped up trying to remember if Jamie needs a snack for after school or if it’s my week for soccer drop-off. I know I should be grateful for shared custody, the breathing room, but honestly it just feels like I’m always switching gears, never really landing anywhere. My head was foggy, and even the strong coffee felt weak against it. I looked at the scribbles in my notebook and realized half of them were just doodles of knives and pans instead of actual to-do items. Maybe I’ll try again tomorrow morning when my brain’s less mushy, but for now, I just want to stare at nothing and let the noise wash over me.

Just re reading the Emotional Abuse link on my menu
Picked out this as a reminder, to myself and to others.
1. The brainwasher keeps the victim unaware of what is going on and what changes are taking place.
Your partner might control your finances, make plans for you, or not tell you what his plans are until the last minute. He may talk about you to others behind your back, to isolate you from them.
2. The brainwasher controls the victim's time and physical environment, and works to suppress much of the victim's old behavior. The victim is slowly, or abruptly, isolated from all supportive persons except the brainwasher.
Your partner might have insisted that you stop certain social, hobby, or work activities. You might have gotten moved to a new location, farther away from your family and friends. Or you may have been asked (or told) to reduce or stop contact with specific supportive people in your life.
3. The brainwasher creates in the victim a sense of powerlessness, fear, and dependency.
Verbal and emotional abuse creates these emotions, and they become stronger and stronger over time.
4. The brainwasher works to instill new behavior and attitudes in the victim.
Your partner trains to you behave in ways that he wants you to behave. He gradually makes you feel differently about yourself, and erodes your confidence in yourself.
5. The brainwasher puts forth a closed system of logic, and allows no real input or criticism.
In other words -- What he says, goes.

This morning, I remember staring at my phone for almost an hour, flipping between email, my project management app, and the news, trying to will some new work to appear. Even as I was making oatmeal, my mind kept running through the list of invoices still unpaid. Now, after dinner, I’m at the table, dishes pushed to the side, and my laptop open. There’s this odd stillness in the house, but inside my head it feels like a race—like I’m darting from idea to idea, chasing the next project lead.

My focus tonight is sharper than usual, almost like a physical tension in my jaw and shoulders. I spent the last two hours deep-diving into a proposal for a potential client, tweaking every sentence, and researching their company culture to make it perfect. It’s weird how I can get lost in this zone, forgetting how hungry or tired I am until I stop. I know the uncertainty of freelancing is wearing, especially with bills coming up and no guarantee that this pitch will even get a response. Still, I can’t help but feel hopeful. Each time I send something out, I imagine it’s the one that changes everything. The pressure is real, but so is the possibility. I keep telling myself that if I just push a little harder, focus a little more, something good will land. For now, I’m going to try to let my mind slow down and maybe watch a dumb show before bed. In the woods, things go by a LOT slower. You can get aquatinted with the scenery and even sit down on it when you’ve a mind. There are dozens of things you can bring home with you. Pine cones, leaves, interesting stones, fungus, lichen, gnarly sticks, mossy bark and if you have remembered to bring your shovel, you can even get yourself a small tree.
I’ve done it. And I can show you the yard where those transplanted trees are growing today.
In the woods a person can think. The smell of pine needles is way better for thinking than a bunch of cars breaking wind let me tell you. Now if you have decided to have a sit down on a log for a good think in the woods, you might be distracted by a few carpenter ants. If that happens, move to a rock. Solutions to problems are a lot simpler in the woods.
Now it IS true in the woods you might run across some local characters that could startle you. The only ones I would worry about are the mountain lions and the bears. And come to think of it, you might as well not worry about the mountain lions anyway because most likely he will be watching you first and you won’t have a clue what hit you, till he hits you. So instead you might just want to worry about the bears a little, but not too much. Usually you have to go WAY into the woods to run across a bear, and we are just talking about a little stroll, not a wilderness adventure.
It’s possible that you might be startled by a lizard in the woods. They like to run through the dry leaves just to see humans jump. And if they are lucky the human will jump AND let out a squeaky “EEK !” They really like that, so I don’t do it. I just do the jump thing because it’s a reflex and I can’t help it. But then I go over and poke the leaves with a stick to show them I know what they’re up to.
Otherwise, the remaining creatures you see won’t be alarming. Deer, hawks, jackrabbits, pheasants all just take off when they see you. But we wish they would hang around so we could get a better look at them. But you aren’t in charge in the woods. You pretty much have to take what comes.
So next time, bring your basket and we’ll gather some pine cones and I’ll show you a really great spot to see wild orchids. And there is a place up by the creek where I planted an Atlas cedar once, we will go see if it is still growing there. Because I know that in a few more days . . .I’m going to need to take a walk in the woods.

...to steal, lie, harm, judge, or hate; I was not properly set up for a world where everyone makes mistakes, so when I entered the adult world after going no contact with my mother, my life was at an extreme risk. When you're a young black woman, to be perceived as unassuming and harmless is to have a target on your back. To be solipsistic is frowned upon and unladylike. Charm and elegance attract insidious men with evil eyes. Perhaps the only thing I learned that helped me survive after I took the plunge into the real world from an abusive household was how to obey, and I despise that. My freedom is the triumph I have fought hardest for. Giving it up to survive in various circumstances throughout my life has disheartened me.

The times that I have lost my breath and crumbled to my knees with grief and guttural sobs were when I had my right to choose ripped violently away from me. It does not feel like breathing but rather death. I have died many times.
Despite the distance now between my mother and I and our mothers before us, we all share this particular sorrow in a manner near identical.

I just finished a quiet lunch break in the teacher's lounge, which was surprisingly empty today. The quiet gave me a chance to replay the conversation with my sister from last night. She asked if I’d noticed changes in my new relationship, but I wasn’t sure how to answer her. It felt like she was fishing for some deep insight or maybe judgment, but all I had was uncertainty. I didn’t want to admit that I’m restless, that things seem fragile and undefined, and frankly, that I’m scared of where this might go. 

Work has been the usual whirlwind of grading and meetings, but underneath it all, there’s this lingering feeling of imbalance. My health hasn’t exactly been a priority, which probably explains why I’ve been more tired than usual. I joked to a colleague today that I’m one bad coffee away from developing a caffeine addiction, and they laughed, but maybe there’s some truth to it. Sometimes I wonder if I’m overthinking every little signal, every hesitation in a text or a voice message from her. It’s like I want to read too much into things because I need to understand what’s happening or figure out what I’m supposed to do next. Deep down, I guess I want clarity, but I’m uncomfortable with how slow and unsure this feels. Feeling a dull weight in my chest, not quite worry but not peace either. Last night, after finishing my coding assignment, I wandered into the kitchen around 1:30am. The fridge light was too bright. I stood barefoot on the cold tile, eating a piece of leftover bread, just letting my mind run. I kept thinking about whether I’m still the same person I was before I started these classes. I used to be certain about where I was heading—stable job, decent routine, but now everything seems up in the air.

Balancing work and school is harder than I expected. My thoughts keep skipping ahead to deadlines and meetings, and then back to these questions about what I’m actually building toward. It’s a strange mix of feeling focused on the tasks and totally unsure of the bigger picture. I catch myself zoning out during lectures, then snapping back, worried I missed something important. The kitchen at night is the only place that feels still, but my mind won’t settle. The hum of the fridge and the ticking clock almost make it worse.

I keep wondering if this is just a phase—if other people my age feel this restless, questioning what their work really means. I want to believe the effort is worth it, even if I can’t see the end result yet. I wiped the crumbs off the counter, filled my water bottle, and went to bed, still turning it all over in my head. Maybe tomorrow will feel clearer. For now, I’ll just try to keep moving forward, even if the path feels blurry.

I went to my daughter's house last evening to hand out goodies. She wanted to go out with her daughter trick-r-treating. This will most likely be Rena's last year, since she just turned 13. I think that's a reasonable cut-off date.
There weren't as many kids as I thought there would be, considering this is a residental neighborhood, and the nearby elementary school is well populated. Some of the kids were mere babies, and costumed so cute. The cutest ones got a double portion of treat. Some pretty ghoulish costumes too.
Which brings me to reminiscing about Halloween when I was growing up. We did a little bit ot trick-r-treating, but mostly we got together at community or neighborhood parties.
Anybody remember dunking for apples? You could darn near drown yourself trying to snag an apple floating in a tub of water. No hands allowed. There were games, taffy pulls (remember those?), some pairing off, too, but we were pretty closely chaperoned.
Chaperoned. That was the whole idea of the neighborhood or community parties. Kids had easy access to alcohol in those days, and snitching from the parents' cigarette supply was not unknown. Of course, small towns were more inclined, I think, to have community gatherings. There's a greater sense of community when you know your neighbors, the mailman is a personal friend, you know all the businessmen by their first names.
A lot of adult activities took place in private homes, and kids went along because the host/hostess had kids the same age. Babysitting was almost unheard of.
And so with Halloween. The churches had their own parties, and no one took exception to witch costumes. Parents got together and helped each other with their kids' costumes. I don't remember seeing ready-made costumes in the stores.
Oh, yes, and we never had to worry about razor blades stuck in apples, or poisoned candy. Homemade cookies were accepted without question, but of course, they were wrapped in waxed paper, if only for the sake of neatness.
There were a lot of things we didn't have then--technological advances we take for granted now. But we were a lot safer, too.
Shalom

Well, here we are in eastern North Carolina once again, facing snow! Being where I am in the Coastal Plains, it seems like we're always on that fine line of snow or not. This time it's looking really good. Do I want it to snow? Hell yeah! I love snow. They're comparing this to the 1979 blizzard we had. How many of you remember that? I was about four years old, and I remember my grandpa shoveling the snow from the back porch to the outside shed (AKA detached garage) where he had a wood stove heater. And although we had power, he just did that to be doing something. I can remember running back and forth from the house to Grandpa. I also remember seeing the snow drifts all the way up to the roof of my uncle's house.
Then there was the snow of 1993. I barely remember it, but I do remember seeing the Christmas lights and the snow and my sister having to go to work at the convenience store in her small town. It's funny how I can remember the one when I was four years old a lot better than I could when I was seventeen. I have a 17-year-old daughter, and she is so excited about seeing a snow like we used to see growing up because it seems like in the past 17 years, the snow has been very minimal here. So here's for good luck. Hope we get snow here in Wayne County, North Carolina. I hope we get 6 inches or more because we probably won't see it like this again in a good while.

I would definitely say - after Ha Long Bay Ninh Binh is my second favourite place in Vietnam. It has so much to offer and not so much contaminated by the tourist traps...In Ninh Binh you do three things: boats, mountains and caves. I have visited no more no less, but 9 various caves in my 3 days in Ninh Binh, three mountains and have taken 3 boat rides on different rivers...
The other wonders I've seen in this province were:
Bich Dong Pagoda - lovely spiritual place, especially, when you go there after 4pm, when all the tour groups left for a day. The name means "emerald pagoda". And the most of this pagoda is actually in a cave! It is, in reality, is a complex of pagodas, the way to each next one is through the previous one...dated from 15 century, this Buddhist marvel radiates a timeless beauty and tranquillity. And if you make it all the way to the top, you're rewarded with the view!
Another cave I visited separately, called Galaxy Grotto and it is slightly off the beaten path in Ninh Binh, but all so worth the effort to get there! A scenic boat ride and a walk through a 700m cave filled with colourful, illuminated stalactites.
I was so lucky to be the only one in that cave! The experience was out of this world! A cave of wonder - Thien Ha - Galaxy Grotto...
Few more caves visited en route to one more local attraction - The Bird Garden, Thung Nham.
The garden itself is not something I would've gone to see, as it is a well kept, manicured to perfection, "designer garden". and, while gorgeous, you can find equally attractive gardens everywhere else in the world.
What does make this place special - a reservation area where lots of wild birds, like cranes, storks, egrets can be observed in masses...
Well, that would be a very (and I mean - VERY) brief record of my Ninh Binh time.
This is a place so worth visiting, and if you choose to stay slightly out of the centre, you're as close to the amazing nature as you could possibly be...

I’m sitting at my desk. The rain is falling outside in a thick, drizzly way. The wind is blowing in an off hand manner. My neighbors are packing up their car with suitcases and bags. A chickadee just landed on the front porch railing among the roses, or what’s left of the roses. I guess he wants to get out of the rain for a bit. What a little marvel he is. Little flying ball of feathers with a black hat.
From the looks of things I am not in the vortex of ‘where it’s happening’ in the world today. I am off in the corner, tucked up in the broom closet like Harry Potter. Only no one keeps me locked up. I kind of like it in here although I won’t tolerate any spiders as perhaps Harry might.
Are quiet people the glue that holds the world together? Do we keep it from flying apart at the seams when the noisier people are jumping up and down and shouting? (not to mention showing their belly buttons)
Maybe so. I’m going to go make some hot cocoa and think that over.
Quietly.

This morning I remembered walking past the kitchen table and seeing Mom’s old planner sitting there, still open to last week. It made me pause for a second, thinking about how much she used to write in it and how I always thought her color-coded notes were overkill. Now I wish I had that kind of structure because lately my head feels like a spinning top, especially since moving here. The kitchen feels too big and empty this morning, with only the hum of the fridge and the weird ticking sound the clock makes.

I keep trying to write out a new schedule for myself and for the house stuff but all I’ve done is scribble half-formed to-do lists. There’s the grocery run I was supposed to do yesterday, the calls we need to make about Dad's next appointment, and I still haven’t found the right box with the insurance papers. I keep thinking I’ll sort out the bathroom closet too, but I just open the door and close it again. It’s like the more I try to get organized, the more things I remember I haven’t done. I know I said I’d help with meals this week but I’m not even sure what’s in the freezer anymore. I think my sister expects me to just know what needs to be done, but half the time I can’t even remember where we put the extra towels.

There’s a sticky note on the fridge with a reminder about a prescription pickup, and I’m afraid I’ll forget that too. I wish I could just wake up and have a plan, or a list that actually makes sense and isn’t just a bunch of half-finished thoughts. I guess I’m supposed to be the responsible one now, but it doesn’t feel real yet. Maybe I’ll try to make a new list after breakfast, or maybe I’ll just stare at the planner again and hope something clicks. I know things will settle eventually, but right now it’s just a lot all at once.

The patience I’m supposed to have feels like a mask some days, especially when I catch myself snapping at little things, like forgetting to buy milk or the TV being too loud. I wish I could talk to someone about this, but I always chicken out—nobody wants to hear about middle-aged guy problems, right? There’s a part of me that misses being spontaneous in a good way, not just reacting to emergencies. Even now, I feel calm, but underneath is this restless energy, like I’m waiting for a sign or a push. I’m not sure what I want from the next year, but I know I don’t want it to look exactly like today. The streetlights flickered on as I walked back, and it made me think about how routines can be comforting and stifling at the same time. Anyway, I should go check on Mom and heat up dinner. Maybe tomorrow I’ll walk a different route, just to see if it feels any different.

sometimes old school advice is just really good advice. i don't believe life was actually better for most people back in, say, the 50's (for example, not a good time to be gay) but i find some social advice from back then to not only be charming, but relevant. still, somehow, i'm sure i would have resented _a lot_ of these well-intentioned lessons when i was a youth because these videos are a little judgmental. to be honest, though, i still sort of appreciate how straight and narrow it is. like, a slap on the head and a 'straighten up!' sort of appeals to me as part of the advice i get. makes me think, i guess. 'well, ya, i guess when you put it that way...' somewhere in this house i have a relic of social etiquette called 'the polite pupil' which covers everything from how to eat a boiled egg properly to the proper greetings of your fellows according to social standing, so it covers all the important topics a child should know. anyway, if you're not really defensive about getting told how shitty you look or that you're a moron, these types of lessons might be for you. put in a softer way, i guess it's that sometimes you need other people's judgement to mold you into something not only socially acceptable, but something socially _desirable_ for whatever space in society you would like to occupy. one of the instructional videos i watched today, which again, is not terrible advice, is just about emotional maturity, which is something i for sure didn't have when i should have, which, consequently, would have made me very resistant to even the idea. another was for girls, literally 'how to be pretty' which, you know, _is_ socially and developmentally kind of important but still, damn, calm down. most of the advice was harmless and basically 'be healthy and put effort into yourself' which again, the whole emotional maturity aspect, would _not_ have sat well with me as a young person. so how does this get romantic? i don't know, there's just something about this sort of advice that, when i'm receptive, strikes me as though i'm valuable in a way that more permissive attitudes don't. like, sometimes the message of unlimited personal freedom can come off as 'i don't give a shit what you do', which is sometimes nice. every now and then, though, it's nice to be held to certain expectations and i find that sort of romantic. the idea of structure and respect and propriety and personal grooming and being considerate and open to criticism and guidance and personal requests without getting needlessly defensive, i find that all to be very romantic. also i love the idealized language. the 'oh, mother, i had hoped so terribly that johnny would be attending sunday service, but it seems he's been called away for the weekend. whatever am i to do?' there's even an accent in old movies called the 'transatlantic accent' that is this blend of english english (the king's english) and american english. what is the most romantic movie i know? lady and the tramp. and there's a transatlantic accent in there too. oh the charm of it all. i ended up eating more last night and don't regret it but i do still want to get back to a calorie deficit. i had my regular breakfast. dinner was cabbage and tofu in a garlic cheese sauce. got a little runny, but nice. i think it would actually work out really well as a sort of 'baked spaghetti' deal, following the same idea as a cabbage roll. i will be eating more, i'm still hungry. i'll just add whatever i have as an eddit because i already wrote all this out and i don't want to lose it while i'm making food. edit: guess, what it was a bean burrito and hot chocolate. i'll say calories are at about 1,700.
