My breath fogs up the windshield while I wait in the parking lot. I’m just sitting here, replaying the conversation from last night with Casey. It started as some offhand joke I made about her friends, which she didn’t find funny at all. I thought she’d get my humor by now, or at least not take it so personally.

When she got quiet, I tried to push past it, but it hung between us the rest of the night. I hate those silences where you know you said something wrong but aren’t sure if it’s really worth apologizing for. Even now, I can’t tell if I was out of line or if she’s just more sensitive than I expected.

Honestly, I’m not sure how serious this thing is supposed to get. I like her, but I keep running into these weird walls where we don’t get each other. Is that just how it goes in the beginning, or is it a sign we’re forcing something?

I guess I’ll see how things go tonight. Not planning to bring it up unless she does. For now, I just need to get through work without replaying the whole thing again in my head.

Anybody watching the Speilberg series Taken ?
We have been watching because we are suckers for science fiction.
But I am having to work at staying with it on some levels. Perhaps it's because there are a few too many characters. And last night it occured to me they are a bit like CARDBOARD characters ! The thing about telling a good story is getting people to relate to the people in it. Then whatever happens, you have the connection. In a way it makes me feel better as a writer to know that even the really GREAT storytellers sometimes struggle to find this place too.
Yes Virginia, I just called myself a writer. One who WRITES. I have confered upon myself the title ! I will stop apologizing for it, like it's a secret little 'thing' I do in my spare time. A hobby. It is becoming much more than that.

It's fucking cold. I'm tired of the cold, but we still have many months to go. I also have some sort of plague, my second of the winter season. I guess this is my new normal, I can't say that I'm alright with it, but I'm not really sure what I can do about it. Dad said I need to go to the doctor, which I'm going on Monday for a follow-up, but I'd fully expect the diagnosis to be, yes, plague, rest and time as the treatment. We also got snow. Started Monday, snow plus high winds, they clocked 79mph at the airport. That made the drive home interesting as you go from normal visibility to barely seeing a few feet in front of you, combined with slippery roads. Fun times. Yet there were still morons driving like it's a normal summer day, and other morons driving with their lights off. Tuesday was moderately better, there were only a few stretches of road that the plows decided to skip. We had several call outs that day, less than 50% of our team showed up. Wednesday was the big snow day for this area. It snowed all day, it was bad enough that I opted to skip going to see Mom, and stayed under layers of blankets. Thursday morning I was up a little early because I knew I'd need to clean off the car. As I was cleaning the car off, fully intending to go to work, I watched a plow come by, twice pushing more snow into the driveway. It was at that point that Dad stuck his head out the door asking if I was going to be able to get out of the driveway. I told him I originally thought I was going to, but after watching the plow take the snow bank from 2ft to about 4ft, seeing that, I was staying home. It turned out I was not the only, apparently even less people made it in than on Tuesday. Friday was closer to normal, but we still had people missing, combine that with a back up of freight because of the weather, and a lot of areas didn't get picked (freezer & cooler) and it was a hectic day. Friday being my freezer/cooler day, my coworker & I didn't finish the freezer until almost 2pm, something that hasn't happened in probably a year at this point. --- It's Sunday now. The nursing home called this morning, Mom had another (minor) seizure. They let the doctor know, and said she was "blank" initially, but had come out of it and was eating and drinking. This plague is seriously kicking my ass. Congestion, sore throat from nasal drainage. Cough. Wheezing when I'm trying to sleep. I'm supposed to go out to dinner with Mr Angry & the Italian on Saturday, but unless I have dramatic improvement this week, I'm not sure I'm going to go. I'm already a little annoyed at the venue of choice, I asked for closer and not downtown. Well technically it is closer, but it's on the North side of Buffalo, not directly downtown, but pretty damn close. They are talking snow or possible freezing rain on Saturday, so I'm not sure decent food and good company will be enough incentive if I'm not feeling 100%. --- I'm hoping to use this year to right the floundering ship that is life these days. I need to make positive changes, drop weight, cut out the crap. I need to severely cut back on my drinking, I've had way too much in the last year, for a multitude of reasons, none of them valid enough to justify it. I want to write more. When Spring arrives, I'd definitely like to get outside more, it's just too miserably cold right now. I'd just like to actually enjoy life again, instead of just existing. ---

I connected with my Asian neighbor down the street, saw her leaving the house to get her mail as I was driving by, so I pulled over. Communicating was difficult, as she speaks very little English. I pointed to where I live so she knew who I was and she understood. Then I said I would help her, food, shopping. She looked confused. I said ICE. And then she understood. She pointed in a circle and said much family, and shook her head, looking sad/concerned. I understood it to mean she had family nearby. I pointed to myself, then extended my hands toward her in a cupped giving gesture and the lightbulb went off. Oh! Thank you! she said.Then she gave me a hug!! I told her my name, she told me hers. Just before she turned to go back to her house she asked, "You Catholic?" No, I replied. (But I was raised Catholic lol!) We parted with smiles. I'm so glad I tried.

While waiting for this stupid server to complete what it's doing, found some "encouraging" quotes (got to print them out and stick on the wall):
1. When computing, whatever happens, behave as though you meant it to happen.
2. When you get to the point where you really understand your computer, it's probably obsolete.
3. The first place to look for information is in the section of the manual where you least expect to find it.
4. When the going gets tough, upgrade.
5. For every action, there is an equal and opposite malfunction.
6. To err is human. . .to blame your computer for your mistakes is even more human, it's downright natural.
7. He who laughs last probably made a back-up.
8. If at first you don't succeed, blame your computer.
9. A complex system that does not work is invariably found to have evolved from a simpler system that worked just fine.
10. The number one cause of computer problems is computer solutions.
11. A computer program will always do what you tell it to do, but rarely what you want to do.

A week or so ago when the smoke from forest fires covered the sky, the sun took on that same burnt gold look that the moon had tonight.

First I went out to my daughter's workplace to have a few words with her and show off the shawl I just completed crocheting. It was chilly with a spit of rain every now and then, but she's worth it.
I thought it would take forever to get to D&D's, as the traffic is usually bad at that hour, but I went sailing right along. Got most of the green lights. I was the first one there and got to get the first whiff of bread fresh out of the oven.
These WNGTs are pot-luck, and I gotta tellya, there are some mighty fine cooks. We sat around the table chatting after cleaning up our plates, then all of a sudden D-Himself got out the cards and we started playing poker. Five-card draw. D-Herself had never played, so I sat out and coached her for several hands. After she began to show some understanding of how to hold her cards and how to bet, I began playing.
I can't remember the last time I played poker. I love card games. I don't often run a bluff, but I do know how to psych-out another player. For awhile I wasn't hitting very well, then all of a sudden the cards started coming my way. It was strange, though. It seemed that whatever I threw, I got back in another suit. F'rinstance: if I threw an eight of clubs and a 4 of hearts on the draw, what I got back would be an eight of diamonds and a 4 of spades. If I could have seen a minute or two in the future....ah well. I cleaned out everybody, anyway.
We didn't have any chips, and declined to play for money, so D-Herself got out a jar of dried rose hips, and we used those for betting. So now I'm the hippy card shark.
Well, hey! can I help it if good cards are dealt to me?
All that excitement gave me an asthma attack.
D-Herself sent me home with some of her wonderful rye bread, and a container of the yummy noodles one of the other women brought. So I'm set for lunch tomorrow, and a piece of my cake for a mid-afternoon snack.
I was going to let y'all in a secret, but my sister reads this blurb, too, so I guess I won't write about what she's getting for Christmas.
Now it's time for a pill and bed.
G'nite and Shalom

Closed my laptop at 1:15 AM and just let my head rest on my arms for a minute, feeling the hum of the coffee shop’s fridge and watching the barista wipe down counters. I was the last customer, nursing a cup of peppermint tea because coffee was out of the question if I wanted any chance at sleep. My mind kept circling back to the phone call with Mom earlier—she sounded so small, her voice fragile in a way that made me ache. I wanted to ask more, to fix something, but she just wanted to talk about the weather and the new neighbors. Maybe she’s protecting me, or maybe I’m protecting myself. I keep telling myself I have time to breathe and process but everything feels like it’s stacked on top of me lately: deadlines, group projects, the empty side of my bed when I get home, and the soft click of my roommate’s door closing at night.

I noticed the smell of cinnamon from someone’s pastry lingered long after they left, and it reminded me of baking with Dad when I was little. The ache of missing him comes in waves—sometimes sharp, sometimes just a dull ache in the background. Grief is strange; it makes me more observant, like I’m searching for pieces of him in everyday things. I wiped away tears before leaving so the barista wouldn’t see. Walked home under the streetlights with my backpack heavier than it should be, wishing I could trade a little of my exhaustion for some peace.

Closed my laptop after handling another customer complaint, and now I’m just staring at this half-empty mug of cold tea on my desk. My brain won’t stop spinning tonight, even though my body feels tired. I keep wondering if freelancing was a terrible idea—it’s always a toss-up if I’ll get enough gigs to pay rent, and sometimes I honestly feel like I’m just faking it, that someone will call me out for not being good enough. My friends all seem to have some direction, or at least stable jobs, but I can’t tell if that’s just how it looks from the outside. Maybe everyone is just kind of bluffing their way through things? I wish I could ask, but I never do, it’s not really my style to talk about this stuff and I doubt they’d actually be honest about it anyway.

I get stuck in these loops where I question if I’m even the kind of person who can build something steady. Maybe I’m too gentle or not assertive enough for this hustle—people always say you have to be aggressive to get by as a freelancer. My room’s messy, papers everywhere, receipts from last week’s groceries still on the corner of the desk, and I just keep letting it pile up. Even writing this feels a bit pointless but maybe it’ll help me sleep if I dump my brain out like this. The radiator just clicked on and I’m weirdly grateful for the distraction. I think I’ll brush my teeth and try to shut my head off for a few hours, even if I know I’ll probably just lie there thinking about all of this again.

Pretty drained right now, just staring out the grimy window as the bus rattles down Main. Work was the usual chaos—register freezing, customers griping about the sale signs, and my manager snapping about folding standards. I honestly don’t know how people have the patience to ask for the manager over a $2 price difference, but I guess everyone’s got their thing. The fluorescent lights are still buzzing in my head. It’s almost 7 PM and I can’t stop replaying that conversation with Alex from lunch break. We’ve been texting less and less, and today she seemed distracted when I tried to make plans for the weekend, almost like she was just going through motions. Maybe I’m reading into it, but it’s hard not to when you’re still trying to find your footing in a new city. I was hoping she’d be one of those friends who’d stick around, but lately it feels one-sided and I’m not sure if I should keep pushing or just let it fizzle. I don’t want to come off as needy, but also, if I don’t reach out, who will? This city feels huge and anonymous, and sometimes I’m not sure if I’m making any progress at all. I keep telling myself that it takes time, but when the only people I talk to all day are coworkers and customers, it’s easy to feel stuck. My feet hurt from standing, my phone battery’s almost dead, and the weird guy in the seat across keeps humming to himself. I should pick up groceries but I doubt I’ll have the energy. Maybe I’ll just order something unhealthy and watch TV. I don’t know—today just felt heavier than usual, and all I can think about is crawling into bed and not talking to anyone for a while.

My sandwich is still a little cold in the middle, but I’m too tired to care and just keep chewing. The warehouse is pretty quiet during lunch, except for the hum of the vending machine and the occasional footsteps in the hallway. I checked my phone for messages from Sean about tonight’s pickup, but nothing yet. My fingers are sticky from the peach I packed this morning, so I wipe them on my napkin and try to focus on my food.

Tonight is one of those nights where both work and home need my attention and I’m not sure how to split myself in two. I need to finish my shift, then grab groceries, and coordinate with Sean about who’s taking Mia to her dance class. Our shared calendar is color coded, but we still manage to double book or forget little things, like who’s picking up snacks for her class. I feel like I’m always thinking a few steps ahead, but sometimes I miss the obvious stuff when I’m this tired.

I notice the way the afternoon light comes through the window, falling in a stripe across the breakroom table. It makes the dust motes look like glitter. I wonder if anyone else notices things like that, or if I’m just trying to find something nice to look at in the middle of a long day. The quiet makes it easier to think, but also reminds me how little downtime I actually get between work and coparenting.

Even though I’m exhausted, I’m optimistic that we’ll figure out tonight’s logistics like we always do. We’ve had worse weeks and made it through. At least Mia seems happy lately, and I know that’s what matters most. I just need to get through the rest of my shift and try not to overthink everything. Maybe, if I’m lucky, I’ll get to bed before midnight. One step at a time.

I remember catching the look on his face just before he left last night. That pause when he hesitated at the door, like he was trying to decide if he should say something more or just go. He didn’t say much, but the silence between us spoke loud enough. It’s frustrating how this apartment, our routines, and all the little scheduling clashes build walls without us noticing until it’s too late. This morning, as I stood in the kitchen half awake, the smell of coffee wasn’t enough to clear my head or that tight knot in my chest. I keep running scenarios in my mind about what I should have said or done differently. But thinking doesn’t help if we don’t actually talk, and I’m tired of circling the same conversations that get us nowhere. I want to find a way back to something solid between us, but right now, it feels like we're just two people living parallel lives under one roof. I need to stop overthinking for a minute and just be present, even if it means sitting with the discomfort. Maybe if I can focus on the now, the scattered pieces won't seem so impossible to put together.

Plastic fork in one hand, salad in the other, my phone screen lighting up with unread messages from her. Lunch break is strangely quiet, just the hum of the old fridge in the staff room and the occasional rattle from the vending machine. I keep thinking about last night—her voice was softer than usual, not angry, but something off. She asked where I thought this was going. I didn’t answer right away. I said I was tired, which was true, but also a way out. I stared at the ceiling after we hung up, tracing the cracks, listening to the faint traffic outside my window. Not sure who I’m supposed to be in this relationship, or if I even know what I want out of it. Part of me wants to just let it ride and see what happens. Another part wants to hit pause and figure myself out first. She joked about my "mystery" this morning, but I could tell she meant it. Being private is easier than being honest, at least for me. Maybe I’m just not ready to let anyone in all the way. Focused on work now, but the questions keep looping in the background like a bad song on repeat. I wish I had a better answer for both of us.

This afternoon, Mom asked if I’d help out with dinner, but somehow the way she said it felt more like a demand than a question — maybe I’m just reading into things again. I was already in that half-space of thinking about a case and my brain was doing somersaults trying to untangle someone else’s mess while also trying not to snap at her. I said yeah, but maybe later. She looked annoyed but didn’t say anything, which made me wonder if I’ve been distant lately, even though I try hard to keep it together around her. Now, sitting in the kitchen early morning while everyone sleeps, I’m replaying that little interaction and wondering if I should have just said yes immediately or asked if she wanted company while cooking so it wouldn’t feel so cold. It’s weird because I’m so used to hearing clients’ feelings and needs but then I turn into this awkward mute with my own family. There’s this tension between wanting space and feeling guilty for needing it. And I probably sound ridiculous because it’s just a small thing, but the silence after my reply stuck with me. Maybe I overthink things but sometimes I feel like I’m walking on eggshells at home, even though it’s the only place I’m supposed to relax. I wish I could just say what I really mean without worrying about tone or consequences, but that would require a level of bravery I don’t have before coffee. Anyway, maybe I’ll make an effort to chat with her tonight, or maybe I’ll chicken out and just keep scrolling on my phone pretending to be busy. It’s exhausting trying to balance being the helper for everyone else and feeling like I’m invisible when I need help too. Okay, I’ll stop spiraling before the day even starts. Maybe just one more sip of this ridiculously strong coffee and try to breathe.

This morning, I spilled my coffee while trying to scan a bunch of documents at work—classic scatterbrained move that instantly set a stressful tone. Now, on this crowded bus ride home, I’m trying to untangle the thoughts racing through my head after the endless emails and last-minute schedules piled up today. It feels like I was on autopilot most of the afternoon, just ticking boxes without really absorbing anything. I told myself I’d update my to-do list more regularly, but somehow I still lost track of a few tasks. I hate feeling so stretched thin and worried I’m letting my partner down by not communicating well enough as we promised to fix. We had a pretty quiet dinner last night, and I left some things unsaid, which I know probably isn’t helping. I keep thinking maybe if I write down what I want to say first, it’ll come out easier next time. Sometimes I feel like I’m organized in theory but lose it when pressure piles up. It's weird how I can be so grounded but also overwhelmed almost at the same time. The bus is noisy, people chatting and the hum of traffic outside, yet my mind keeps spinning around every little thing I forgot today. I have a notebook in my bag with some reminders, but it feels like that’s just a band-aid. I wonder if tomorrow I’ll finally get a handle on it. At least the ride home gives me a moment to slow down and breathe before jumping back into everything again. It’s exhausting but maybe also necessary to feel this way sometimes.

LAUDS UNDER THE DAWN AND A SWEATY HAND
North Of Italy, 7:15 PM
Last night
I slept about seven hours
, which is not bad at all by my recent standards.
At 5:30 AM the birds 🐦 were already singing — something that wasn’t happening just a few weeks ago — which means
spring is truly near.
😃
At dawn I put God first.
I don’t always manage to do that, nor do I always feel like it, I must admit.
But waking up with
Morning Lauds
is incredibly sweet — it gives the whole day a sacred tone. 🕊️
And I often discover new meanings in the same prayers.
It’s so moving.
I also
took a hot shower
🚿, something I don’t do often enough out of laziness, yet once I’m in, I never want to get out.
I was in a hurry, so I couldn’t stay under the water as long as I would have liked, but it was already something.
My skin itches less now.
I should set aside specific days during the week for this — maybe in the evening, so I can go to bed more relaxed.
But if I don’t feel like it in the evening, mornings will do too, even if I have less time to enjoy it.
It was an
interesting morning
at
work.
I
learned something new
(you truly never stop learning!), and above all,
a new colleague arrived.
He was hired as a driver, but when he’s not out, he’ll help the offices.
For now, they’ve placed him in R. 's office.
He’s from the south of Italy, just one year older than me, and he doesn’t have a family yet.
That was enough for M. and F. to immediately try to set us up.
They asked me if I liked him at the very moment I was thinking he wasn’t bad-looking, but I didn’t feel what I “should” have felt — I mean, there was no spark.
I shook his hand 🤝🏻 and noticed
it was sweaty and sticky.
He was probably a bit nervous.
My immediate impulse was to wash mine.
I’m curious to see how he works and what kind of person he is.
He gave me the impression of being quite
emotional
— his expression was so focused it almost looked like he was sulking.
I didn’t leave any backlog today either
, thankfully.
Tonight the
Sanremo Festival
🎤 begins.
I’m not sure whether I’ll watch it or not — I haven’t followed it in years!

Dear C, A year ago today I was sitting in the emergency department, taking anti nausea meds and praying for you to stay put. I'd woken up vomiting Christmas night and the triage nurse told me to get comfortable because I'd be there for hours. You did stay put, and now you're a year old. I love you so fiercely it almost hurts. You are strong willed, determined, and absolutely hilarious. You spent this evening opening presents at Grandma and Grandad's house and you were far more interested in the wrapping paper than any of the gifts. You got so many lovely things - books, toys, clothes. But what you really wanted was to eat the paper and throw the bows. You started walking unassisted this month and now you won't stop. You toddle everywhere, arms outstretched for balance, grinning like you've just discovered the greatest secret in the world. You love to climb - on everything. The couch, the chairs, the dog. Nothing is safe from your tiny determined hands. Your vocabulary is growing too. You say "Mama," "Dada," "dog," "cat," and "no." Especially "no." You say it with such conviction, like you've been waiting your whole life to tell us all off. You love music. Whenever you hear a song you like, you bounce up and down and wave your arms. You've started to dance more intentionally now, swaying back and forth with the beat. Your favorite foods are strawberries, pasta, and cheese. You will eat cheese any time, any place. You've also recently discovered chocolate and now you point at it and say "dat" repeatedly until someone gives you some. You're still nursing, though I know our time is coming to an end soon. I'm trying to savor these quiet moments with you, knowing they won't last forever. You are the light of my life, C. I can't believe you're already one. I love you more than words can say. Happy first birthday, my darling girl. Love, Mama

Today I spent at least twenty minutes looking for the box with the kitchen towels, only to find it under a pile of winter coats by the front door. I swore I’d be more organized after the move, but it’s like every system I try to set up gets interrupted by a crying baby, a spilled snack, or just my own wandering attention. The living room still smells faintly of cardboard, and the couch is lumpy because I haven’t found the right cushions yet. It’s early afternoon, and there’s a patch of sunlight on the rug that I keep staring at while I think about what this place is supposed to be for us. I keep wondering when this house will feel like home, or if that’s even something that just happens on its own. Sometimes I feel like I’m playing house rather than actually living in it—especially when I catch myself making mental lists of what I should be doing instead of just being present with my kid. There’s a weird kind of calm here, almost like I’m waiting for some switch to flip so I can settle in for real. A distant ex of mine used to accuse me of being 2% gay based on a phenomenon that she noticed back then, that many have noticed before and since: I hit it off with almost every gay man that I meet- no flirting, or fake bullshit- just genuine warmth and friendship. I hit it off similarly well with women who are exclusively into other women, assuming I have some kind of introduction from a trusted mutual. They're often more closed off and defensive, which I totally understand, no aspersions cast AT ALL there, but with guards lowered I find a lot of laughter. With women and gay men thoughts have a very chaotic fluidity to them, which churn and stir undescribed in this cloud between the two of us, obscuring objective meaning and allowing us both to draw whatever we wish to see from it, while still maintaining connection. A connection of pure feeling, with the specifics of how to arrive at that feeling somewhat veiled, necessarily. With men and gay women thoughts are crystal clear, and synchronized. It's the feelings that churn undescribed in a cloud between the two of us. It's an interesting dichotomy. I wonder if anyone else experiences this? I don't think it has much to do with why I get along better with gay folks than I typically do with straight folks, despite being straight myself. I think being an outcast is what makes that happen. Not directly. Not through camaraderie, but through an indirect mechanism of it. If there is one thing I, or any outcast I imagine wants, it's to be known and accepted. Known and accepted. Why? It's the only path to not being alone. The most telltale sign of an outcast isn't what you think. They aren't the people with their noses down lost in propaganda like you imagine. At least not most of them. The true sign of an outcast you can see immediately. Within 5 seconds of meeting them. Their eyes will be wide open, but soft. Not blank doe eyes, but not sharp predatory eyes either. Something in the middle. Something that feels mischievous, even though it isn't. It's just desperate openness. A full throated and constant willingness to be seen and known, completely compulsory based on a lifetime of not having it, and the inversion of fear that occurs in adulthood- from "what if they see me?" to "what if no one sees me?" I promise the warmest people you meet, the most generous and genuine, the most eager and willing to help types that you know- that you might think hold the world together- actually feel very far away from it, and everyone deep down.

Closed the fridge door a minute ago, having just grabbed the last yogurt. The sun barely comes through the tiny window above the sink at this hour, just enough to remind me that I should have slept more. I stood there for a while listening to the hum of the refrigerator, thinking about the string of messages I need to answer this afternoon—clients waiting for updates, a couple of invoices still hanging in limbo. I don’t know why, but the more work comes in, the more I feel like I’m getting away with something. Maybe that’s just freelancing: never quite sure if you’re busy or just scrambling.

My to-do list is already half-scrawled on a sticky note stuck to the microwave, and I keep glancing at it as if it’s going to rearrange itself. It’s oddly satisfying when small things get crossed off, though. Still, I can’t help but worry about whether this streak of steady projects is going to dry up. There’s a weird comfort in the chaos, but it’s also exhausting. I’ll try to get a run in before noon to clear my head, but for now, I’m just hoping the rest of today goes as planned and that nobody throws me a curveball. At least breakfast is sorted, even if everything else isn’t.

The hum of the fridge is the loudest thing in the kitchen this afternoon, besides my own thoughts rushing around. I tried to get the old truck running again but kept hitting the same dead end. It’s frustrating that I know the parts like the back of my hand, yet sometimes it feels like the engine itself is a puzzle I can’t solve anymore. Maybe it’s me, not the truck. I keep wondering if this job still means what it used to. When did I stop feeling like the go-to person for tough fixes and just start feeling like I’m going through the motions? There’s a restless itch in my chest, like I should be doing something else, something new, but that “something else” isn't clear yet. I grabbed a cup of coffee, black, no sugar, just to slow down my thoughts, but they’re still sprinting. Life’s steady routine is both a comfort and a cage. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try a different approach on the truck, or maybe just take the day off. I don’t have answers, just questions that pile up louder than the sound of this kitchen right now.

For now, I’ll just sit with this feeling, try to accept the chaos, and hope that a little order finds me soon.

The toaster wasn’t working again this morning, which shouldn’t be a big deal, but somehow it felt like the last straw, at least for that moment. I stood there barefoot in the kitchen, the floor colder than I expected, just staring at the stupid machine and wondering why nothing feels settled anymore. The sunlight came in at a weird angle—maybe the windows here face a different direction than the old place—and I just kept thinking about how nothing is quite where it’s supposed to be. I tried to make a list in my head of what I need to get done this afternoon, but the ideas kept slipping away, replaced by random thoughts about whether I should try that new grocery store or unpack the last box in the bedroom.

I do like that there’s always something new to notice, like the neighbor’s wind chimes or the way the fridge hums a little louder in the morning. I’m curious about the people here, but haven’t worked up the nerve to say hello—maybe today I’ll just go for a walk and see what happens. Work feels like it’s pulling me in a dozen directions, but I’m optimistic that I’ll find my rhythm again soon. For now, I just wish I could remember where I put the can opener.

Just finished rinsing out my mug and the kitchen is still half-lit by the streetlights outside, making everything look a little unfamiliar. I can hear the hum of the fridge and the faint creak of the floor when I shift my weight. It’s early, way too early, but I couldn’t sleep again, mind racing over every awkward conversation from today. Work wasn’t terrible, but I keep feeling like the new kid even though it’s been almost a month since I moved. There’s this sense that everyone already has their routines and circles, and I’m stuck on the outside trying to find a way in that doesn’t feel forced or fake.

The break room was a minefield—people talking in little groups, mostly about things I don’t know or inside jokes I’m not part of. I tried to join in on a conversation about the local sports team but realized fast I didn’t know the players or even the rules well enough to keep up. I hate that feeling, like I’m faking interest just to seem normal. Maybe if I just keep my head down and show up, things will settle, but right now it just feels exhausting. At least the work itself is straightforward. Stacking boxes, scanning barcodes, keeping my hands busy so my mind doesn’t wander too much. Sometimes I wonder if everyone else feels this out of place or if it’s just me overthinking everything again.

I miss how things used to feel familiar. Even the way the kitchen smells is different here, and it’s such a stupid small thing but it gets to me. I know it will take time, but tonight, standing here in the half-dark, I just feel kind of tired of starting over. Maybe tomorrow will be easier. For now I’m just going to try to get a little more sleep before the alarm goes off.

This morning, just after 6:30, I was standing by the toaster waiting for my bread to pop up, and I could hear the kids arguing upstairs about who gets the last blueberry yogurt. I tried to tune it out and focus on the smell of coffee, but my mind was already spinning with what I knew was coming this afternoon. The kitchen was dim, with just a streak of sunlight hitting the counter, and I remember staring at the crumbs and wishing I could just have five minutes without someone needing something from me.

Today, there’s this neighborhood gathering scheduled, and I’m already dreading it. The idea of forced small talk with people I barely know, the obligation to act interested in conversations about lawn care or school events—I can feel my chest tighten just thinking about it. I always wonder if everyone else actually enjoys these things, or if they’re just better at pretending. I keep running through possible awkward moments in my head, like what if someone asks me about work and I ramble on too long, or if I say something that comes off as aloof. My wife says I overthink these things, but it’s not like I can just switch it off. I wish I could be more relaxed, but every time I try, I end up second-guessing myself later. Sometimes I envy people who just seem to float through these social things without a care. Maybe I’ll find a way to step outside for a break if it gets too much—just a few minutes of quiet would help. Even now, as I write this with the hum of the fridge in the background and the faint sound of cartoons from the living room, I’m trying to mentally rehearse for this afternoon, even though I know it probably won’t go according to plan.

Dialysis Memory
Dialysis went smoothly today. Deb and Jackie are relearning and reevaluating how to do dialysis at home, which we have been trying since November and December, but I ended up in the hospital because I had gotten another blood infection (my second one) and was at Mercy for 8 days. Well, after my 9th catheter needing to be removed, we went where Fresenius patients go. The place is named Azura, and the place is pleasant and friendly --- even more friendly and NOT judgmental, according to what I saw and heard around me. I have ALWAYS felt like a number at Mercy, but at Azura, I was treated as a patient who needed care that was urgent this one Friday afternoon, and my tenth catheter placement, because I have no more access points in my body to have a fistula or graft anymore. The graft I did have worked only for 9 months, while the fistula never got strong enough to be used, and then it stopped doing what it was supposed to do -- thump as my heart beat. That is how I perceived it to feel and sound, by the way my heart beat went.

I'm playing catch-up here with a few things, which is my excuse for throwing what promises to be a quite disjointed entry out here today.

No cavities, the existing fillings do not need replacing, the one cap I have may cause problems in the future, but it's a wait and see thing at the moment. I now have absolutely no signs of gingivitis, and my gum depths are all within healthy, normal limits (except for around the previously mentioned cap, which is why we'll be keeping an eye on that). I got a pat on the head and have another appointment set up in three months time. After this year, if things continue normal, I'll be able to return to six month appointments. I still hate going to the dentist's, though.
The Professor returned home Saturday night toting an extra bag and a few extra things of his from back West (he bought me his old Spirograph set, the darling man!). I expected him to be exhaused, but he was absolutely wound up. We got back to the apartment aroun 11:00 that evening, and I was ready to go to bed by that point, but he stayed up for another four hours or so. It's good to have him back.
His grandfather remains in the hospital with heart fibrillations. It sounds like they are going to try and get it under control with electrical stimulation, possible going so far as to implant an pacemaker. I put (slight) pressure on The Professor to call home yesterday to see if there were any changes, but he resisted and I am reluctant to push further at the moment.
Sunday he slept until about 3:00 in the afternoon. I snuck out around noon-time to get myself a calendar at the half-price sales all the bookstores were having. I knew exactly what calendar I wanted: the Magnetic Poetry calendar for 2002. I have several boxes of magnetic poetry words in my office, and thought it would be fun to have the calendar by my desk to play with. Of course, all the magnetic poetry calendars were sold out, though. I do this to myself every year. I'm too cheap to buy a calendar I see for full price, so I wait for the half price sales, when the only calendars left are of Elvis Presley (the fat version), race cars (the NASCAR edition) and so-cute-they-gag-me Anne Geddes (sp?) babies all dressed up like bananas and butterflies and sunflowers. I did manage to pick up a nice Edward Gorey day book at half price (yay!) but I had to settle for a "Star Trek; Ships of the Fleet" wall calendar for my office. When I got back, The Professor was up and hungry. He really wanted to go out for Indian food, but I've been suffering from a bit of persistent diarrhea recently (I did warn you that this was going to be a "share too much" entry) and really didn't think that was a good idea. I conned him into going to Appleby's instead, where I could at least get something with minimal seasoning. The Professor elected to get their garlic steak (served with whole garlic cloves), with a side order of garlic mashed potatoes and garlic bread. That man is going to reek for a week. It didn't slow down the welcome home festivities later that evening, though. (Like I said, "share too much").
Freezing rain and sleet, switching over to snow, were the offerings for last night, so after dinner we rented a DVD and returned home to watch it. It was the Professor's turn to pick, and I was treated to "Heavy Metal". I vowed revenge, and I shall have it. I get to pick next, and I think I'm going to inflict "Maltese Falcon" on him. He'll probably hate it, but it's the equivalent of movie comfort-food to me (like Casablanca, or the Third Man).
Meanwhile, I've been trying to get through to my doctor's office all morning, but their phone has been chronically busy. This persistent diarhhea I've been enjoying has led to other complications of the nether region, and I am distinctly uncomfortable at the moment. (Remember, I did warn you about the "share too much" aspect of this entry.)
I also have a less painful, but somewhat more alarming problem I want to get checked out. Just before we left on vacation, a small lump on my back next to the shoulder blade suddenly blossomed out into a much larger bump. It's probably just a cyst, or maybe a small infection, but its rate of expansion was rather rapid and I'll feel better just getting it checked out.
If it isn't one thing, it's another.

I just closed my laptop after scrolling through job postings for what felt like the hundredth time today. It’s past midnight but my mind is still spinning with everything I need to do tomorrow. I promised myself I’d apply to at least three positions, but I only managed to finish one application because I kept second-guessing my cover letter. I also need to follow up on that email from last week and update my resume with those new skills I learned, but the to-do list keeps growing faster than I can keep up. On top of that, I remembered earlier that we have to finalize plans for the weekend with his family, and I’m not even sure what we’re supposed to bring. Communication with him has been better lately, at least, but there are still moments when I can tell we’re both tired and trying not to snap at each other. I wanted to talk more about how we’re dividing up chores, but we ended up just watching TV in silence instead. It’s hard to bring up little frustrations when I already feel like I’m barely keeping my own head above water. Earlier tonight I skipped dinner because I was so caught up in tasks, and now my stomach is grumbling. There’s laundry waiting in the basket, dishes in the sink, and the bathroom really needs to be cleaned but I can’t find the motivation. I keep thinking if I just get more organized, I’ll finally feel on top of things, but every day something new pops up. I wish I could turn off my brain for a bit or at least feel like I’m making real progress somewhere. Maybe tomorrow I’ll manage to cross a few things off the list, but right now it just feels endless.

TV is on but I’m not watching, just the hum in the background mixing with the dishwasher going in the kitchen. It’s late, almost 10, and the living room lamp throws that kind of yellow light that makes the whole place look tired. I should be thinking about getting to bed, but my mind’s running through the list of bills I paid today and the ones I still have to handle. The envelope from the electric company is still on the coffee table, I keep glancing at it like the numbers will change if I stare long enough. 

Work was normal, nothing big broke down, which is good. I like fixing things, but there’s a part of me that wonders if I’ll be crawling under cars forever. I’m good at what I do, but sometimes I catch myself wondering if that’s all there is. Maybe that’s just the anxiety talking. I try to stay positive—at least I’ve got work, and I can keep the lights on for now. Sometimes I wish I could just say screw it and take off for a weekend, but tracking every cent makes that feel impossible. Still, I know I’m lucky compared to some, and I have to remind myself of that. Maybe I’ll feel different in the morning. For now, I’m just going to sit here and let the boring sounds fill up the room until I’m tired enough to sleep.

Failure…
It’s such a loaded word. Weighted. Dark. And yet… do I even really know what it means? Does anyone? Or are we just repeating what we’ve been told?
Who decided what failure is? And whose set of rules are we being measured by? Why are we so quick to make failure about identity instead of the event itself? And when did we allow these moments define who we are?
Is it because we live in a society that measures everything…? Targets, grades, promotions, likes, outcomes... Its as if perceived status and achievement equals worth. And when things don’t go to plan.
It becomes personal. You
failed.
You're a failure
. Or worse… "
I failed".
"
I'm
a failure".
Rarely do we ask why. And often, if we’re honest it’s circumstance… or standards imposed on us either by ourselves or by others.
And the measure isn’t just abstract. How we view failure affects not just how we feel, but the choices we make. It shapes how we think and act. The fear of failure can twist our judgement, make us doubt ourselves, push us to rush decisions, or leave us feeling overwhelmed by what might happen. Sometimes we catastrophise about what could go wrong, or get stuck in the worry loop of thinking we won’t measure up.
The dictionary definition says failure is “lack of success”. What exactly does that imply? We only get one shot, one moment, pass or fail… as if life were a single door? But life isn’t like that. Life is a long winding corridor. With a myriad of doors. Some locked doors, some swinging wide open. Others cracked open. And many leading to places I never planned to go….
So how can not fully opening one door suddenly mean “no success”?
When we were children, we fell hundreds of times learning to walk. Nobody called us a failure. We were encouraged to keep trying. We called it growth. Learning. Development. Adapting. Skill building. So when did trying become failing?
Maybe it’s time we all ask ourselves these questions…
Perhaps we should look to learn from other cultures, the cultures that value the process, mistakes the trial and error. The ones that accept missteps as part of learning, not a reflection of identity. Where imperfection is expected and repeated practice matters far more than a single outcome. Continuous improvement over a lifetime, rather than one single verdict.
Maybe failure only exists when we stop questioning. When we stop trying. As long as we are still moving… still curious… still willing to try again, even when we have no idea where we are going or the results were not what we expected …
So… lets ask the question again.... is it really failure if we get up more times than we fall? If we keep learning, refining, adapting and trying?
Could it simply be a new or unexpected chapter unfolding, like one of those "choose your own adventure" books I loved as a kid, or just a moment to pause or recalibrate?
Every so-called failure carries information. A map of what didn’t work. A clue about what might. An experience to call on later. The people we consider successful, the artists, entrepreneurs, inventors…. they’ve all “failed” more times than they’ve succeeded. And yet… they didn’t stop. They didn’t accept the label. They learned. They adapted. They tried again. Is that failure? Or is it
determination, resilience and courage?
Perhaps it’s time to stop buying into the trap…. believing that success is a destination. Maybe it’s an elaborate construct, designed to keep us cautious, restrained, slaves to conformity… holding us back from thriving.
Life was never meant to be linear. The point isn’t to skip to the end. Or to fall on the sword when the outcome isn’t what we expected. The point is to live the journey. To feel the highs and lows. To experience. To learn its lessons. To grow.
Could it be that the real failure is believing the story ends when a door closes, when a path takes an unexpected turn or when we didn’t get the result we expected?
And maybe it’s time to reframe failure altogether.... t

Dialysis Day
Today, a normal dialysis day every Monday morning had found an unusual time of getting on and off and home today. I got on before 11:30 AM and out the door and downstairs at 2:28 AM, and my ride was here by 2:45 AM. It was an amazing day that I experience once in a great while. Today was one of those days. A good day for dialysis. I don’t get days like this too often.
Also, with that said, dialysis went through until 20 minutes before getting off. I started getting cramped in the left side where my kidneys used to be so long again before I learned of total kidney failure at age 17 when I learned that my right kidney had been gone and my left kidney was functioning only at 4% and had my creatinine at 13–in double digits. I became a kidney transplant patient in the making in October 1987 at the age 17, and it became a journey in the making that lasted 32 years before being diagnosed with kidney disease with the transplanted kidney with kidney disease for three years before having hemodialysis three times a week in April on the 24th in 2019 at Mercy Hospital. Have been dialyzing ever since May 7th of 2019, but the first 5 years was done on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays at the clinic until 2023 when the clinic moved to Sister Michael Barry building in July 2023. That was when I was finally able to get my days switched to Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays. The time is not always described as desired, so when I get on early like today, it is a very big treat for me and the dialysis techs and nurses, and the doctors who make their rounds on Mondays and Tuesdays. Dr. Anjum saw me at my 10-minute left mark of treatment for the day. For today, I was gone and out of clinic, and downstairs by 2:28 PM waiting for my ride with You Buy We Fly
(YBWF)
.
Visit With Dr. Anjum
Every Monday, except when he’s on vacation or on the 5th Monday in the month, he takes his time to see his patient in each cubicle to discuss how each patient is doing. He got to me when I had 15 left to dialyze foe the day. I was sitting in my chair #18 today after a two day stint sitting in chair #19 this week. I find this a big treat once in a while.

Just finished washing last night's dishes, letting the hot water run over my hands and staring at the window while the sky slowly turned from black to this faded blue. I kept thinking about Dad this afternoon, how I caught myself reaching for my phone to text him about the stupid car making that rattling noise again, and then I just stood there, phone in hand, feeling this heavy drop inside me. It’s so weird how the smallest things punch you in the gut when you aren’t ready. I tried to shake it off by looking up cheap car parts, making notes in my expense tracker app, but my brain kept looping back to how he always knew what to do, or at least acted like he did. Now it feels like there’s this blank space where advice used to be, and I keep circling it, hoping it’ll fill in with something if I just think hard enough. I made eggs on toast because I read somewhere protein helps with mood, but honestly, it tasted like cardboard. I keep overanalyzing every choice lately, like saving a few bucks here or there will somehow fix the bigger hole left by missing him. The kitchen was quiet except for the hum of the fridge, and I realized I barely notice the silence anymore. Mom called and I almost didn’t answer because I was worried I’d sound too off, but I did, and she just wanted to know if I was eating okay. I said yes, even though I’m not sure that’s true. I wish I could tell her how scattered I’ve been feeling, but I don’t want to make her worry more. I’m trying to keep it together, keeping busy with lists and tracking every cent, but sometimes it all just feels kind of pointless. Maybe tomorrow I’ll feel a bit more focused. Or not. Either way, this morning feels heavy and I don’t really have a fix for it.

Earlier this afternoon, I caught myself staring at Mom’s old mug on the counter while packing up my supplies for another shift. It made me think about how she used to fuss about me running late, and now the house is so quiet. I keep expecting to hear her voice or find her notes left for me, but there’s just silence and the low hum of the fridge.

Now I’m at my desk in my room, laptop open but barely touched. The freelance gigs have been unpredictable this month, which only adds to the constant anxiety simmering in my chest. I keep checking my emails and messages, hoping for some certainty, but it’s just more waiting. My hands are restless, fidgeting with a pen, and my mind jumps from work to worrying about Dad’s upcoming doctor appointment. I’ve tried making lists to regain some control, but it only helps for a few minutes at a time.

Maybe I just need to accept this restlessness for now. I know I can’t fix everything or bring her back, but I wish I could at least feel less scattered. It’s hard to balance being strong for the family and managing my own worries, especially with the financial stress looming. Tonight I’ll try to read a few pages before bed, even if my focus is shot. Maybe that will help me wind down, just a little.

Not saying Maduro didn’t have it coming, but I thought conservatives wanted us to get out of the business of ousting foreign leaders and occupying their countries? Didn’t they complain that we’ve done too much of that in the past? I guess it’s only okay when Trump does it? That’s rhetorical. I know they’ll suddenly support anything when Trump does it.

January brings two looming worries for me. One is taxes. Will we owe? Probably. But how much? One silver lining of this administration is supposed to be taxes. I’ve heard they raised the standard deductions but it’s unclear what our own final numbers will look like. It’s also possible that anything we save in federal will come back to bite us in state, since the administration has been pushing so much funding back to the states to deal with, and they’ll need to find that money somewhere.

Which leads to my other much bigger concern, the upcoming state legislative session and what they’re going to do with higher education funding this year. A boring and irrelevant topic for most people, but my job hangs in the balance. Cuts would have to get really bad before I start worrying about actually losing my job, but it’s not completely out of the question. A more likely scenario would be that they would nudge more highly paid older employees into early retirement plans, which could sweep up my boss and one of my coworkers, turning our team of four into a team of two. And given morale is already souring under the modest cuts they’ve made so far, it could trigger some to flee what they see as a sinking ship. Even if my job is safe, it could change. A lot.

And that’s just my life. I can’t be too worried about the world at large, not because I’m not worried, but because I don’t even know WHAT to worry about. The last year has been so unpredictable, I can’t even begin to guess what the next one will bring. But I will say that midterm elections have never seemed more important than they do this year.

The streetlight outside is leaking in through the blinds, kind of yellow and annoying since it’s making my desk look like it’s stuck between night and day. I keep hearing cars outside, probably people heading home or out, and it makes me wonder how they’re all just getting by. I’m sitting here with receipts spread out, trying to figure out if I can actually swing taking my brother out for lunch this weekend like I promised. We talked earlier, and he made some offhand joke about how I’m always counting pennies, which stung more than I let on. It’s not like I want to have to say no to stuff, but there’s just not enough room in the budget for surprises right now. I tried to explain but he brushed it off, like it’s just a phase or I’m being dramatic. Maybe I am, or maybe he doesn’t get what it’s like to have to add up every little thing. There’s this sense that I’m missing something or making things harder than they need to be, but every time I look at my bank app, it’s all right there in black and white. I wish I could be more relaxed about money, or at least convince him that I’m not just being stingy. I know he means well, but sometimes it feels like no one actually hears what I’m saying. Or maybe I’m not explaining it right, but honestly, how do you make someone understand what it’s like to be constantly checking your balance? I keep replaying that conversation, wondering if I should’ve just agreed to lunch and figured it out later, but then I imagine seeing my account drop and I get that tight feeling in my chest again. It’s like there’s no good way to handle it. I want to be the fun older brother, but right now I’m just the one with too many spreadsheets and not enough answers. Maybe I’ll text him tomorrow and try to say it better. Or maybe I’ll just leave it and hope things feel lighter in the morning.

The hum of the old ceiling fan barely stirs the thick air in this tiny kitchen where I’m grabbing a quick lunch, trying to catch a breath between sessions. It’s quiet except for the occasional distant barking dog — a stray, maybe, or just the neighborhood’s usual cacophony. I keep glancing at my phone, half expecting a message from my sister, but nothing new. She’s been quieter since Mom’s anniversary passed last week. I guess grief has a funny way of settling in, not quite disappearing but folding into the spaces where routine used to live. I’m still juggling the blurred lines of work and life, feeling like a counselor who needs counseling, if only to shake off the scattered thoughts that keep poking at the edges of my focus. Sometimes I wonder if the intensity I bring to my clients is a shield for my own restless mind. I’m tired of pretending I can compartmentalize perfectly when all the tabs keep opening on their own. I didn’t cry today, but the lump was there, stubborn, when I pictured Mom’s empty chair at the dinner table. I caught myself cracking a dry joke about it, maybe to keep the silence at bay or to remind myself that humor is still a lifeline. The clock says I’ve got ten minutes before the next call, but honestly, it feels like a lifetime. Somehow, in the midst of this scattered afternoon, I hold on to the hope that these tiny moments of stillness add up. That one day, the noise will quiet, the grief will soften, and maybe, just maybe, I’ll feel anchored again.

I was watching 7th Heaven on TV this evening. Annie was determined to have the whole family around the table this year, and everyone had other plans. She refused to accept that she wasn't going to get her way and made life miserable for everyone. But finally she came around, had an early Thanksgiving with whatever part of the family happened to be around. And everyone was happy.
I got to thinking........
Thanksgivings were very often at my grandparents' house. All the aunts and uncles and grandkids. Sometimes Aunt E would have thanksgiving at her house, but not all the relatives came. But no matter where, the dinner was well attended and enough food for a garrison.
My first Thanksgiving away from home was miserable. I had moved to Los Angeles in June or July, had a job and lived in a rooming house. But no friends with homes who would invite me to share their joy. Didn't have enough money to go home to Idaho, but I did make a long-distance phone call. And blubbered.
By Christmastime I had a fairly serious boyfriend, but not serious enough to be invited to his parents' home for any celebration--or any reason, for that matter. But it was better by then. I'd gotten over the lonelies, and had presents from home to open.
But back to Thanksgiving.... I remember two in particular. In-laws, husband, 4 kids and a couple guests. That was the year I used the beautiful banquet sized tablecloth my mother-in-law had given me. We set up the table in the living room because it was large enough to accommodate everyone. Even though I had a "country kitchen," it still wasn't big enough. I did enjoy that.
I seldom cook a real meal for myself. It's boring. But I love cooking for company. But now, I don't have any room for a dining table.
The second Thanksgiving I remember was here in Sacramento (Carmichael, actually, but that's beside the point). There were 13 of us at the table. My sister and her daughter came from Tucson, which was wonderful. I have pictures of that day, and I surely do enjoy remembering friends and family around a table loaded with goodies.
Well, in-laws, husband, and one child have departed this life. One son has his own family in SoCal. The other son is somewhere, but not here. Sister will remain in Tucson, and her daughter is in Connecticut (wonder if she'll come home for the holiday?). Friend with whom I was sharing the apartment at the time of Thanksgiving #2 is off in the wilds, out of contact. His son is sharing a home with his mother and sister (and her baby). Another friend who was at the table is probably still around, but I have no idea where. Daughter now has her own home and two children, and is planning dinner at her place.
Daughter hasn't informed me yet, but I'm expecting a repeat of last year. She'll cook something in a kosher pot that she has put aside specifically for me, and she has dinnerware set aside specifically for me. And I'll probably go and nibble at the aperitifs and whatever veggies she cooks. It just occurred to me, as I sit here typing, that I can fix a salmon steak for myself and take it. For those of you who don't already know, I don't eat meat, including fowl.
Dang! it's tough being kosher in a non-kosher family.
My first Thanksgiving as a married woman was spent in Ada, Oklahoma. Husband was stationed at Ft Bliss. I don't recall that I cooked anything, and we probably had dinner at the O-Club.
So that's it for Memory Lane tonight.
Shalom

Feeling a bit off today, like my thoughts are all over the place while I walked around the block this afternoon. I tried to focus on the rhythm of my steps, something grounded, but the memories kept intruding. Passing that old maple tree where we used to take the kids after school brought a strange mix of comfort and quiet ache. It’s weird how a simple spot can hold so much weight, the laughter and the small fights all echoing back. I caught myself wondering if the way I handled things was good enough, or if I missed signs that could have changed everything. Sometimes it feels like the time since she’s been gone just shrinks and stretches unpredictably. I noticed how the light hit the pavement differently today, casting longer shadows, and it made me think about how life keeps moving even when you want to freeze certain moments. I suppose that’s the thing that unsettles me most—the inconsistency, not just with work but with the way grief settles in waves. Organizing my thoughts is harder when the house feels emptier, even if I keep busy. The emails and project drafts are waiting, but my mind keeps wandering back to the quiet spaces she left behind. I told myself to finish this walk and grab some water before diving into work again, hoping some fresh air would clear the fog. Instead, I’m still here, stuck between wanting to sort it all out and feeling like it’s slipping through my fingers. The scattered feeling might just be part of the process, though that doesn’t make it any easier. Maybe it’s okay not to have all the answers right now, to let the moments be what they are, even if they’re messy. At least I’m still walking, still moving forward, even if slowly and with uncertain steps.

I've decided to start journaling as an outlet for how I've been feeling since the fire a few weeks ago. In the years before I started seeing Madelaine I'd have likely bottled all of this up. I'm finding myself incapable of doing so right now; I'm unsure if this is because I would talk to Madelaine about literally everything, or if this is just too much to try to contain? Likely both.
There are many ways I'm incredibly fortunate considering the circumstances: I have a place to stay after the fire, I have a community of support to help while I try to rebuild my life from square one, and I have a job where I'm not overly worried about the financial aspects of this. Even with all this on my side I've never felt so lost as I do right now.
I've never felt so supported, and I've never felt so incredibly, cripplingly alone. Feeling and being alone has never bothered me like it does right now. I feel guilty for feeling like this right now; so many people have come out to offer support in one way or another. I have people checking up on me regularly to see if there's anything they can do to help. By all accounts I shouldn't feel like I'm alone surrounded with an all encompassing darkness; one of the greatest lights in my life is gone now, and I'm struggling to see the others in this agony.
I know Madelaine wouldn't want me to struggle like this now that she's gone. I want to keep being the person she would come to when she needed support. She supported me just as often, and her absence is something I'm having to face constantly. Every time I see a picture of her smile, every happy memory that comes to mind, every reminder of Madelaine brings with it the fresh realization she's gone. I'll never get to see her smile again. I'll never get to hear her voice excitedly detailing her latest interest again. I don't get to start and end my day with Madelaine anymore. I don't get to spend my life working to make her happy anymore.
It feels like my world stopped that night. I'm trying to move forward. I'm trying to be who Madelaine loved, but I'm struggling to find that person right now.

This morning I kept checking my phone during my break at work, waiting for a reply from my brother about taking Mom to her appointment next week. He never answered. Now it’s hours later and I’m on the couch, laptop in front of me, trying to juggle next week’s calendar and feeling like I’m missing something obvious. There’s paperwork to fill out for Mom’s insurance and I keep putting it off. I told myself I’d call the pharmacy before five but now it’s almost four and I feel frozen, staring at the list of things I meant to do. The living room is quiet except for the hum of the fridge in the other room. I keep thinking about how Dad used to handle all of this, like it was nothing. Now every call feels like a chore, every reminder a small failure. The groceries I bought are still in bags by the door. I should probably eat something but it’s easier to just sit and scroll through messages that I don’t want to answer. There’s a doctor’s voicemail from yesterday that I haven’t even listened to yet. I know I’m supposed to keep everything in order but it feels like all the little tasks are multiplying. I wish I could just cross off one thing and feel done, at least for a day.

Put down my sketchbook a few minutes ago and now just sitting here on the couch, staring at the ceiling. The apartment is quiet except for the hum of the fridge and some traffic outside, but my brain feels anything but quiet. Tried drawing something about how I feel but it came out disjointed, like I couldn’t even decide what the subject was supposed to be. She texted earlier, something about plans for the weekend, and I still haven’t replied. Not because I don’t want to, but because I actually don’t know what I want to say. Been thinking a lot about what it even means to be in a relationship again at this age. Part of me wants to just let things flow and stop overthinking, but then I get caught up in wondering if I’m just drifting or if I’m actually moving toward something real. It’s strange, I feel organized in my work, my art supplies all in place, my projects mapped out. But this other part of life feels messy and unresolved. I wish I could just ask her where she sees this going, but I know that’s not how these things work. Maybe I’ll answer her tomorrow, after some sleep. For now, I’ll just try to let the quiet settle in and hope I can actually rest tonight.

I was just reading another diarist's comments about her mother, and how close they were. And she mentioned her sister, with the comment "I need family. She needs family."
She's fortunate that she has the memory. Now I don't mean to be maudlin about this, but the fact is, I don't remember my mother. Or my father. I was raised by relatives who had good intentions, but it really isn't the same as having at least a memory.
I'm grateful for my sister, and we're close emotionally, though we live two states apart. But never mind that, in the age of Instant Messaging. We chat for a couple hours just about every day.
We have cousins, but we're not particularly close, and they live in other states, besides.
I wonder how families become so fragmented? I remember when we were kids, the whole clan would meet at the grandparents' for thanksgiving. I think occasionally one of the aunts would open her dining room, but mostly it was the grandparents. I remember the year I thought I was too big to eat with the "little kids" in the kitchen, and someone must have agreed with me because I ate in the dining room that year with the grown ups.
But back to the fragmentation. There's one cousin and his wife in Washington, but as far as I know the rest of the cousins and spouses are in Idaho. No, that's not right. There's a cousin and her husband in Las Vegas. And I don't even know if the cousins in Idaho ever get together. Isn't that pitiful? I'm closer to my friends than I am my own relatives.
I've heard it said that you can't miss what you never had, but that's not true. I don't remember my parents, and I miss them. Even after all these years, there's still that hole in the relationship-thing that's empty. I wonder frequently what it would have been like to have my own parents instead of sharing someone else's.
But, you know, I think I was a better parent for missing that in my life. I think I showed my kids a lot of physical love (one of them thought I was smothering, but that's another story). I have some things of my mother's and I treasure them. In fact, I think I'll take that sapphire ring to the jeweler and get it resized so I can wear it again.
I have pictures of both parents, and stories told by aunts and uncles, and that's enough for now.
Shalom

I need to go for a walk in the woods. Mostly to get away from cars. I have had it with cars lately. A horse would be okay, I’d take a horse with me in the woods. A nice quiet horse, one that didn’t have anything to prove and without any neurotic attachments to the barn. It’s so annoying to ride a horse that’s always thinking about going back to the barn. Just about the time you get engrossed in enjoying the way the light is bouncing off the quaking aspen leaves, or noticing the color of the big leaf maples, a horse like that will have nonchalantly turned around on you. (If horses could whistle while doing this, they would) It’s like going for an outing with someone you are having a mild disagreement with the entire time. Riding a barn sour horse can turn a normal person into a wild eyed demon in about 15 minutes. So I would take a kind of slow, dumb horse that would forget all about the barn until I told him it was time to go home. THEN I would expect him to be able to find his way back in case I get lost. If you ever meet a horse like that, let me know.
Anyway, up in the woods away from cars would be good. Up beyond the fire break road where all you can smell are pine needles and red clay, maybe some rotting leaves, that’s an okay smell. Especially compared to car exhaust. I hate cars.
Well, being the scrupulously honest person that I am, I will admit that I like being able to go places and do things with cars, but I hate ‘em anyway. They cost a cotton pickin’ fortune. They sit in the driveway and lose their value at a rate that can only be called precipitous. They are noisy. They use petroleum products that come from countries where the people hate our guts. And the really weird thing about cars is how different they are than the ones in the television commercials. Those cars almost always seem to be on a stretch of road somewhere in Iceland without another human being within 300 miles. The vast majority of cars that I see are going about 5 miles an hour on an 8 lane freeway that is LOADED with cars. I wonder where you can get one of those cars in the commercials ? If you ever find one, let me know.
And listen, when some people get into their cars, scary things begin to happen. They get in there like mild mannered Clark Kent and by the time they get to the freeway a transformation has taken place. They think they are Genghis Kahn or something. Napoleon, Sadaam Hussein, maybe and they start doing incredibly stupid things like seeing how close they can drive to the car in front of them at 75 miles an hour and live to tell about it. Or practice basket weaving using their car as the shuttle cock.
Cars can give you a false sense of security. You get in one, pile a bunch of your favorite stuff in there with you and drive far, far away from home. What happens if this modern contraption decides to break? There you are stranded alongside the road with no one around except a bunch of people who think they are. . . . Genghis Kahn !
But I WAS talking about the woods. I need to take a walk in the woods….
To be continued. . . . .
