Keys jangling in my hand, I lingered in the car a little longer than usual, watching the early sunlight hit the dashboard. My phone buzzed with a reminder about tonight’s dinner with Mark, and immediately my mind started spinning through everything that still needs to get done before then. The apartment is a mess, laundry is half-finished, and I promised my sister I’d call to check on Mom, but I’m not sure when I’ll actually have a quiet moment.

Work doesn’t let up, either. There’s a project review this afternoon, and I have to sync up with my roommate about who’s picking up groceries since last night’s attempt to plan meals for the week fell apart. I keep thinking I can squeeze in a quick run to the pharmacy for Mom’s prescription, but it’s always just out of reach with all these overlapping schedules. Mark texted late last night about wanting to talk after we eat, which just adds to the knot in my stomach. I know we’ve both been snappy lately, probably because neither of us is really getting enough downtime, but I dread another round of going in circles about who’s not listening or who’s busier.

I wish I could just press pause on everything for an hour and catch my breath, but today is already stacked. Maybe I’ll feel better once I get through the first meeting of the day and have a chance to regroup, but right now, it all feels like a scramble. The car is strangely comforting, almost like a buffer before I have to step into the usual rush. I keep telling myself it’s just a phase, but it feels like it’s been going like this for months. At some point, something has to give, and I really hope it’s not the relationships that matter most to me.

Crickets and the hum of a distant car were about the only sounds walking around the block late last night. The streetlights made these weird overlapping shadows on the sidewalk, and it actually felt kind of peaceful for a couple minutes, which I didn’t expect. My mind kept circling around the next few days, though. There’s this big exam coming up in class, and then two shifts at the restaurant back to back, plus the food cost inventory I still haven’t finished. I tried to map out how I could prep for the test during the slower moments at work, but I don’t know if I’ll have the energy to focus after dinner rush. My backpack is always loaded with notes and recipes, but I keep feeling like I’m forgetting something important, like a form I was supposed to fill out or an email I still haven’t answered.

Sometimes I wonder if I’m actually keeping up, or just treading water and hoping nothing sinks. I know I’ll get through the week, but the list of stuff just keeps growing. Still, walking in the cool air helped clear my head a little. Maybe I’ll try to squeeze in a few more of these walks, even if it’s late and I should be sleeping. At least it feels a bit more manageable right after.

The fridge light is too bright for this hour and the hum seems louder when everything else is quiet. I’m standing here staring at a half-empty carton of eggs, thinking I should probably order groceries but I can’t remember if I already did. Last night was a mess of emails and shipment updates, everything blurring together after 10 pm. I kept thinking I’d log off, just one more thing, but the notifications kept popping up and I guess I lost track. It’s weird working retail from home, like the store has crept into my house and refuses to leave. I’m tired, really tired, but my mind keeps spinning about whether I missed something important for the morning shipment. Maybe I’m overthinking, but mistakes always seem to find me when I’m not paying attention, and I don’t trust that everything’s actually handled. Remote work sounded like it would be easier than being on the floor, but now I feel like I’m always on the clock, never sure when to switch off. Got to remember to make a list for later, but right now all I want is another hour of sleep, just to clear my head. Why does it feel like there’s always more to do, no matter how much I finish? The kitchen is cold, and I’m still in pajamas. Guess I’ll try to shake this off and get on with it.

My phone buzzed at 7:10 this morning and I just stared at it. I didn’t want to check if it was a message from them yet. The light from the window was too sharp and I felt my stomach twist, even though I hadn’t eaten anything. My desk is cluttered with receipts, some loose change, a mug from last night’s tea. I keep worrying I’ll say something wrong and they’ll just quietly fade out of my life. It makes me pick at my fingernails until they hurt.

We’re still so new, but sometimes it feels like I’m always one wrong word away from things ending. I replay last night’s conversation in my head—were they being distant, or am I just overthinking? I want to ask where this is going but every time I try, my throat tightens and I just change the subject. It’s weird to care so much about someone and simultaneously want to hide. I keep reading old texts, looking for patterns, checking if there’s a shift, anything. I wish I could relax and just let things be, but I don’t know how. I haven’t told anyone how much space this takes up in my mind. I wish I could just hit pause long enough to breathe.

Tired and restless, I just sat on the couch last night, feeling the day sitting heavy on my chest. I kept replaying that argument with Marco in my head, the way his tone set me off and how I probably snapped back too fast. I can't shake the feeling that I overreacted, but things have been so tense in the kitchen lately. Every order feels like a test, and I catch myself watching every ingredient, every ounce, thinking about the numbers more than the flavors. Maybe that's why I took it personal when he said we were moving too slow. I know everyone's stressed with the new food costs, but I want them to know I'm still giving everything even if the money is tight. It's like I keep trying to prove I'm still the leader, even when I feel unsure about where things are headed. There's this fear that if I don't keep it all together, I'll lose what little hold I have on the team. I wish I could just sit and talk honestly with them about how scared I am, but I don't want to look weak. I miss the days when cooking was just about the food, not bills and egos and all this pressure. I keep hoping tomorrow will feel different, that I won't wake up with this knot in my stomach. But tonight, it just feels like I'm falling behind on all fronts, and I don't really know where it's all going anymore. Maybe I just need a few hours of sleep to clear my head. Or maybe I need to figure out who I am when I'm not standing behind that stove.

I still need to call the pharmacy about the medication refill before the weekend. It slips my mind every time I think I’ll get to it later, but now it’s pressing. Mom’s appointment got pushed to next Thursday, and I’m not sure how I’ll fit that in with work and everything else. The living room couch feels like the only place I can sit down without immediately feeling like I should be doing something else.

Trying to sort out who’s taking care of what this week is a puzzle. Dad called earlier, frustrated because he feels left out of the plan and that Mom’s health is a mystery to him now. I get where he’s coming from, but it’s another conversation that saps my energy. I want to be patient and clear, but the backlog of unfinished tasks – bills needing attention, groceries to reorder, the car servicing appointment – just piles up.

Sometimes I wonder if I’m juggling too many roles, but there’s no one else stepping in right now. I am curious about how others cope with this stretch of unpredictable demands. At least the chaos forces me to stay somewhat spontaneous in handling issues as they come, even if it’s exhausting. I hope to catch a break soon, maybe with a quiet evening and no calls, no schedules to rearrange. ☕

I spent most of the evening trying to sort out my new schedule for work and figure out the city’s confusing public transit routes. It feels like every simple errand here comes with a dozen extra steps, from finding the right bus stop to deciphering the local grocery store’s layout. Dinner was quick, just leftovers, but at least I got to sit down and breathe for a minute. I keep hoping that once I’ve settled into a routine, things won’t feel so overwhelming. Part of me is excited by the challenge, but I’m also skeptical that I’ll ever feel fully at home in a place where I still need GPS just to get to the pharmacy. I miss having friends nearby who could just come over and hang out without planning it a week in advance. There’s a meetup for nurses next weekend, and I’m debating if I have the energy to go or if I’m just making excuses to stay in. Maybe I’ll push myself to go, even if I’m tired. It’s weird to feel both optimistic and drained at the same time, but I guess that’s just part of starting over.

Kept thinking about Dad’s old mug as I poured the coffee, still can’t bring myself to use it since last winter. Stupid how an object can make things sting again, I guess.

My mind keeps bouncing from bills to Mom’s next checkup to whether I sent that document to the client or not, and then back to memories. The house feels really quiet today, almost like it’s waiting for something. I’m restless, keep opening drawers or looking out the window just to do something with my hands. Thought about calling my sister but I know it’s early and she probably doesn’t want to talk about hospital visits before breakfast. I keep telling myself I should have visited more last year, even though I know it wouldn’t have changed anything. Hard not to replay.

I left my shoes by the fridge again, which makes no sense, but that’s just how my morning brain works. Going to try to make a list for today but I know I’ll lose it or forget what was on it. Still, got to keep moving, even if it feels like I’m only half-there most mornings lately. Maybe I’ll go for a walk before work starts, just to clear my head a bit. Or maybe I’ll just sit here and watch the toaster for a while. Haven’t decided yet.

The clock on the microwave glows 11:47, and the hum of the fridge is the only noise cutting through this quiet apartment. I was drinking chamomile tea but let it go cold, again, distracted by old photos I dug out of the bottom drawer. It’s been two months since Mom passed but I keep expecting her to call, or to see her handwriting on a stray envelope. The practical part of me knows she’s gone, but the rest of me still waits for proof.

I thought grief would be more dramatic, but it’s just an ache that slips into the routine—making my bed, washing dishes, checking emails for school assignments. I keep up with my studies, probably even more focused than usual, because it fills the time and keeps the messier thoughts at bay. Sometimes I wonder if I should talk to someone, but I don’t see how that would change anything. People always say it helps, but I’m not convinced.

Tonight I noticed the light in the hallway flickers, and I made a mental note to change the bulb tomorrow. Living alone means no one else will do it. Maybe that’s not such a bad thing—at least I can have my small griefs and memories without having to explain them. I’ll probably try to sleep now, although I know my mind will wander for a while. That’s just how it is lately.
Just a quick entry before bed. Today was good. Nothing extraordinary, but solid. Sometimes that's all you need.

Feeling kind of tense this afternoon, not sure exactly how to shake it off. The bedroom desk is covered in the usual mess: post-it notes with reminders, my planner open to the week, a mug with cold tea I forgot about. I keep glancing at my phone, waiting to hear back from him about the pickup time for Ava. It’s always a negotiation, never smooth, because his schedule is all over the place and then I have to scramble to change mine. I wish I could just let things slide but I keep thinking if I was more organized, or if I could just anticipate his weird last-minute changes, then maybe Ava wouldn’t have to be shuffled around so much. It’s probably not even a big deal in the long run but it feels like a failure every single time something doesn’t line up. I keep replaying our texts in my head, analyzing if I sounded annoyed or if I should have just agreed right away instead of asking questions, but I can’t help but want some clarity. Part of me wants to just say yes to everything and be easygoing, but the other part is tired of always being the one who adjusts. Sometimes I wonder if I’m making it harder than it has to be, or if I’m just kind of stuck in this pattern of trying to control things that are basically impossible to control. The sunlight through the window is making the dust in here really obvious and I’m noticing every little thing that’s out of place, which is probably not helping. I guess I’m hyperfocused and it’s making me pick apart all the small stuff, like if I had just left work on time or if I had prepped dinner earlier, then maybe the evening wouldn’t be so rushed. I know I’m being self-critical but it’s hard to stop, especially when there’s this constant pressure to make life smooth for Ava. My mind just keeps looping through the schedule, the handoffs, the little frictions, wondering if it’ll ever feel easy. Maybe I just need to step back and let some things go, but that feels so much easier said than done. Wish I could just hit pause for a bit and breathe without thinking about the next thing I might be forgetting.

Keys are digging into my thigh through my jeans while I wait for the office doors to unlock. I’m early, which is ridiculous because I don’t even technically work here yet, but the temp agency said I should show up anyway in case they need someone. I’ve just finished reading Exodus by Leon Uris. And my mind is in a whirl of doubt, grief, speculation, anger, disappointment, and some other emotions I haven’t identified yet.
How can I have the effrontery to call myself a Jew? I’ve never laid down my life for my country. I’ve never fought enemies on all side of me for the sake of my country. I’ve never fought against all odds on all sides of me, never had an implacable enemy who wanted me dead. I’ve never even been to Israel.
I’m angry because of all the declarations, treaties, and so-called friends who deserted Israel when her enemies struck her on all sides on the day of the Declaration of Independence on 5 May 1948. The Balfour Declaration turned out to be a piece of paper with a bunch of writing on it.
When the Arab nations surrounding Israel attacked on that day, did the British come forth with help? Oh, no, we couldn’t possibly offend the Arabs. We need their oil.
A small, poorly armed army of mostly volunteers held off and beat back their sworn enemies, and even their friendly Arab neighbors stood by and watched. These very same Arab neighbors who were the recipients of their Jewish neighbors’ kindness in sharing their farming expertise; showed them how to build sturdier homes; shared sanitation, irrigation expertise, and generally improved the lives of their Arab neighbors. And, presumably, expected to live in peace with them. But when push comes to shove……
When Hitler came into power, did anyone think “Oh, my goodness! We have to help the Jews get out of Germany.” No, in fact most countries refused Jewish immigration. The British even blockaded Palestinian ports to prevent Jews fleeing deadly persecution. Eventually, even the United States, my beloved United States, limited Jewish immigration. Most countries turned a blind eye to what was happening in Germany, Poland, France, Belgium…everywhere the Germans invaded. The full horror wasn’t known until Allied troops discovered the concentration camps, and the graves, and the furnaces. Even now people are denying that the holocaust ever happened. “Jewish propaganda.”
Time and time again the Arabs attacked the new Israeli nation, and time and time again they were thrown back. Sneak attacks. Full frontal attacks. Coordinated attacks. Attacks on Yom Kippur when Jews are in the synagogues, totally unprepared for war. Yet, the Israelis again defeated their enemies, and even drove them back beyond their borders.
There’s so much more to say, but that’s history. Let’s go on….to the present day.
Here’s an item on the Internet from Council for the National Interest
dated 18 September 2004. Title WHO’S OBSTRUCTING PEACE PROSPECTS?
I quote the last paragraph of a totally one-sided blog:
Why is the United States continuing to insist on sidelining Arafat and embracing Sharon who has rejected American peace initiatives and undermined the war on terrorism?
Whoever wrote that doesn’t read the paper or watch the television news. How many times has Sharon acceded to Arafat’s demands, and Arafat turned around and said “It’s not enough.”? When did Arafat ever rein in Hamas, his organ of terrorism?
Take a look at a map of the Middle East and see if you can figure out why Sharon won’t give up the West Bank. If you can’t see it, I’ll be glad to point it out. The Gaza, OK. That was traditionally Philistia (Palestine according to the Roman translation). Let the Arabs have it. The West Bank, never!
If the other Arabs are so concerned about their poor, mistreated brothers in the Gaza, why don’t they send in medicine, food, clothing, and put up decent housing? And get rid of the terrorist cells in the Gaza. Israel won’t prevent that. But, no, that would spoil their propaganda about Israeli mistreatment of the “prisoners” in the Gaza.
Oh, yes, and the Saudis forbid the presence of a Jew in their country.
Why is it when a busload of Israeli innocents and children is bombed, the world goes tsk, tsk. But when Israel retaliates and bombs a known terrorist area, the whole world gets up in arms about the horrible, vindictive, unreasonable Israelis?
Tell me, now, WHO is obstructing the peace prospects?????
Peace, peace. When? In my lifetime? Unlikely. I mourn.

The scattered pieces of the day’s code bugs and my half-finished tea cup mirror the way my thoughts won’t line up. I want to fix this, but it also feels like trying to hold water in my hands. Maybe tonight I’ll say something, or maybe I’ll just listen harder. Either way, I’m tired of pretending everything’s fine when it isn’t. The apartment feels too small for both our silences, and I hate feeling so stuck between wanting to reach out and not knowing how.

The hum of the fridge is the loudest thing in the kitchen right now, almost drowning out my own thoughts as I eat leftover pasta, fork scraping against the chipped ceramic bowl. Last night spun out longer than I planned—the talk we had about my dad’s health just kept circling in my head. I wanted to say something comforting to her, to both of us really, but the words got tangled and all I managed was a long, quiet hug. She seemed tired too, her eyes heavy, and I kept wondering if she felt as adrift as I did. I know I should be more present, more open, but sometimes it’s like my mind is jumping from one half-finished painting to the next, and I can’t hold a single thought for long. The phone buzzed with a message from my sister, just a simple “call me when you can,” and I still haven’t replied. Guilt sits with me, just behind the ribs, because I don’t want to talk about hospital visits or test results anymore, but I know I need to. I promised myself I’d try harder to let her in, to not shut down when things get heavy. Maybe tonight I’ll try again, softer, and just listen more. Breathing slows a little now, the kitchen clock ticking steady as if reminding me to just take things one moment at a time.

What the heck is wrong with me? I'm getting thin skinned and edgey again, and taking offense at things that aren't worth the calorie expenditure.
On a forum yesterday, run by a friend in cyberspace, I encountered a person who personified the reason I don't want to do private practice. Let's call her CanineExpert. (My God, I'm giving pseudonyms to pseudonyms now.) My friend's dog is having skin problems, and CanineExpert was giving advice on ways to approach it. There was nothing wrong with the advice, which centered around dietary changes. I'd have gone about things a little differently, but nothing the CanineExpert said was incorrect. Then I came across this post from her:
CanineExpert: Doesn't surprise me. Corn is a known allergen.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
while it doesn't bother every dog, mine have a problem with it, and both dogs have pigmentation. Dogs that have a lot of white background color, are much more prone to skin problems, than those with pigmentation.
Wheat has been a problem for some dogs too. Unfortunately, we have to do our own research regarding foods. Veterinarians have little knowledge about nutrition. If they did, they would not recommend some of the foods they do...Science Diet being one of them IMHO, which uses suspected cancer-causing chemicals as preservatives. A very over-rated food IMHO. Vets only get a few hours of "education" regarding nutrition, which is usually taught by a food manufacturer. My vet is the LAST person I would ever ask for advice regarding nutrition.
Huh? If her vet is the last person she'd ask for advice, then she needs to change vets. Anyhow, this is where I made the tactical error. I should have just walked away from it. She's a little off-base with things, but then people who have negative experiences with something (like a specific brand of pet food) tend to be prejudiced toward or away from things. But no, my nose was out of joint. Besides, she had far too many opinions for them to be considered "humble".
Salamander: Who told you THAT?
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I'm a vet. My vet school had a full semester's course in nutrition, and another full semester's course in skin diseases that featured atopy heavily because it is such a common problem in dogs. Lamb protein and rice carbs were recommended as a good first start for any suspected food allergy.
By the way, I never had ANY class taught by a manufacturer, be it food manufacurer, pharmacological representive, or breeder. And I don't know any fellow veterinarian who has, unless it was post-grad continuing education, which we all take with a grain of salt.
Of course, that was either the first or second salvo (depending on how you look at it) in outright incivilities.
CanineExpert: Who told me that? A vet told me that, and even spoke about it
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
in front of a large breed group meeting out of State, that I personally attended. This vet was well-known in his State, and owned more than one clinic, and was highly-respected. I have also been told this by other vets. And this vet had no qualms about stating how little education he received in a top vet school about nutrition.
I'm no kid, I am 61, have had many vets over the years, and I have yet to meet one, who had any real knowledge about nutrition. I handle pets for many people, and have for a number of years. And I can tell you that they often have "no clue" when it comes to food.
So she personally attended (as opposed to impersonally attended) this meeting and is now an expert based on what this vet (who apparently has some problems with his fellow professionals) said. Frankly, I'm sorry he didn't get any education in this department, but it was unfair of him to paint the whole profession with his own personal paintbrush. Part of me wonders when this guy graduated, since many nutritional courses were only instituted fifteen or so years ago. But that's neither here nor there. Checking the AVMA convention schedule, which arrived in my mailbox yesterday, there are over fifteen hours of continuing education credits devoted to small animal nutrition. If he didn't get the classes in school, he has no excuse for not getting them after graduation. Which isn't the point. I
am
curious how being 61 years-of-age qualifies CanineExpert as a better nutritional consultant than someone who went to vet school, but who am I to argue?
Salamander: Ah, good point.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I am quite disappointed to discover that my semester of nutrition, followed by three separate rotations in different species nutritional requirements, supplemented with two years of of working with a prominent zoo's animal nutritionist (board certified) has done nothing to advance my knowledge in the field. I'll have to write my alma mater and complain about that.
I still have a decade and a half to go until I reach 61. My comparative youth and my lack of education (as pointed out by a fellow veterinarian) forces me to tender an apology to you.
Now, let's face it, there's a lot of self-made experts out there. Some are actually quite knowledgeable. I've learned a lot from people who raise the animals I see. But this person's attitude about my profession simply boiled me. And now I'm not even in a position to tell my friend about the proper way to go about an elimination diet to check for food allergies because I've been rude on her board to one of her friends.
I should have stayed a paralegal.

It's a quiet morning for me, full of cozy introspection. There's coffee in my mug, and I'm wrapped up in a blanket with the Christmas lights giving off this warm glow around me. The house is calm. It feels peaceful. Yesterday was a whirlwind. We hosted Christmas Eve at our place, and even though it was smaller than usual—just my parents, D's mom, and us—it felt full. We had prime rib, mashed potatoes, roasted vegetables, and this cranberry-orange tart I made that turned out way better than I expected. The tart was a gamble since I've never made one before, but I'm glad I tried. Everyone seemed to enjoy it. D's mom brought cookies she'd made—snickerdoodles and these almond shortbread things that were incredible. We ate too much, laughed a lot, and exchanged gifts. It was simple and lovely. This morning, D and I exchanged our gifts to each other. He got me a beautiful journal with a leather cover and some fancy pens because he knows I've been wanting to write more by hand. I got him a new watch and a book he's been eyeing for months. We're both happy. It's funny—Christmas doesn't feel like it used to when I was a kid. It's less about the presents and more about the quiet moments. The way the lights look in the early morning. The way D's face softens when he's opening a gift. The way my mom laughed last night when we were playing cards. I'm grateful for these small, tender things. I know not everyone feels peaceful today. Some people are grieving. Some are lonely. Some are stressed or overwhelmed. I'm thinking of them, too. Sending love to anyone who needs it today. I hope you find a moment of peace, even if it's just for a second.

Tried to piece together what I’m feeling about my work lately, but honestly, the thoughts kept jumping around — like I want to push in new directions but also keep some stability. Family noise was faint but present, reminding me privacy here is rare, so moments like this walk are more important than I usually admit.

The walk helped a bit, but the jumble of feelings about identity and purpose in my work and life didn’t settle fully. Maybe I’m just overthinking because of the buzz at home. I learned fast in a day and still can to some point. Waiting for my chair to become available and my on time is 11:45 AM.

I am not pretending I know everything. I am not giving advises for people to follow. It is not necessary to take up my point of view, nobody obliged.
I know where I stand and I know what I believe in. And so does anybody around. It is a “problem” of interaction that “causes all the problems”. We interact in many ways, on many levels: informative, emotional, physical, spiritual, godknowswhichelse…
If we would’ve been more “simpleir”, we would have much less of a pain that normally accompanies any relationship, friendship or love or kindred…I am not saying for all – to start to be unsophisticated at once. Just we need to be aware and allow some tolerance for this.
Where two can share something very special on emotional level, they might follow different religions; where two can have same interests, they might be completely “deaf” to the body language of each other; where two live together in perfect harmony as a couple, they might not share their dreams with each other…
What defines close friends – how many interactive links they’ve got in synch, how many bridges they’ve built and also – how much tolerance they have for each other.
Be kind to your friend, despite of opposite views on certain things. ACCEPT them as they are and be there for them no matter how universally far apart your views might be.
Tolerance could serve as a measure unit for the value of the friendship. [*not that I believe one should ever wonder about its value anyway – friendship should be either there or not, doesn't it?]

There’s a chipped mug in my hand and I never noticed that before, maybe it’s always been like this or maybe I’m just more distracted than usual. I told myself I was going to apply to at least five positions today but after the weird conversation I had with Marcus this morning, my head’s just buzzing. He was mad about the shower schedule again, or at least I think he was, but halfway through explaining why he needs the bathroom at 7:15 sharp, he switched to asking about my job search and then back to the water bill. I tried to answer but my words came out jumbled and he just gave me that look, like he’s annoyed but doesn’t want to say it. I kind of snapped, which I regret, but I was already feeling off balance and there’s something about the way he hovers that makes me defensive. Not that I was even sure what we were arguing about by the end. Did I agree to cover his half of the bill this month? I can’t remember, and I don’t want to bring it up again because that’ll just make things more awkward. I keep thinking about how much easier life would be if I had my own place, but then again, I don’t even have steady work right now, so that’s just wishful thinking. My brain feels like it’s running in circles, bouncing from job sites to roommate drama to wondering if I should just get a coffee refill or go home and nap. I saw an email pop up from a recruiter but I haven’t opened it yet, not sure if I’m ready for more rejection or even another interview. I wish I could just focus for more than a few minutes at a time, but today my mind is foggy and I keep getting distracted by the noise around me and my own worries. Maybe tomorrow will be better. For now, I guess I’ll just sit here a bit longer, try to collect myself, and maybe actually start the next application if I can remember my login details.

Still, I pulled together enough focus to finish the most urgent reports on time. The fridge hums a little louder than usual, and the afternoon sun is slanting through the blinds, making weird stripes on the kitchen counter. Lunch break, but it doesn’t feel like much of a break. I just microwaved leftovers and scrolled through emails with one hand while eating. My tablet is sitting open next to the sink, mocking me with half-finished sketches and a long to-do list. Sometimes it feels like the days just blur together, each one packed with video calls, client edits, and messages that need replies right away.

I thought working remotely would give me more space to breathe, but lately it’s just meant the boundaries are gone. I’m trying to focus on the positives—at least I don’t have a commute, and I can wear paint-stained sweatpants all day if I want. Still, I can’t shake this tired, restless feeling, like I’m never fully caught up. Maybe I’m just being hard on myself, but I need to figure out a better system before I burn out. For now, I’ll just finish this cold rice and hope inspiration hits before my next call.

The hum of my old desk lamp is louder than usual tonight, or maybe I’m just noticing it more because my brain won’t shut up. There’s a pile of textbooks on the left, grease-stained work gloves on the right, and my planner somewhere under the mess. Sometimes I wonder if I’ll ever figure out how to juggle all this. Work at the garage ran late again because some guy’s truck wouldn’t start and he was in a bad mood, but honestly, I kind of liked the challenge. I feel more at home around engines than I do with most people at school. Still, I have a paper due tomorrow, and my head is full of torque specs instead of essay ideas. Balancing shifts, classes, and homework is starting to wear me out, but I keep telling myself it’s temporary. Once I get my certification, maybe things will slow down, or at least I can afford to work fewer hours. I know I’m lucky to have a job I actually care about, but that doesn’t make tonight’s workload any lighter. My roommate poked her head in a few minutes ago to ask if I wanted dinner, but I just grabbed a granola bar and waved her off. Some days, I’m proud of how much I’m handling, and other days, I want to just drop everything and sleep for a week. I guess that’s normal. Anyway, I’m going to try to get through a chapter before I crash. If I can just keep moving forward, that’s enough for now.

This morning, I was filling Dad’s pill organizer at the kitchen table, and realized I’d done it out of order again. The clock on the microwave said 6:13, but it felt much earlier. I could hear the refrigerator humming, louder than usual, or maybe that was just me. The cereal boxes were stacked unevenly on the counter, next to the crossword puzzle I’d half-finished last night. Dad shuffled in, asking if it was Saturday. I told him it was Thursday, but he looked at me blankly, so I just nodded and helped him sit down. The tea kettle whistled, and I actually jumped—my nerves are shot lately. I handed him his morning meds with a glass of water and tried to remember if I’d taken mine. There’s a heaviness in the kitchen, not just from the damp air, but from the routine itself. I keep thinking I should be able to manage this better, being a therapist, but the practical side of care is different than giving advice to others. I miss things—appointments, calls, sometimes meals. It’s hard to keep track. My mind feels thick, like everything is moving through molasses. Still, I caught myself hoping today would be a little smoother, maybe Dad will have a good day, maybe I’ll remember to eat lunch. I’m tired but trying to stay grounded. There’s no big insight, just the slow work of getting through the morning, one task at a time.

Well, hello there! It’s been a minute, eh? More like 20+ years, I think, but I still remember and think about many of you fondly.



As the entry title suggests, I’m presently unsure what I want to do with this new writing pad. I'm thinking it will be a personal journal-commonplace book combo – a diary of sorts, but also a place to store and share quotations, photos, recipes, etc. If I remember correctly, my Open Diary entry titles all included an ampersand (e.g., This & That, Pride & Joy, etc.). These days, though, I’m fond of six-word phrases, and that’s what I plan to use.



You’ll no doubt be pleased that I don’t intend to recap the last 20 years in this entry. Let’s just go with ten “me now” bullet points, instead:



• I have a milestone approaching in September 2026 -- my 70th birthday!



• I’m still married to Hubster, and this year we’ll celebrate 42 years of (mostly) wedded bliss.



• I’ll need find a new handle for Teenster here since he’s now a husband, father and CEO.



• I’ve lived in Mexico for the past six years, moving here shortly before the pandemic hit. We’re on the Baja Peninsula – where the desert meets the sea – and I love it… most of the time...



• The summer months are brutal here with Heat + Humidity + Hurricanes. That first year, because of the pandemic, we had no choice but to stay here "sweltering in place." After things opened back up, we escaped to and explored some of Mexico’s cooler, mountainous regions. A couple of years ago, tired of spending my summers in ill-equipped airbnbs, I used inherited funds to buy a “summer place” in the Lake Chapala area. It’s a 45-minute drive from the Guadalajara airport and claims to have “the second-best climate in the world.” While I can’t find confirmation for that, it is temperately lovely, charmingly artistic and quite popular with U.S. and Canadian expats.



• I’m still working on learning Spanish, even though it’s possible to exist at both of those locations without it. If that hadn’t been the case, I suspect I’d have used something other than Duolingo for my tutoring. That said, I’ve been a consistent Duolingoist, and my current streak is at 2080 days. To put that in perspective, if I do another 2080 days the date will be Sunday, September 14, 2031. 😯



• As of Summer 2025, we have a new “summer place” and I’m now a landlord for the first time. A lovely couple from Colorado recently leased my Lake Chapala property and will move there later this year. Our new condo is in Washington State, where I was born and where my adorable granddaughter lives with her parents. We live on an island there, in a cute little downtown area that’s about a five-minute walk to the ferry terminal. Most of this summer was spent making our new place comfortable (thank goodness for Amazon since we moved in with nothing but suitcases), but I plan to explore and enjoy the area thoroughly in 2026.



• All of those abodes are in areas with excellent walking scores. I prefer not to drive these days. My mom and stepdad were involved in a horrible automobile accident in 2008; happily, though, both recovered (eventually… somewhat) to live a few more years. I was in charge of the accident aftermath, however, and the event traumatized me.



• This introductory entry is A LOT longer than I intended it to be.



I also intended to end this with a photo of this morning's sunrise, but it looks like I still have some things to learn about Prosebox. I'm off to do that now...

I can hear the hum of my laptop fan as I sit at my bedroom desk, finishing up another round of shift schedules. My phone keeps buzzing with messages from the team about shift swaps and coverage, and it feels like I’ve spent the whole evening answering them. The new inventory system rollout was supposed to make things easier, but now there are more questions from the night crew than before. It’s hard to keep everything straight when the notifications never stop.

Remote work was supposed to give me more control, but it’s like the workday just stretches out into the night. I caught myself snapping at Jen earlier when she asked if I could help with the dishes. I feel bad about that. We barely talked at dinner, mostly just sat in silence while I read emails on my phone. I know she’s frustrated with how distracted I am lately, but I don’t know how to switch off work when it’s always here.

I keep telling myself I’ll set better boundaries. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try leaving my phone in the other room after 8pm, at least for a night. Right now I just want the team to stop messaging for a couple hours so I can actually unwind. Even as I write this, I’m thinking about the morning’s call and whether I missed anything urgent. It’s exhausting, but I’m not sure what else to do.

Cold air against my face walking past the neighbor’s hedge, phone buzzing in my pocket. I keep glancing at emails because technically I’m on work hours, but my brain refuses to focus. Kind of pointless to take this walk if I’m still half in the spreadsheet, but staying inside was making me twitchy. Noticed the same delivery truck I saw two days ago, driver waving at me like we’re old friends. I should really set firmer boundaries with work, but I keep telling myself I’ll try again tomorrow. Hard not to feel guilty for not being more productive, even though I know no one is watching except me. Listened to a podcast for a minute, couldn’t keep track of what they were saying, so I turned it off and tried to just walk. Sometimes I wonder if this is what burnout looks like, or if I’m just lazy. I made a mental note to check the mailbox and forgot until I got home. Back now, shoes still on, thinking about dinner and whether it’s worth checking Slack one more time. My thoughts feel scattered today, but at least I got some fresh air.

Today in the warehouse, the conveyor jammed right when I was trying to clear it fast enough to meet the quota. Got a bit of sweat and cursing out of me. On the bus ride home now, staring out the window but not really seeing anything. My head’s spinning over that conversation I had with her last night—trying to figure out if she’s really into this or just being polite. It’s weird how you can analyze every little thing someone says when you’re unsure. Meanwhile, I’m supposed to be decompressing after a long shift, but all I can think about is what this means for us, if anything. The weight of work is still on my shoulders; my back aches, and my feet are killing me. Every bump of the bus makes me flinch, reminding me how physical the job is. I wonder if I’m just overthinking the whole relationship thing because it’s new and unfamiliar. Maybe I should just drop it and focus on what I know, but my brain won’t let me. I keep replaying our last moments together and trying to read between the lines, which probably just makes a mess of it all. I feel like I’m stuck in this loop of doubt and need some clarity, but it’s not coming anytime soon. How do people handle this stuff without breaking down? Tomorrow’s shift is early, and I know I’ll be dragging both physically and mentally. Wish I could just shut the noise off for a bit.

I can't sleep, which is not unusual. My mind is a mass of thoughts and emotions. 
36 years ago, at this time of night, I was at my cousin Tony's house, spending the night, knowing that my father and brother were leaving for Louisiana during the night. The last words I remember hearing Daddy say were the familiar "Goodnight and goodbye" he would say when he'd be leaving while we were asleep.


And at this time that night, he was probably already on his way to Louisiana, thankfully without my brother, whose asthma had decided to flare up suddenly, as it did a lot when we were kids.
The next morning, I woke up when I heard a car pull into the driveway at Cleta and Kenneth's house (Tony's parents). I looked out the window and saw my cousin Donny driving Mama's car, with my little brother in tow. The first thing I thought was, "Ooooh, Daddy is gonna be MAAAD that he's driving that" He didn't like anyone but Mama, him, or my sister to drive any of their vehicles. 


I raced back to the bed, once I realized Johnny was coming to get me. If anything, I was just irritated, because Mama had a habit of wanting us to come home what felt like the crack of dawn, when we spent the night anywhere. So I dashed back to the bed and pretended to be asleep. 


My baby brother, who was only 11 years old, came in to talk to me, and after "waking me up", he said, "There was an accident. One of them is dead, but we don't know which one."
I was not confused. There was only one person he could have been talking about - our truck driver father. In a move that completely surprised me, I said a prayer for my father, asking God to let him be alive. 


I knew better when we got to our home. The first person I saw was my sister coming out the door I was about to go in, her face red and puffy, with tears streaming down her face. That's when I knew, somewhere inside me, but I didn't want to believe the hunch, until someone said it.


Someone took me into my bedroom, where my Mama and Memaw (her mother) were, and Mama told me that Daddy had been killed in an accident on the highway in Jennings, Louisiana that morning. I still remember how blank my head felt, not knowing what to think, say, or do. I think I cried with my mother and grandmother a little, but I couldn't swear to that. 


Then I went out of my room and saw Nanny, Daddy's mother. That was one of the worst experiences of my life. She was FRANTICALLY pacing all over the place, repeating "Liebe Gottes" over and over and over again. She looked insane, and I have no doubt that at that moment, she really was.


I really don't remember too much more about that first day, December 20, except that I realized my mother was on auto-pilot and not able to think clearly at all. That actually continued for a few years afterwards, though not to the same extent. 


Meanwhile, I got the present Daddy had gotten for me - The Supremes's Merry Christmas album, and I played it about forty million times in a row, without pause. To this day, I still cry when I listen to that, because it helped me keep myself going during what I would later call "The day my world exploded."


I miss my father. A lot. We only had about one truly peaceful year with each other, when we'd finally started working out our differences, and then he was gone. I was 14. I still needed him there. 


All these years later, I still keep a portrait of him hanging on my wall, and my great-grandson, Alex, is totally fascinated with that portrait, which makes me happy. I keep wondering if Daddy can see his little look alike great-great-grandchild. It's curious, since there is no genetic connection, how Alex turned out looking so much like Daddy and me both. 


I'm sad, but I'm not destroyed. I just miss my dad, and I wonder what he'd be like right now, at age 79, when he only got to live to be 43. It still gobsmacks me every time I realize I'm older than him.


I wonder if he'd like me or approve of the way I am with my family. Would he and Laurie have liked each other, or would they have been mortal enemies? But I guess I won't ever know.
It gives me some peace and happiness to think they've met now, and they are both nothing but love anymore, so all is well, and they are happy to know one another. 


When I get to go home, it will be a most happy time for me, because I believe I will be with them and so, so many others I have known, loved, and lost. That has removed a fear of my own mortality, too. 


Rest in peace, Hermann Friedrich. I love you and miss you.

Maybe it's the roundness of the number. Maybe it's because I know a lot of people who are 24 now, and so I'm confronted even more thoroughly with what it means that she never got older. Mostly it's that as I build my life, every good piece of it forces me to recognize again what was stolen from her. I wonder what kind of adult she would have been. Would she be the kind of person I'd call when I was stuck in my head? Would we still laugh at inside jokes from second grade? Would we still know each other at all? I wish she were here to ask. I am on an antibiotic that's making me feel pervasively like shit. As though it must work by pervasively toxifying all of my tissues in a way that I can survive but the bacteria (hopefully) cannot. I am extremely sensitive to antibiotics. I'm allergic to a bunch of them and have dreadful side effects from all the rest. I'm not going to complain of it to my doctor though. ...Maybe I should, but I know that it always results in me having to stop my current course and restart a new course of a different antibiotic, back at day zero. Only to discover that I have equally bad effects from the new drug. And then maybe be advise to quit that one, and start yet another new antibiotic, again at day zero. Only to get equally bad effects. Only to eventually be told that I'll just need to power through it. So I'm skipping to the "just power through it" part. Instead of prolonging the total time I need to suffer through antibiotics. Because I really do need to get rid of this infection. Which I have because, I am biological and therefore I am food. I'm just protein. I am decaying. Everything is decaying. Due to entropy. And we can only fight entropy for so long. But we will fight it. Because it is an inextricable feature of our make up. Predetermined since the inception of the universe. Programmed into our genetic code by billions of years of natural selection. A cold and egoless clockworks which there is no satisfaction in trying to defeat or one-up. And no possibility of defeating. Every move we make, is the move we were predetermined to make. Nothing is an error or glitch or side-effect. It is only an effect. An outcome. The only outcome. But still we must fight. Even the ego involved in throwing down ones arms and renouncing the fight would be a combat strategy. Uh oh. Recursion again. I'll get stuck in a loop. This fight is like a fever dream I'm stuck in. And time passes very slowly. I can hardly sleep, and when I do my restless dreams are marked by constant urgencies to resolve, so I wake up entirely unrested in a puddle of perspiration. And with a massive headache. My chest, my throat, my esophagus burn with the sort of acid I normally only get when there are problems to be solved. During my limited free time at the college, I have been looking for what psychologists have to say about diaries and people who read them. Unfortuately, I only found one good article. *@ keepmedia.com* I found it interesting and I think you will too.
Ever since teenagers discovered sex, they've hardly been able to think about anything else, and that has had a major effect on the psychic life of girls. For them, it's been one long downhill skid for their sense of self-worth.
This anguished view of adolescence emerges from the mouths of babes themselves, and Cornell University social historian Joan Jacobs Brumberg has been listening to them, studying the diaries girls have written over the last 150 years.
In bygone days, girls routinely revealed rich inner lives with talk about spirituality, books, intellectual and creative activities, and the pursuit of arts and games. A typical teen of 1890 confided to her diary her dance and calisthenics activities, her elaborate plans for nature walks to collect botany specimens--a passion she shared with her friends--and long talks with female teachers who served as mentors.
Today, inner life has been overtaken by the quest for boys' attention, and with beauty and grooming. It's strictly "Joey told Suzie that David loves Linda." No provocative ideas. No interest in creative activities. Girls first began to cut loose in the Roaring Twenties, and being attractive to the opposite sex has since become the top teen interest.
Adolescent girls today are "overwhelmed with insidious feelings of unworthiness and low self-esteem as they obsess about boys and body image at the expense of more fruitful activities," says Brumberg, who calls it a national tragedy, since it occurs at a time when all kinds of new opportunities and freedoms are open to young women. Girls today wind up tense, uneasy, and vulnerable to a variety of behavioral problems and diseases, including eating disorders and sexually transmitted diseases.
Not that she would even consider putting the genie back in the bottle. She'd keep sexual liberalism but give it feminist footing, and she'd pay the creative efforts of young women some higher compliment than "I love your shoes."
Well, that's all for now. I got to go. Later, I real entry. Later

Maybe that’s what being patient actually looks like, not the calm kind but the adjusting kind. Still, I can feel this jittery energy in my legs, like I want to get up and run somewhere, but here I am chewing slowly and trying to remember if I emailed my professor back. I wish I could just do things in the moment, drop everything and take Maya to the park if the weather’s nice, but it never lines up that simply. I left the conversation feeling both relieved it was over and annoyed at myself for not being more open. There’s this nagging feeling that I’m missing some step in how to build a life here. Setting personal boundaries are like identifying the gates in our invisible fence lines which protects the precious heart and soul inside our bodies. Many people look at boundaries as walls, but rather when we establish healthy boundaries it provides a way to distinguish what we choose to let in and let out. They form flexible gates, not stationary walls It is important to learn about setting healthy boundaries so we can make decisions about what is and what isn’t permissible in all relationships.
Boundaries are valuable
All relationships work more harmoniously when the participants know what to expect and what is expected of them. Being kind, but firm when stating what you need from a relationship allows the other person to reciprocate. How other people act and think often has nothing to do with you, but rather with their own perceptions. You can only take care of yourself.
It doesn’t matter how elaborate the fencing and eloquent our statements are, if we don’t honor ourselves enough to draw the line and stick to it consistently. It is just as valuable to the other person that they learn how to be with you and what the guidelines are for the relationship.
Body Language and tone of voice
Verbal communication is the language of information and only 20 % is absorbed. Body language and tone of voice is the language of relationships and 80% is remembered. Make sure you appear confident and you speak with a neutral, calm and non-accusing tone when establishing your boundaries. Use “I” statements which reflect on how things affect you, rather than “you” statements which put people on the defensive.
4 Step model for setting boundaries
1. Calmly inform the other person by stating, “I feel uncomfortable and want to shut down when you yell at me.”
2. Request that they honor your boundary. “I ask that you talk to me without yelling.” Or ..For me to listen and hear what you are saying to me, I need to you speak to me in a calm voice without yelling.
3. Insist that they honor your boundary, again with a firm but kind voice, “I insist that when we are talking we talk in calm voices.”
4. Leave the situation. Now is not the time or place to continue communicating with someone who refuses to respect your boundaries. Leave the door open to talk later in a more respectful manner. Continue to maintain a calm but firm voice and say, “I will not continue this conversation in this way. I welcome an opportunity to talk with you without yelling or screaming at another time. Let me know if you decide to visit without raised voices.”
Don’t take it personally
You can not assume responsibility for other people’s feelings, agendas or methods of communication. You can only state how you desire to be treated in life. If there are old patterns, it may take some time to convince others that you are serious about sticking to your boundaries. Everyone has the right to be treated with respect and courtesy.
People you know may be surprised at first when you tell them they have crossed the line, but will respect you more in the end. Hopefully, they will model this communication style and it will make for more honest and open relationships for all.

The remote for the TV went missing again tonight and I spent like twenty minutes digging around in the couch cushions, pulling up old wrappers, a pen that doesn’t work, even a sock I thought I lost last week. It’s honestly annoying how nothing ever stays where it’s supposed to in this house. I keep thinking about how I want my own space, my own room at least, but with my brothers and parents all crammed in here, privacy is just not a thing. I ended up sprawled on the couch after everyone went to bed, just staring at the ceiling and letting my head buzz with all the stuff from work today—so many boxes, the endless beep of scanners, the heavy thud of pallets on concrete. Sometimes when I get in the zone at work, nothing else matters, I just focus on moving fast, stacking things right, double-checking the labels. Hours skip by and I barely notice, and yet when I get home it’s like everything slows down and I’m hyperaware of every tiny noise in the house. The fridge kicked on around midnight and I nearly jumped. I wish I could just turn my brain off, but instead I end up running through lists in my head—what I need to do tomorrow, what I could’ve done better today, whether I’ll ever get out of this rut. Still, I try to remind myself that I’m young and things can change. Maybe I’m just impatient, but I want more, and I keep telling myself that just working hard now is going to pay off. The TV remote turned up in the laundry basket, of all places. I laughed out loud, but no one was awake to hear me. It felt weirdly good to be the only one awake, even if it was just for a few minutes, with the house quiet except for the hum from the fridge and the streetlights shining through the blinds. I need to sleep but my mind’s still racing, thinking about how tomorrow I’ll do even better, maybe save a little more money, maybe get a little closer to moving out. I don’t know, I just have to keep believing things will get better.

Ermygosh, I'm tired! I feel like I need one more day to recover from our full Christmas break! Friday afternoon/evening we did our trip up to winter park and The Glide skating loop with Tom & Nic's family and it was really fun! The roads were still terrible, but we just took our time and made it there & back safely. The full moon was really pretty on the ride, though! The park was pretty busy when we arrived, but darkness was starting to set in and most people were wrapping things up and heading out. It worked out great! The park was on the edge of town and host to a regular skating rink, a sledding hill, and The Glide, the .8 mile skating loop thru the woods. The Glide is new within the last 2 years and has become a pretty big attraction since it's the first of its kind in our state. Here's a quick vid from YouTube to give you a better idea … WeWisconsin Travel Subscribe We changed into our skates right away and hit the ribbon first. The sun was just finishing to set and so by the time we got into the woods to skate, we appreciated their motion-activated lights scattered throughout. We also brought some headlights to wear and between the two it helped light our way. The ribbon itself is maintained by a zamboni and it was fairly smooth for an outdoor sheet of ice, but still quite the work-out between the natural bumps and the gradual inclines thru the woods. It was so pretty skating thru the woods, though – especially with all the snow on our trees right now! My friend, Nic, and her daughter, K (Chance's "girlfriend"), skating hand-in-hand. Hubs & I. The kids REALLY loved the loop and went around at least 5x! Our tender, adult feet - LOL - were still getting used to being in our skates again for the first time this year, however, and so we didn't quite make it that many times. This morning I nearly walked out the door still wearing my slippers. The kettle was whistling, my phone dinging, and I couldn’t remember if I’d packed my lunch or not. Sometimes it feels like everything I need to remember just slips through my fingers, and by the time I get to work, I’m already exhausted. I had to laugh at myself as I stood there in mismatched shoes, but honestly, it was a close call.

Now it’s lunchtime and the classroom is finally quiet. I’m sitting at my desk, picking at a tuna sandwich and trying to keep my eyes open. There’s a stack of ungraded papers next to me, and I keep glancing at them, but I can’t bring myself to start. The hum of the old radiator is the only sound, and for a second, I just sit there and let myself breathe. My mind keeps drifting to him and the uncertainty of everything.

I replay snippets of our last conversation, wondering if I came across as too needy or not interested enough. He texted me late last night, just a few lines, and I’ve been analyzing every word since. I want to trust what’s happening, but it all feels so fragile, and I’m not sure if I’m protecting myself or just pushing away something good. Being in a new relationship at this age is nothing like I expected—it’s both exciting and terrifying, and I wish I could take a break from second-guessing everything.

There are still lessons to plan, emails to answer, and a parent meeting after school, but all I want is an hour to nap. My head aches a bit, and my body is heavy. Maybe tonight I’ll just order takeout and let myself watch something mindless. I keep telling myself to take it one thing at a time, but today that feels impossible. I hope tomorrow is a little lighter.

Just got back from a slow walk around the block, the kind you take when your thoughts are too loud to stay inside. The streetlights cast that yellow glow over the cracked sidewalk and my shoes scuffed in a rhythm that kept me a little grounded. It was late, probably close to midnight, and the houses were all dark except for a few fuzzy blue TVs flickering through curtains. My phone buzzed in my pocket—her name on the screen—but I didn’t answer. Couldn’t decide if I wanted to talk or just keep walking forever.

I keep replaying our last conversation in my head, going over every word I said and everything I wish I’d said differently. Why is it so hard to know what I want? I analyze every gesture, every silence, wondering if I’m too much, too intense, not enough of something else. I think I’m afraid of this going nowhere but also afraid of it going somewhere I can’t predict or control. The night air was chilly, and I kept my hands stuffed in my jacket, wishing I could just shut my brain off for a minute. I’m tired—tired in my bones—but even after the walk, I don’t feel any closer to answers.

Today *or should I say yesterday, the entry says tomorrow, anywho* while chatting with honey, I decided to go more into my past. One reason for it is so you can better understand me. It may not always be chronlogical, but try to stick with me. Maybe one day I'll put it in order.
Well, since it's the fourth of July, I thought it'd be approiate to talk about when my brother got shot. WHy that, cause, he got shot 5 years ago on this day. Here's how it happened. Ok, so we move into this new area right. We don't know that many ppl. But my brother has to associate with some Northtianos. *northerners (it translated to english), mexican gang of young ppl born and raised her in America* FOr awhile things were ok till he start fighting with Southtianos. *southerners, mexican gang of young ppl born in Mexico, and raised there* And won every fight. THey did not like that. So on July 4, 1996 they decided to come at night 5 cars deep. THey start coming out their cars. I run in the house, I'm like what do I do. * in the meanwhile they surrond my big bro and his friends out there* So I decide to do one of the dumbest things I've ever done. Serious. So we call ambulance after seeing the bullet in there.
When the ambulance comes, they ask what happen, he refuses to tell. So later, after going to the ambulance, we found out why he survived. It was hollowed tipped!!! He goes but protects them. *why you ask, to stop the threats we received* So homeboy gets in trouble only for evading arrest, possenion of a gun, and speeding. The first thing on my mind this morning was the scramble to confirm who’s picking up Alex from band practice, and whether I remembered to put the signed permission slip in his bag. The kitchen was still quiet except for the ticking clock, but my phone had already pinged twice with calendar reminders—one for the dentist, one for the parent-teacher meeting. I tried to map out the week on the back of an old grocery list, but it quickly devolved into a mess of arrows and crossed-out times. I can’t help but notice how every small change—an extra rehearsal or a rescheduled meeting—ripples through both my own classes and my coparent’s schedule, turning coordination into a high-stakes game of Tetris. By dinner, I’d managed to get all but one appointment squared away, but I still have a nagging feeling I’ve missed something crucial. Maybe it’s just the usual anxiety, or maybe there really is a field trip I’ve overlooked. Either way, I wish there were a way to sync brains, not just calendars. For now, it’s back to the spreadsheets and shared apps, hoping tomorrow’s less of a logistical circus. At least the dishwasher’s running on time, which is more than I can say for the rest of us.

Put my phone down after texting Alex about the groceries. I thought it was my turn, but the way he replied, maybe he assumed he was supposed to do it. We always end up circling around these small things, making them feel bigger than they are. I don’t know if it’s just the way I phrase things or if he’s actually annoyed. It’s weird because I try to be clear, but sometimes I worry I sound too blunt. Sitting on the couch now, listening to the fridge hum, I’m thinking about how much I overthink these small roommate interactions. I want to be easy to live with, but I also can’t help wanting things done a certain way, especially with our clashing schedules. The kitchen feels like neutral ground most days, but every now and then, it gets tense. Maybe I should just ask directly next time or let it go. Not sure which is better. I don’t want to make things awkward, but I also don’t want to keep guessing. Sometimes being gentle feels like tiptoeing. For now, I’ll let it settle and see how it feels in the morning.

The leftovers from last night's pasta are cold but I don't feel like warming them up. I keep replaying the conversation we had this morning, and it's honestly making it hard to focus on anything else. Sometimes I wonder if I'm just overthinking all of this—he says he likes me, but then he goes quiet for hours and I start spinning out. I want to trust it, but I don't even know what "it" is yet. Maybe I'm just not cut out for this kind of uncertainty, or maybe I want too much too soon.

My phone keeps lighting up with notifications, but none of them are from him. I'm trying to remind myself I have worth outside of whether he texts back or not. I know I should probably use this downtime to look for jobs, but my head feels all over the place and the idea of another rejection email makes me feel tired. I wish I had more answers—or at least a better sense of what I even want from all this. The refrigerator hums and I just stare at the kitchen tiles, wondering if I'm supposed to feel more sure of myself by now.

The fridge is humming again, louder than usual, or maybe it just seems that way because the rest of the apartment is so quiet. It’s late, I’ve got tomorrow’s reading spread out all over the couch, but my brain keeps skipping back to what happened this afternoon. Got a call from my sister while I was halfway through my stats homework. I could tell from her voice it wasn’t just a check-in. Turns out Dad’s test results weren’t great. Not surprising, honestly, but it hit harder than I expected. 

The rest of the day was a blur after that. Tried to focus on the online lecture, typed a bunch of nonsense in my notes. Kept thinking about the last time I saw him, how tired he looked, but also how he still tried to crack that stupid joke about the hospital food. I think my way of dealing is to overanalyze everything, run through all the possible scenarios in my head, as if I could plan my way out of feeling useless. I did manage to get a few assignments submitted, but it felt mechanical, like my hands belonged to someone else. 

Now it’s almost midnight and my brain won’t shut off. I’m supposed to be prepping for a group project tomorrow but instead, I’m staring at the ceiling, wondering if I should call home again or just wait. I don’t know how people manage to keep living their regular lives when stuff like this is happening. It feels like everyone else is moving on a conveyor belt and I’m stuck sorting through old family photos in my mind, trying to figure out if I missed some warning signs, or if this is just how things go. Maybe I’ll email the professor about an extension, not sure yet. For now, I’ll just try to sleep, or at least pretend I can.

I just finished wiping crumbs from the counter for the third time tonight. Everyone else is asleep, the house is finally quiet, and I can hear the fridge humming behind me. I keep coming back to this kitchen like it’s the only place I can breathe, even if the air smells like last night’s soup.

Today was another round of dodging questions from my mother about how I’m “really doing.” She means well, but I’m so tired of talking circles around the obvious. Grief has taken up space here, even in the cabinets somehow. I noticed my son left his homework on the table, half-finished, and I thought about how much I wanted to just leave things half-done, too. But I picked it up and set it on his backpack anyway.

I barely wrote anything useful all day. The words just wouldn’t come, or if they did, they sounded hollow. I wonder if this is what it’s going to be like from now on. The restlessness isn’t helping. I tried making lists, thinking I could wrangle my brain into productivity, but mostly ended up doodling in the margins. Sometimes I think I’d get more done if I locked myself in the bathroom, though someone would bang on the door within five minutes.

Late nights like this, I start to overthink everything: my work, my health, how we’re all supposed to move forward without her. I keep telling myself that tomorrow will be easier, but I know that’s not guaranteed. For now, I’ll just listen to the fridge and hope the morning brings some clarity, or at least fewer crumbs.

After discussion with friend I've been left with a question that burns inside my mind since yesterday. I'd like to say straight away: I do not know the answer to it. I hope someone does. I'd like to hear opinions, if anyone can offer a logical explanation please.
Can Love Be Grown?
I do not mean - when two being best friends and have their mutual friendship grown into more with time. I'm talking purely - about "Love Greenhouse":
Can one decide to "cultivate" love for the other and actually do it? Is it possible to make a decision to love and just start to do it? Maybe - in response for the love towards you, maybe - out of gratitude, or - as a result of someone's love and devotion, that may melt your heart eventually?
Say, in a situation, when one loves another unrequitedly. Would it be right for them to hope that by their loving they will make another person to grow love in return?
For my personal opinion, love can never be "grown" on demand. It just happenned or not happenned. And no matter how much of someone's love you can have, there is no way that you can feel love for them "in response". Therefore, to expect and to hope that love can be grown in situation of "unrequited love" is wrong.
What would you say, wise people?

The fan is buzzing in the background and the light from my laptop feels a bit too harsh on my eyes right now. I keep thinking I should get up and open the curtains, but it’s easier to stay slumped in this chair and hope the next email isn’t urgent.

My phone has been pinging non-stop all morning. Group chat with the team, messages from the warehouse, and the daily rundown from upper management. I thought remote work meant more flexibility, but it just means I’m on the clock all the time. I have a spreadsheet open with everyone’s shift changes for the rest of the week, but every time I update it, someone pings me with a new request or a complaint about coverage. I’m worried I’ll miss something important or double-book shifts again. The to-do list is a sticky note graveyard next to my keyboard, half crossed out but mostly scribbled over. Lunch was just a granola bar because I lost track of time. I keep reminding myself that I’m supposed to be patient, that this is just part of the job, but it’s hard to feel organized when everything is coming at me sideways. Even now, I know I’m probably forgetting something, but I can’t seem to focus long enough to figure out what.

This afternoon I spilled half my latte while trying to juggle sketching and answering emails—typical scatterbrained move. Now I'm huddled in the corner of a coffee shop, the only place I could find open this late, laptop humming, but my brain feels like it's running in circles. I keep revisiting that same pitch deck, tweaking details that probably no one will even notice, and yet I’m stuck second-guessing every font size and color choice. The inconsistency of freelance income gnaws at me more when my workflow is this chaotic. I’m supposed to have another call tomorrow, but I’m still unsure if my proposal will land well or if I’ll just seem like an amateur fumbling through ideas. Sometimes I wonder if I’m too self-critical, or if that’s just what keeps me sharp, but right now it’s just making me freeze. The place is mostly empty, except a few late-night regulars, and their quiet presence is oddly comforting. I wish I could organize my day better instead of these last-minute scrambles. I need a plan that actually sticks, but thinking about it only adds to the overwhelm. At least the coffee is strong, and I guess tomorrow is a fresh chance to try again.

Today I was in the kitchen sorting through the newspaper, finding the coupon sections, throwing out junk mail and generally straightening up. Suddenly over in the corner something started to beep and buzz and crawl across the counter. I jumped, squeaked and tip toed over there to see what was going on. There was my husband’s cell phone beeping, vibrating and dancing around in it’s power cords. He had forgotten to take it with him this morning.
I can only assume it was throwing a cell phone tantrum.I don't think it LIKED being left behind. I picked it up and realized I didn’t even know how to turn it off. It finally calmed down and I think it took a message. I dropped it back in it’s snarled cord pile and walked off shaking my head and laughing.
I find technology annoying most of the time, amusing some of the time and amazing about once a month. But having grown up in the low tech world, I don’t think I will ever take it for granted.
I DO appreciate the ability to email my friends and family. And let’s face it, here I am writing an on line journal. Communication is a wonderful thing. But I wonder about being ‘plugged in’ all the time.
Turn on, tune in and drop out was the slogan of the 60’s.
Plug in, plug in more, and ‘Here let me put this implant in your brain’
seems to be the slogan for today. I wonder if ‘separation anxiety’ will take on another meaning in the psychological dictionary. . . .
definition #4. Intentional or unintentional lack of cell phone, internet, television and radio access. Marked by heart palpitations, fingernail biting and hyperventilation. In severe cases, patient may even resort to reading old Microsoft Word user manuals. Hospitalization is indicated if this happens.
But today, I only have to worry about the left behind cell phone. And listen, if that thing lets out another peep, I’m pulling it’s plug. Yeah, I’m a Ruthless Technophobe. Deal with it.
However brave I may sound though, I’m begging you don’t touch my DSL connection.
No, really, leave that alone.
Please !
Honest, don’t touch that modem.
I’m NOT KIDDING !
STAY AWAY from my computer! Ahhrrrrrggggg!
I think I’m hyperventilating!
Pass me the brown paper bag will ‘ya ?
….thank you.

The air was cool tonight as I walked around the block, my mind wandering even though my body felt so tired. I noticed the familiar porch lights flickering on as families settled in for the evening, and it made me think of how much has changed since Mom’s diagnosis. Work was non-stop today, a steady stream of clients with heavy stories, and I could feel my energy flagging by the time I got home. I tried to check in with my partner as soon as I walked through the door, but I think I came off distracted. Communication has been a project for us lately, and I keep reminding myself to be more present, but sometimes I just feel drained. During my walk, I called my brother to see how he was holding up with everything at home. He sounded tired too, but he was grateful that I asked. I wish I had more to give both at work and with my family, but tonight just feels like one of those nights when I’m running on fumes. I grabbed some groceries on the way back and thought about making soup, but ended up just microwaving leftovers. I’m hoping tomorrow I wake up with a little more energy to face the day, to be a better partner and daughter. For now, I’m just glad to have a quiet moment outside under the streetlights, listening to my own footsteps for a bit.

When I was younger, I remember being quite attached to some of my possessions. Record albums, books, plastic models of horses that looked almost real, my favorite pair of orange shoes with the teardrop cutouts on the toes that matched an orange dress with a scalloped hem, my diary.
That diary, ha ! Back then I had many an entry that said ‘just a day’. I didn’t seem to have the vocabulary or skill to put down anything interesting about my day. I think I might have been worried that my little brother would read it or something.
I read two quotes today about writing and diaries.
‘We write to heighten our own awareness of life…..
We write to taste life twice.'
The Diary of Anais Nin
‘We do not write in order to be understood; we write in order to understand.’
C. Day Lewis
(how does he know when to use a semicolon?) I never do… :-)
To taste life twice. I like that. It re-enforces the idea that life is to be paid attention to. It’s not something that’s happening while we are on our way to something else.
We write to understand. I think I have spent a lot of my life thinking that I was writing to be understood. But when I read this quote, a light bulb went on over my head. I have been writing out of puzzlement, and uncertainty.
Trying to figure out the world, and my place in it. And you know, sometimes in the writing, answers come….. sometimes they come.
But ! I was talking about being attached to possessions!
Now a days I hold things so much more lightly. My things do not define me, I define my things. I suppose that is a natural progression in the human journey. This of course is not good for the gross national product.
And might even be a subversive stance to take in America. But I think the economy will plug along without my input for a while don’t you ?
Today I am happy just to have a scrap of paper and a pen to scribble with. I hope this is a trend that continues, just think of all the money I will save ! Maybe I will save enough to get a beautiful leather bound journal and write more than ….. ‘just a day’ in it’s pages.
