The sunlight sneaks in just enough to warm the kitchen windowsill where the plants mostly survive on neglect. It's quiet now, a rare pause in the usual chaos of the house. I spent the evening fiddling with those abstract ideas for the new canvas, but my mind won't settle long enough to really dig in. There’s a sketch with jagged lines scribbled on a napkin somewhere, but finding it feels like a small quest I don’t have the energy to undertake. I keep thinking about how the kids’ laughter feels both like a balm and a relentless tide pulling me away from my own headspace. I crave the solitude that never quite comes, even when they’re asleep. Last night, I caught myself staring out the window, tracing the shapes of the trees against the stars, wondering if I’ll ever get a moment to just be without noise. I suppose this restlessness is part of the process, but it’s exhausting. I wish I could bottle one perfect stretch of peaceful hours to revisit when everything feels scattered. For now, I’ll settle for this quiet lunch break, the hum of the fridge, and a slow, imperfect breath.

The stark winter moon illuminates the dry grasses in the field next door, washing out the color until it looks like a field of snow. The fallen garden plants cringe in the contrasting rays, hunkering down in the chill air, knowing their glory days are over. So much has transpired around them this season and they would like to pause and think a few things through, but the moonlight is keeping them from doing so with laser like beams disturbing their reverie. They are busy instead lifting up their limp, frost damaged leaves in dismay, remembering how beautiful they were in July.
I too would pause for some serious reflection but my mind is sluggish from lack of sleep and filled with trivia taking up valuable space while larger matters tap their toes outside waiting in line. While I should be contemplating the mysteries of the universe, I ponder when I will have a few moments to go out into the fields and gather some dried grasses and branches with red berries to make winter arrangements in the house. Always, always, I am making my nest. Wanting to make a beautiful place for friends and family to sit and talk and eat and dream. It seems like such a humble goal. Yet getting to that quiet space will take all the energy I can muster on this chilly night, illuminated by the stark winter moon.
The very shape of my own hand, holding this work of art that is the pen that Daniel has given to me makes me pause in wonder. Maybe these simple things ARE the mysteries of the universe and the moon is trying to tell me so.

Steam fogged up the window over the sink as I ran hot water for the dishes, even though it was barely past six and the sun had just started to push through the clouds. The kitchen still smells like cardboard and unfamiliar soap, nothing like the old place, but I guess that’s what happens when you pick up your life and drop it somewhere new at my age. I should be reviewing my notes for class later, but my mind keeps drifting to whether I made the right call going back to school now, of all times. I keep hearing the clock tick, and it’s louder than usual, almost like it’s reminding me that there’s not as much time as I’d like to figure things out. The fridge hums, and my backpack is slumped against the wall, half-open, with highlighters and crumpled handouts poking out. I keep thinking about what I’m trying to prove—maybe that I’m still able to change, or that I can fit in with people who probably don’t even remember the 90s. It’s weird being the oldest guy in the room, trying to act like I’m not worried about grades or being called out in seminars, but I am. There’s this low-level anxiety running in the background all the time, even when I’m feeling hopeful that this is a fresh start. I don’t know if I’m actually optimistic or if I just have to be, because otherwise the doubts would eat me up. The kitchen table is covered in syllabi and sticky notes, and I keep wiping at a ring from my mug, like I’m trying to clean up more than just coffee. I hear the neighbors moving around upstairs—new sounds, new routines, none of it feels like mine yet. I promised myself I wouldn’t second-guess every decision, but here I am, wondering again if I’m actually cut out for all this or if it’s just something to keep me busy. I guess I just want to belong somewhere again, not float around feeling unanchored. Maybe it’ll get easier once I make a friend or two, or at least stop getting lost in the hallways. For now, I just keep going, because it’s morning, and I’ve got reading to do, and sometimes moving forward is the only thing that makes sense.

Earlier today, I kept replaying that conversation with Jamie in my head. We were both on break, tucked away in the corner of the shop while the espresso machines hissed in the background. She seemed distant, barely making eye contact, and I felt this weird mix of frustration and worry. I tried to ask her what was wrong, but she brushed it off, saying she was just tired. Now, sitting here after my shift with the café mostly empty, I keep wondering if I missed something obvious or if I just made things worse by pushing. I know I can get a bit intense when I sense tension, and it’s hard for me to just let things be unresolved. Part of me wants to text her and apologize for being nosy, but another part says maybe I should just give her space. Living alone makes it easy to overthink all of this. At least work itself went smoothly, but I can’t shake the feeling that I should have handled things differently. Maybe I need to learn to be more patient with other people’s moods, not just my own. For now, I’ll try to focus on winding down and see if tomorrow gives me a better perspective.

I wiped down the counter for the third time this afternoon, trying to keep busy while the quiet tension between us settled like steam on the windows. She said something about me not listening, but I don’t really remember how the conversation slipped into that. I want to hear her, I really do, but words feel like they're swimming just out of reach, drowning in my restlessness.

I keep replaying what she said, looking for where I might have missed the mark or where the sharp edge came from. Is it impatience, or something I said that sounded dismissive? That thought pulls me under more than I'd like. When we finally spoke again, it felt like we were both trying to hold fragile things without knowing how. I nodded a lot, hoping that was enough to show I cared.

She’s probably tired of my silence, but I’m not ready to speak without feeling sure I won’t make it worse. Maybe tomorrow I’ll be more grounded. For now, I’m just trying to keep the line open, even if it’s quiet on my end. This cup of coffee doesn’t taste like much, but maybe that’s okay. At least it’s something.

The steering wheel is cold tonight. I keep flexing my hands, trying to shake off this weird fog in my head, but it’s just hanging around, stubborn as ever. I should be reviewing articles before class tomorrow, but here I am, staring out at a line of brake lights and thinking about Mom again. Last night I dreamed of her, or maybe just her voice, and I woke up with that ache in my chest that doesn’t really go away. I don’t want to dump all of this on the family group chat, but I wish someone would just ask how I actually am, not just whether I finished my paper or if the Wi-Fi is acting up again.

Remote work makes the days run together. I can’t remember if I actually ate lunch or just watched a video about meal prepping and called it good. The house is too quiet, except for when the neighbor’s dog starts howling, and then it’s too loud. I keep telling myself I’ll go for a walk, but the pull of the laptop is strong, and my motivation is about as unreliable as this old car. There’s this restlessness in me lately, but then I get tired just thinking about doing anything different. I know grief comes in waves, but tonight it’s more like fog, and even with the engine running, I’m not sure I’m moving forward.

Earlier today I remembered how I used to just buy that fancy bread at the grocery store without even thinking, but now I stood there comparing price tags like it was some kind of test. Tonight, after everyone was asleep and the house was quiet for once, I slipped on my shoes and took a loop around the block because my head felt full—too many lists, deadlines, receipts. The streetlights made weird shadows on the sidewalk and I kept replaying the conversation with my editor in my head, wondering if my pitch was actually as clear as I thought. I keep telling myself I can juggle all this—the invoices, the word count, the bills stacked on the counter—but my phone buzzed with a reminder about rent and suddenly I was counting days instead of steps. My fingers were cold even in my pockets but the air felt good, like it was pressing pause for a minute. I know optimism is my thing, but tonight I mostly felt practical, just trying to check off what I can and not drop any pieces. I wish work felt less like a treadmill and more like an open window. Maybe tomorrow I’ll find a little more breathing space.

I can not believe that March has left us so quickly! I can not believe it. April is already here? Wow! Let's start the April month out right...writing in my journal here. Starting Monday, I will go back to writing the Chapters of my life during my illness (kidney transplant) but I do have a couple of things I need to do Monday so I will not be able to write in my journal unless I find time in the morning before late afternoon. This weekend, yet March 29th according to my clock and time being after 10:30 p.m...Wisconsin (state) time. I am still getting used to the idea of Dear Diary being about three hours ahead of my time...which I am used to. I am getting used to it though...believe me. I can not believe that April is among us now...I can't! Unbelieveable but so very true. Today was just another Saturday for me. Except going to church on Saturdays, my weekends are pretty much the same and normal. I am always looking forward to the week ending and Friday comes and every weekend I look forward to. It's one of those things. Do you understand? When Saturday night closes in, I look forward to Sunday being quiet and peaceful as I do live in an apartment complex of elderly folk. I am, at age 30, grateful for the quietness and peacefullness of the neighbors at nighttime hours after 10 p.m. and I do respect my neighbors as much as possible even though it is kind of hard sometimes believe it or not. I live on a fixed income each month called SSI because I have a physical handicap called CP (cerebral palsy) and a pre-existing condition kidney transplant of thirteen years. I qualify living at Teamster Manor because I have SSI and a disability.

Feeling a little restless today, but focused. Lunch is just leftovers, eaten at the kitchen table, sunlight coming in through the window and making patterns on the wood. The clock above the fridge ticks louder than usual. I try to keep my mind on work, but it drifts—mostly to that conversation with Sara this morning. We weren’t exactly fighting, but it felt like we were talking past each other again. She says she supports the freelancing, but I sense the worry in her voice when she asks about new clients. I want to reassure her, but honestly I don’t know what next month looks like either. Some weeks I’m convinced I’ll make it work, and other days it feels like I’m just barely holding on. The emails have slowed down again and I can’t help checking my inbox between bites, hoping for something promising. There’s a strange comfort in the routine of emailing pitches and waiting, even if the waiting gets heavy. I know she misses the stability we had when I was working full-time. I miss it too, sometimes, but I also can’t imagine going back. The freedom is real, but so is the uncertainty. It’s like I’m always proving to myself—and her—that this was the right call. I want to believe that the patience will pay off, that the right project is just around the corner, but today it’s just me, the ticking clock, and the quiet. Maybe tonight I’ll try to talk things through with her again, if I can find the right words. For now, I’ll finish this cold pasta and get back to the spreadsheet. One step at a time.

This morning, before my shift, I remembered how my sister used to always text me jokes whenever she knew I had an early start, just something dumb to make me grin before I dragged myself out the door. She hasn’t done that in a while, not since Dad took a turn for the worse. Looking back, I don’t think I ever told her how much I actually looked forward to those texts, even if I’d just roll my eyes at them. Now, during lunch, I’m sitting in the break room, picking at a half-warm sandwich and thinking about the call we had late last night. She said she feels like I’m shutting her out, but honestly, I’m just tapped out and tired, barely keeping up with work and making sure the apartment doesn’t fall apart. We argued a bit about who’s been visiting Dad more and it just left me feeling guilty, even though I know she’s got her own stuff going on. Part of me wonders if it’s easier to fight about chores and visits than to admit we’re both scared about what comes next. I wish I had something smart or comforting to say to her but I end up just mumbling or changing the subject. Maybe I should try again tonight, if I don’t crash as soon as I get home. Someone—maybe Mark?—made a joke about "fancy chef food" and everyone laughed except me. I laughed, technically, but it was more of a dry cough. This morning, I stood by the kitchen window and watched the rain tap against the glass while my roommate scrambled to find her umbrella. For a moment, I was annoyed by the noise and the chaos—coats everywhere, keys misplaced, another morning where I tried to keep everything in order and still felt like I was failing. Now, during this quiet lunch break, I’m sitting at the small dining table, leftover soup cooling in front of me, trying to map out the rest of my day in my head. My calendar is a mess; appointments, reminders to call Mom’s doctor, the job search spreadsheet open on my laptop but untouched since last night.

I can feel my shoulders tensed up. There’s guilt about not being productive enough, about letting myself get swallowed by grief ever since Dad passed. Some days are better, but today isn’t one of them. The smallest decisions—what to cook for dinner, when to take out the trash, how to phrase another cover letter—feel impossibly heavy. I keep glancing at the clock, counting down hours until I have to make another round of phone calls for Mom's medication refills. The apartment is so still right now, but inside my head, everything is loud.

Tonight, I know I’ll be up late, probably shuffling schedules for both myself and my roommate, feeling like I’m barely keeping up. I just want to feel like I’m doing something right, even if it’s just getting through the day. Maybe after dinner I’ll take a short walk, breathe in the night air, and let myself stop organizing things for five minutes. I want to believe that tomorrow will go a little smoother, even if right now that feels far away.

I just want to remember this day. What I did on September, 11th, 2001? That year I was studying for my certificates. That day I’ve been hanging around on discussion board – online forum for techi-crazy folks. We were just doing stuff we always do – discussing the exams, questions, answers, helping each other. It is a big and friendly community… Then the whole world collapsed. There were many from America on our board. There were few from NYC. In a moment things changed and there‘ve been no longer different countries, there was one family coming together, as the day unfolded… It may not be one of those heartbreaking moments, that would find its way to the news, but for me this was – what I remember of that day. And always will. On that day, in 2001 one of the forum members came in despair asking for help - his sister worked in the Tower. He wasn't able to get through to her on the phone and wasn't able to run to the towers either. He was desperate for help. And the people on this board stood up for him all, as one, and did the best they can... Sunlight is coming in through the blinds and hitting the coffee table in weird stripes, and I can hear the washing machine rumbling in the next room. I got home from work about an hour ago and my legs are still sore from running around picking orders all day. There was a big shipment in the morning, so we were all hustling, and it felt like I barely had a second to breathe. Lunch was basically a granola bar at my locker because the line in the break room was too long. I keep thinking about the dumb argument we had this morning before I left for work, and I want to talk about it but I’m exhausted and worried I’ll make things worse. I know we both want to get better at talking things out, but it’s so hard when we’re both tired and stressed. For now, I’m just sitting here, listening to the washer and trying to slow down before I start dinner.

Was washing last night’s dishes in the kitchen before anyone else got up. I tried to keep the noise down but the faucet still echoed, and that made me think about how thin these walls are. The schedule for today is already in my head, even though I haven’t written anything down yet. Dad needs a ride to his appointment, Mom wants me to call the plumber about the leak under the sink, and my sister left her laundry in the washer again. Still haven’t figured out when I’m supposed to join that project kickoff call, because the time zones got mixed up in the last email. I keep checking my phone, but the notifications blend together. 

I meant to finish my own work project last night, but after dinner everyone needed something. There’s no real private spot in the house, so I just try to work at the kitchen table and hope people don’t wander in. The to-do list keeps growing, mostly with things that aren’t mine. I keep thinking I’ll get a handle on it if I just organize better, but it’s like moving pieces around without actually clearing space. Not sure if I’ll ever find a good rhythm with all this. Might try blocking out a chunk of time tonight, but something always comes up.

This morning, I found myself staring at the Google calendar on my phone before I’d even had breakfast, trying to remember if I’d already confirmed tomorrow’s drop-off with Mark. I thought I had, but then my mind started spinning about whether I’d forgotten to update him about the dentist appointment next week. It feels like every day is just a stream of reminders and adjustments, and I’m always worried something will fall through the cracks. Now it’s almost 8pm, and I’m slumped on the couch, laptop open but untouched, because I can’t bring myself to look at job postings right now. The living room is a mess—socks everywhere, a half-eaten apple on the coffee table, and I keep hearing the dryer spin in the background. I keep telling myself I should be applying to at least three jobs a day, but the whole process feels pointless lately. All these job descriptions asking for skills I barely remember having, or weirdly specific software I’ve never even heard of. I know I’m supposed to stay organized, and I have a spreadsheet for applications, but it’s honestly just making me feel more overwhelmed. I feel guilty for not being more productive, especially when I think about setting an example for the kids. Part of me wonders if I’m just making excuses, but then I start doubting whether any of this effort will actually pay off. Mark texted me again about switching weekends, and I wanted to say no, but I can already see the calendar dominoes falling if I don’t agree. I hate that my schedule is always up for negotiation and I never get to plan more than a week ahead. I’m tired—like, bone-deep tired—and still can’t turn off the part of my brain that’s buzzing about what I might be missing. Maybe tomorrow I’ll actually apply for something, or maybe I’ll just reorganize the spreadsheet again. I wish I could just stop worrying for five minutes.

This morning, I remembered how tense things were when I left the house. There was hardly any conversation, just a couple of comments about the kids' lunches and a quick check to make sure everyone had what they needed. I could feel the frustration simmering under the surface, mostly about last night's argument. It was about something small, but it somehow turned into a bigger deal than it should have been.

Now I'm on the bus heading home, thinking about how to approach things tonight. The day at work felt like a blur because I kept replaying everything in my head. I want to talk things through, but I'm exhausted and honestly not sure where to start. I know I should stay positive, but it's hard to keep that mindset when everything feels so heavy. Maybe if I just focus on listening first, we'll get somewhere. I hope that by the time I walk through the door, I've got enough patience left to try again.

Earlier today, I caught myself staring at the empty chair across from me during lunch, like it was supposed to say something it never did. The silence between us has grown thicker these past few weeks, heavier than the grease and grime I deal with at the shop. I kept turning over what I said last night when things got heated, wondering if I pushed too hard, or if maybe I didn’t push hard enough. Now, here I am sitting in the dark, the clock ticking louder than my heart, trying to piece together why saying sorry feels like swallowing something bitter. I want to bridge the gap, to fix this tension before it stretches into something unfixable, but the words stick like oil on my tongue. I’m tired, not just from work and classes, but from carrying this weight alone. I hope tomorrow brings a chance to start fresh or at least a little understanding. It's strange, balancing this job, schoolwork, and trying to keep what matters from slipping through my hands. I guess patience is what I have left, even if it feels like little more than hope right now. I don’t know if I’m doing the right thing or just holding on to fear of losing what I care about most. Sometimes, late at night, the silence answers back and I still feel like I’m the one who has to break it. Maybe tomorrow I will.

I just put my phone on silent and shoved it under a pillow because I couldn’t stand to see another message from Mark tonight. All afternoon, I tried to focus on menu planning, but every time a ping went off, I lost my train of thought. Remote work used to feel like freedom, but now it’s like I’m never able to clock out—work and personal just bleed together. The kitchen table is covered with sticky notes, my laptop, and a cold cup of tea I forgot hours ago.

I keep replaying our argument from earlier. He says I don’t listen, but honestly, he never seems to notice when I’m overwhelmed. Maybe I’m too blunt, but I don’t have time to sugarcoat everything. The truth is, I needed him to back me up when I told my sous chef to stop cutting corners, but instead, he just shrugged it off.

It’s exhausting having to be tuned in to everyone’s moods while I’m just trying to get through the day. The worst part is, I can’t even escape it at home. I used to love the quiet at night, but now it just feels heavy. Sometimes I wonder if I’m the problem, or if I’m just tired of carrying so much all the time.

I know I should probably reach out and try to talk again, but right now, I just want the world to leave me alone. Maybe things will look different in the morning. For now, I’ll try to turn my brain off and get some sleep, though I doubt I’ll manage it.

We do have lots of friends. This is a good thing, right? We do have lots of Good Friends and we happy and we love and loved by them too. Sometimes this is not quite enough tho…
Good Friend is not the same as – Special Friend. And this is that one, which is most often missing from our life. The one with whom we can be as much ourselves, as we are with ourselves. The one, who knows our best and our worst. The one who accepts us just as we accept ourselves. Who would not be gentle when pointing to the mistakes we make and who would not be cruel when lying to please.
I wonder how many of us do have that Special Friend for real? And I wonder why, even having lots of very good friends, we still not set with satisfaction and we keep searching?
I am not talking about love here. Well, in a sense, it is – love, isn’t? Not to be in love, but - to trust one’s soul in someone. To share not just somethings, but to share yourself, whoever you happened to be. In a way – I am talking about – trust.
I’ve been thinking on lately: isn’t it strange that it is generally easier to build that kind of trust between men and women then between same genders? Could this be coz of mutual interest in each other is higher? Coz in effect we are – explorers of unknown and the unknown lies where we can’t reach. In order to understand what man thinks, you’ve got to be a man. And same – for female. Could we be so opinionated that we know everything about our own species and therefore we are not interested in us any more?
Is it really a question of trust when talking friendship between men and women or is it – mere inquisitiveness and concealed yearning for flirting? How much of our “frank confessions” would be without ulterior motive? Even if we are pretty certain ourselves: it isn’t so.
I wonder now, if there is such thing, as men&women friendship?
And getting back to the initial question: I wonder if we really need to have that Special Friend at all or is it better just to keep our deepest secrets safe within? In the end of a day who can be more Special to you, as not yourself?
[And who can love you more then you love yourself, really? Lol…;-)]

I am sitting in front of a technological marvel. Typing on a word processor that can erase my mistakes with the click of the backspace key (oh for such a wonder in typing class in 1966!) There is a midi file playing that I downloaded from the internet a few days ago that is very beautiful. I can set it so that it just plays once or over and over if I want it to. I can change the way my computer screen looks and sounds in a thousand different ways. The spell checker prompts me when I make a mistake so that I can fix them write away….. well, most mistakes…. right away and turn out a document that is not a complete embarrassment in that personally deficient area of my life, (the old spelling area). I am wondering what I would have thought of and done with all these things when I was a teenager. The possibilities for creativity and self-expression may have opened doors for me, or for all we know, may have just made me lazy and peevish. We will never know.
But I think about this kind of stuff. I have to. The world has been altered so much just in my own lifetime. And we race every day to try and keep up with the changes that are taking place even as we speak. I wonder if humans were made to function well under this much uncertainty. Just this year MOST of my close relatives have moved or gotten new phone numbers and email addresses. Including us ! We changed our ISP a couple of months ago. Geeze ! I spend a significant amount of my time updating my address book these days. I feel a nasty case of Future Shock coming on, and I think my immunity is wearing off.
The concept of permanence is quickly disappearing. Perhaps it was an illusion in the first place. Maybe. Probably. – but oh, I don’t want to go THERE….( This way there be dragons….) But our fascination with the “new” in an insidious way is engendering in us a contempt of the stable as stodgy, old, decrepit, non “progressive”. Progress to WHERE ? I ask you?
I have a feeling that none of this is good for us, but have no idea how to unplug.
Although in truth all this whining is funny coming from me, because I live a pretty quiet life compared to so many around me. I am grateful for it too. I know my limits. Growing up in the country, I learned many a humble, non technical skill. How to plant a garden, how to milk goats, care for chickens, make homemade bread and learned how to preserve all kinds of foods. I sewed clothes for myself and my boys. I learned how to make handmade soap, quilts and candles, and we even cut and split our own firewood to keep warm with in the winter. All these things I have done, and done well. And with only a few minor differences, some of these things were done the same way for centuries before me. As we write and read these words, someone in America is milking their goat, by hand ! All these activities had tangible results, food, clothing, warmth. Those bare minimum things that humans need. It is a satisfying way to spend one’s time. Can we say the same about a state of the art digital camera ? Do you know how to fix it if it breaks ?
I’ll bet not.
It’s as if I’m stuck in a slow contemplative style of living yet watching the world whiz by at ever increasing dizzying speed. Even though I try to stay out of the loop, every now and then the mayhem reaches out and gives me a good spin.
Maybe some of my cognitive dissonance comes from watching the ubiquitous teletube that seeks constantly to shape my perception of the world. To tell me I need MORE stuff all the time. New stuff, complicated stuff, cutting edge stuff. Stuff that needs a manual just to figure out how to turn it on and off. Stuff that costs WAY too much money. Stuff that I can’t eat, drink, clothe or shelter myself with. Toys. Complicated, expensive toys.
I should just turn the stupid tube off you say ! But so many of us ARE watching and way too much of it. I worry that so much of our information about the world comes from such a narrow and untrustworthy source, that our conclusions about life are becoming more and more distorted.
Real life does not make good TV, Ozzy notwithstanding. Too much down time, not enough action. But who can measure with a camera the thoughts and dreams and other amazing things that run through the human mind ? How many quiet hours did it take to hammer out the Declaration of Independence ? You know, it doesn’t look or sound like a document that was whipped up in an afternoon committee meeting. Many people had to think some very deep thoughts for quite a while to come up with it. Who is making time to think deeply about things today ? And what will be the consequences of actions taken without a good deep think ?
Oh, I am sure you are tired of reading how I struggle with this stuff. I apologize, and I admit that I am not even articulating my dilemma very well. This is a recurring issue for me and I wrestle with it often. And I just as often throw up my hands in despair. Sorry, but I just don’t have the answers yet, so I “write out loud” to see if it might help somehow….maybe I will go bake some bread. A small act of defiance. Power to the contemplatives !

Specifically, Baensidh.
Anyone who has lived with cats knows that they have a certain dignity about them. Even as frolicking kittens, there's an aura about them. Someone said that cats were worshipped in Egypt, and they've never forgotten that.
Even the most dignified cat can make a misstep and look foolish, and stalk off with a look that says "I meant to do that."
Well, Baensidh's nosiness got him into trouble and caused me a deal of merriment. There was a large paper sack on the floor in the kitchen with a handle on it. Cat's curiosity got the best of him and he finally just had to investigate the sack and the contents thereof. Now, I can't explain exactly how it happened because I was in the living room when Baensidh investigated the sack in the kitchen. But......
All of a sudden there he comes flying down the hall, circling the living room, a white blur at warp speed, jumping over funiture (knocked over some candle sticks), and finally galloping back down the hall the other way. With the handle of the sack around his neck. And the sack flying out behind him. Then utter silence.
Finally I go looking for him. All his usual hiding places. No cat. Now where could he have gotten to? No doors or windows open. So I looked again on the other side of the bed, and there he was, poor baby, all huddle into the farthest corner under the bed. The paper sack in a bunch under and around him. I tried to pull the sack out from under him, but it didn't budge. I finally discovered that the handle was still around his neck.
Well the sack was in shreds, but the handle was intact.
Once I freed the cat, he went somewhere else to hide (and lick his emotional wounds?). I didn't see him for several hours after that, but finally he got hungry and came out to eat. I gave him a little extra treat of tuna to try to make up a little for the indignity.
Wonder how long it'll take for the feline curiosity to get the better of him until he investigates another paper sack.
Shalom
PS: And the contents of the sack (two small light bulb, still in the box fortunately) I finally found in the bedroom and in the hallway.

This morning I woke up too early because I forgot to close the blinds, so the sun was basically stabbing me in the eyes at 6:15. I wandered around my new apartment in a daze, trying to find my sketchbook but I still haven’t unpacked all my art supplies. The boxes are like a maze, and I keep tripping over random stuff. I made some oatmeal but couldn’t really taste it, just kept thinking about how weird it is to start over in a new place. Everything smells different, even the water from the tap.

Now I’m in the parking lot outside work, just watching people come and go. I keep checking my phone, not really sure who I want to hear from. Maybe I’m hoping someone from my old life will message me, but they probably won’t. I’m supposed to be excited about new beginnings, but mostly I just feel floaty, like I could drift away. I keep telling myself to be patient and let things settle, but then I get fidgety and want to do a million things at once. I doodled on the back of a grocery receipt while waiting, just quick messy lines, nothing good. I don’t know if I even like my art lately. I hope I’ll figure out how to feel normal here, but right now it feels like I’m not really anywhere at all.

I just rinsed my plate and set it in the rack, letting the warm water run over my fingers longer than I needed to. The kitchen feels too quiet tonight, just the faint hum of the fridge and the clock ticking above the stove. I keep thinking about how I spent another day scrolling through job postings, jotting down positions that seem doable but never quite clicking the 'apply' button. I tell myself I’ll do it tomorrow, but I’m not sure if I believe that anymore.

Earlier, when I tried to join in on the conversation with my new roommates during dinner, it felt awkward, like I was intruding on a rhythm I haven’t learned yet. They laughed about people and places I don’t know, and I smiled along, but it was mostly just to fill space. I wish I could stop overthinking each little thing I say, but the words get stuck in my head before they ever make it out. Maybe I’m just not used to being the new person, or maybe I’m just tired from uprooting everything.

There’s this weird mix of hope and frustration in me right now, like I’m waiting for something to shift but I don’t know what exactly. My mind keeps circling around what I’m supposed to do next, but for now, all I can focus on is the sticky feel of my hands from dish soap and the way the streetlight outside flickers against the window. It’s not much, but it’s what I have tonight.

Had to squeeze in breakfast in the kitchen before my roommate came in. The fridge is basically empty except for some leftovers, so I grabbed a yogurt and tried not to think about how much I miss Mom’s cooking. I keep expecting her to text me some random tip about eating better, but of course that’s not happening anymore. Grief isn’t as loud now as it was, but it still sneaks in at these quiet moments. I was in such a rush to get my resume updated last night that I barely slept, and now I’m running on autopilot. There’s something weird about going through all these small daily routines when such a big part of life is missing. I haven’t talked to my dad this week, which I keep meaning to do but just can’t seem to make time for. Being patient with myself is harder some days than others. Anyway, I need to check job postings before my roommate needs the table for her meeting.

This morning, I remember accidentally leaving the kitchen window open while trying to pack breakfast quickly, and now there's this chill that I can't seem to shake. I'm sitting here, half-drinking my coffee that’s gone cold, trying to map out the day in my head. The schedule feels like a tangled mess: work shifts, my parent’s appointments, the pharmacy run, and those unresolved calls from the insurance company. It’s like I keep shifting priorities but nothing really gets checked off. Sometimes I start a task and then something else pulls me away — a phone call, a sudden need for help, or just plain exhaustion that creeps in. At the cafe, I try to focus on the rhythm of pouring drinks and greeting regulars, but my mind drifts back to a pile of unpaid bills on the kitchen counter and that half-packed bag for the doctor’s visit. I wish I could be more organized, but the days blend together, and I feel stretched thin. Even when I get a moment's peace, I’m already planning the next thing, which makes it hard to relax. I’m patient with others, yet sometimes it’s hard to extend that same kindness to myself. I’ll need to make a real to-do list today and maybe tackle one small thing before the afternoon chaos begins. For now, the quiet kitchen and a lukewarm cup of coffee are all I have to regroup.

I had the pill organizer in one hand, my phone in the other with three alarms going off for different things. That pretty much sums up most mornings lately. Now I’m finally sitting on the couch, not quite sure if I’m supposed to be relaxing or if I’m forgetting something urgent. There’s a stack of paperwork on the coffee table (insurance stuff for Mom, some bills of my own, a note to call her doctor back). I keep setting reminders but there’s always something that slips through the cracks.

I was supposed to follow up with my brother about respite care options, but we haven’t connected in days. He’s got his own family chaos and I don’t want to push, but the weight of juggling Mom’s appointments, her physical therapy schedule, grocery runs, and actually doing my job is starting to feel impossible. I double-booked myself for a video call at work and taking Mom to her blood draw, so I ended up rescheduling both, which made me look pretty flaky. My manager says he understands, but I know I’m stretching patience on all sides. The calendar on the fridge is a mess of scribbled times and question marks. Sometimes I just stare at it trying to piece together what comes next.

I guess I’m managing to keep things going, but it’s not exactly smooth. I still try to stay positive and remind myself I’m doing the best I can, but there’s always this low-level buzz in my head about what I’ve forgotten. The living room feels like a command center with all the sticky notes and lists, and yet it never feels fully under control. At least Mom seems comfortable today. I just wish I could find a better way to stay on top of it all without feeling like I’m running in circles.

The parking lot is drier than I expected this afternoon, though the sun hides behind some heavy clouds that threaten rain later. I’m parked near the far end, where the potholes have multiplied since we moved here. It’s frustrating how much time slips away just trying to get everything sorted—school supplies, lesson plans, groceries, doctor’s appointments for Mom. I still feel like I’m forgetting something important every time I back out of this lot. The new house is quieter but somehow more hollow. Yesterday I found myself staring at the walls, wondering how long it will take before it actually feels like home instead of just a place to store things. The kids seem to be adjusting better than I am, though maybe that’s because school gives them a sense of routine I desperately crave. I should check in on their homework tonight, but I might be too wiped out again. My head’s scattered with memories of Dad and the funeral arrangements, the way the light caught his favorite chair, the silence that followed. It’s odd to think that grief doesn’t follow a neat schedule, just like all the chaos of moving and working full time. Sometimes I catch a glimpse of something funny or sweet and wish I could slow down enough to hold onto it. For now, I have to get inside and focus on the day ahead, even if my mind runs ten steps ahead of me and my coffee’s gone cold.

The hum of the fridge is louder than usual right now as I eat this cold leftover quiche at my desk. I barely tasted it, just something to do with my hands while I run through all the things I need to finish before the afternoon meeting. My phone keeps lighting up—he sent another text about dinner Friday night, asking if I want to try that new Italian place. I should be excited, but I’m just tired and my mind keeps looping around whether we’re really even on the same page. 

Late last night, after everyone else went to bed, I found myself staring at the TV without actually watching. Mom’s birthday would have been next week, and the ache of missing her hit out of nowhere. Maybe that’s partly why I feel so off-balance about this relationship. I want to move forward, but my head is full of old memories and half-finished tasks. I know I’m practical, but sometimes I wish things just felt a bit more clear. For now, I’ll answer his text after work and try to focus on the next item on my list.

Why does it always feel like one tiny comment can just spiral into this whole thing? Dinner was good tonight, I guess, but I could tell there was tension as soon as we sat down. I tried to talk about the project I’ve been working on, but it was like my words kept getting tangled and I wasn’t really saying what I meant. She kept looking at her phone, which made me feel like I was boring or just too much, but when I asked if something was wrong, she just said she was tired. I know I overthink everything, but it’s hard not to when the air feels so thick. The kitchen light was flickering, which only made me more distracted. I want to be better at this—actually listening, actually saying what’s in my head, but it’s like my thoughts are all jumbled up and I can’t make them line up. I have this hope that tomorrow will be different, that I’ll come up with the right words, but right now my brain’s buzzing and it’s hard not to just retreat. Maybe I just need to write it all out, even if it feels like rambling. I love her, and I want to make this work, but when nights feel like this, I question if I’m just fundamentally missing some key ingredient to good communication. Maybe we’re both just tired. Maybe I just need to breathe and try again tomorrow.

The other day I went to the grocery store. One of the items on my list was jam. This seemed like a pretty straightforward errand, easily completed. Until I stood with my shopping cart in front of the jam section at my local Ralph’s.
This store was new to me and I was curious to see what they had, as I was in the mood to try something different . So I passed up the first jar of strawberry jam I saw and scanned the shelves for other choices. I quickly realized I was in deep trouble.
There were probably 10 or 12 different brands and each brand had about 5 or 6 kinds and each kind a sub-kind….etc. Jams with no sugar, jams without seeds, jams with seeds. Imported, domestic and mystery jams. Several sizes of jars and I had a choice between organic and chemical filled. Jams mixed with peanut butter. Jelly from Hungary, England and Spain. Marmalade, lemon curd, grape, current, cherry, pineapple, apricot, raspberry, strawberry, plum, mint, apple butter, apple jelly, peach, blackberry, loganberry, and boysenberry. I felt myself breaking out in a cold sweat.
Then I started comparing prices ! I was paralyzed with indecision.
I became aware that I had been standing there with what was probably a particularly vacant look on my face. I grabbed a jar of strawberry, my usual brand even, and bolted for the checkout stand. I haven’t been down that aisle since, but my jar of strawberry is already getting low. . . I should have bought two of them, because now I am going to have to go back.
And I’m feeling like trying something different. . . .

I felt a little unsettled tonight as I walked around the block after dinner. The air had cooled down, which made the houses seem quieter than usual, and it gave me some space to think about Mom. It's been months since her diagnosis, but it still catches me off guard when I remember how quickly things changed. I keep noticing small things she liked, like the smell from that jasmine bush near the corner, and it makes me pause. Sometimes I worry that if I get too locked into my routines, I’ll miss these details, but at the same time, having structure helps me manage the restlessness.

I tried sketching a bit earlier, but my mind kept wandering back to the family group chat and the updates about her next doctor’s visit. I want to be hopeful for her, but I can’t help running through possible outcomes in my head. I wonder if my organized streak is actually helping anyone, or if it just gives me something to do so I don’t have to sit with all the uncertainty. I’m grateful for the quiet tonight, though. It’s easier to listen to what I’m actually feeling when the world slows down a bit.

To this day, I don’t think I could explain my attraction to horses as a teenager. I can only stumble around at vague guesses of the underlying magnetism. I suppose some Freudian type would infuse my obsession with my nascent sexuality, but that just seems convenient and conventional psychobable. Besides, I want a second opinion from Jung anyway. I think he had much better ideas. But that is another story.
Here are my theories. Horses were BIG, I was small. They were powerful, agile, and could run like the wind. I was clumsy and a really bad runner, (still am). They had beautiful long flowing manes and tails. I had short curly hair that had a mind of it’s own. It took a really stiff wind to make my hair even consider flowing. Whipping around in circles was more like it.
In any event, these irresistible forces drew me into the field across the street from our house where the day before someone had turned out about six horses. I went out to see if I could bribe them into letting me touch them with carrots stolen from our refrigerator. The ultimate fantasy was to jump on one and hold on while he ran. Twelve year olds don’t have much in the understanding consequences department do they ? But this day, I would be content just to sit on a big rock with carrots and make friends.
My bribe worked. Pretty soon I was surrounded by six horses milling around trying to get in the best position for carrot hand outs. One of them sidled up to me in an alarming way. Sitting on the rock, my eyes were about level with his flank. He was a big brown and white pinto. The edges of his spots were all jagged, an unusual pinto. And had I been more experienced I would have taken better note of the white showing around his eyes. He pushed closer to me and I put out my hand to shove him away, right on his flank. Bad idea. He whipped around and kicked me off the rock. I involuntarily shielded my face with my arm, so it took the brunt of the kick. The horses thundered off and I picked myself up off the ground. My right arm wasn’t working properly so I cradled it with the left and headed for the house. I almost passed out on the way to the fence, but managed to make it home.
Well, I had a nasty broken elbow and spent the next several weeks in a cast. I was in the sixth grade at the time, and had to learn to write left handed. Which was actually kind of fun. I can still write rather decently with that hand, although the writing looks curiously like a sixth grader still.
Even after the six weeks of healing and the month of exercises after the cast was off, I was still in thrall to the horse spell. I was just a little more wary. I still went into fields with horses in them and one day I actually did get on my neighbor’s horse without as much as a string for a bridle and rode pell mell down the fence line. I was crazed. Horse crazy.
I finally did get my own horse a year or two later, and I stopped fooling around with other people’s thank goodness. After a few years, I sort of grew out of it. Very strange. Oh I still love horses, but I don’t feel the need to ride them or even hang out with them any more.
I got a good look at my old affliction though last summer when I spent a week with my niece who spent every spare moment, and a few we couldn’t spare, at the house next door where a neighbor keeps….horses. She knew all their names and ended up riding two of them before the week was up. At least this time we made sure she had permission. Yep, she has it too. The horse crazy gene. It must run in the family.

Three trips. Last month I went to the past. A place from my past. It seemed almost blasphemous that the place still existed in space though no longer in time. My hometown. I guess a little like the setting of a hallmark movie. It reminded me of who I am. What I was constructed of. What I rebelled against and what I integrated into my matrix. My husband was going to go too, but he wound up coming down with a cold and we couldn't risk exposing my elderly step-grandmother. So, just my son and I went. It was my first time doing a big road trip with just my son and me. …Actually it was my first time ever driving so far. We stayed for two nights and it was my son's first time ever staying a night away from his dad. It was so nostalgic and sentimental driving around my hometown. It felt like being in a dream about the past. Long, winding country road. Uncanny. I'm used to being in the city. The road itself curved both up and down, and side to side in these long snaking arcs. My ears would pop from the changes in altitude. And we were surrounded by pitch-black except for the reflective lines and markers on the road and the occasional traffic lights out in the middle of nowhere. It was almost like driving through outer space! I didn't sleep well at all. I felt nervous, being away from home and being the only adult to protect my son. I felt very vigilant all through the night, like I could hear every little sound in the adjoining hotel rooms. But my hometown was less foreign to me than where I am now. This is my sister's and mother's home but I have no roots or connection here. I am homesick here. The journey was long and turbulent. Our connecting flight was delayed by three hours. My son was a trooper. Someone in the airport approached us to compliment us both. Told him that he was doing a great job being adaptable and helpful, and that I was doing a great job being a patient and accommodating parent. It meant a lot to me. My husband is in India. I had no time to prepare for this trip. My son got sick right after my husband left for his trip. So my son had to come to work with me every day. I am exhausted. I am homesick. I don't think I like it here. I think...my sister did not know that i hate Christmas. I hate Christmas. I hate the sight of Christmas decorations. I tend to have a panic attack every year on Christmas. My sister, trying to dig up what little magic there was in our childhood, and wash it of all the dung it was coated in and forge a better version of it in the fires of nostalgia, had turned my living quarters into an explosion of Christmas festivity. My normal Christmas strategy is to fly to a country where it isn't as widely celebrated. But I simply couldn't make that journey this year. But this town, this state, is alien to me. Much more foreign to me than my husband's country. This place is cold and unforgiving. And imposing mountains loom everywhere in the distance, boxing us in on all sides. I miss my home in the present. With the vibrance of the city skyline greeting every distant gaze. The ever present heat of the heartbeat of the city ever thrumming with human life. There are no neighbors here. The night is pitch black and endless, the beam of my cellphone's flashlight cannot even cut through it, it bleeds away into nothingness. There are no sounds of neighbors upstairs or downstairs or to the side. I'm sure there is life here. My instincts tell me to be wary that it may be the sort of life that perceives me and my offspring as prey. And that I have no safety in numbers here. Cannot rely on the inherent goodness of the vast majority of my species. Anyone out there is a lone and rogue agent, with no predictability. Anyone out there may well be a grizzly or a mountain lion. Everything feels very difficult. Not in my own home, things do not work the way I expect. Even the logistics of hygiene and sleep and making coffee and daily routine are a challenge. My sister had done such a commendable job. Filling up this space with things for me and my son. Like offerings, like tokens of friendship and closeness, like well wishes, she has stuffed the place with well-wishes. But now the place is so cluttered and there's no room for our own things that we packed. I am homesick. I am alone. My sister has left my son and I to our own devices, out in the middle of nowhere. She has put in so much effort, I know I should not complain. But I feel alone and unhosted. I don't know how to drive here. I don't know what to do here. When I return to my city, I will feel whole again, I think. But it's seven more days.

Its been just over three months since the fire now. It's weird how unreal so many things still seem. Time is still crawling by at a snail's pace, but it feels like the world around me is zooming by. Nothing feels real, and I hate that I can't really focus on things that mattered to me. The world (or at least the country) is basically on fire and I'm struggling to care like I used to; it feels like it doesn't matter anymore (in a dark way I almost welcome the end of it all).
Day to day is muscle memory at this point. It's auto-pilot. It's like I'm LARPing as myself. It feels like I'm wearing a mask of "Will" and doing the things playing that role entails. My body is going through the motions it knows it's supposed to, but it's like I'm not the one controlling it anymore. I'm struggling to find the motivation to be "Will" anymore; whatever that means.
I still find myself getting blindsided with reminders of Madelaine and the life we shared. I can't see a black cat or a black/white mix cat without tearing up. There's a giant pit I'm staring into where our life once was. I can distract myself sometimes if I focus on what I'm doing hard enough, and even in those times I can feel that abyss just behind me; patiently waiting for my gaze once more. The quiet, dark solitude which once brought comfort and introspection brings dread and sorrow now. I suppose the dread and sorrow could be the introspection I'm accustomed to in these quiet moments.
I'm trying to get back into things I enjoy as I can. I've been playing Final Fantasy XIV again on a new character so I can play with a friend. It has been nice getting back into the game we enjoyed together, but I've had to stop more than once when something reminds me of our time together. Even when nothing reminds me I'll find myself wishing we were still playing together like we used to. It just doesn't feel the same.
The new apartment is two weeks away. I'm looking forward to having my own space again; it feels like a "Will" thing to want/do. More than anything I'm looking forward to having my own bed again, and a room with blackout curtains. I don't think it's going to feel like home for awhile, though, if anything ever really feels like home ever again.
Been thinking a lot about my relationships and how I want to nurture them better next year. I want to be more present, more intentional, more connected.

Regarding monstergirl's question:
I got the Kitten from Hell the end of last July. Clueless Wonder's breakout started about a week and a half ago or so. While feline acne can be contagious between cats, it is highly unlikely I can blame this one on the KfH. As much as I'd like to.
Cats have oil glands all over their body to help keep their hair waterproof and their skin in good condition. They have extra large ones on their chins and at the bases of their tails though to help mark their territory. Sometimes too much oil can be produced, and just as in humans, this can cause blackheads to form. Bacteria on the skin can multiply and cause infections because of the excess oil. You can end up with acne breakouts that make the cat's chin hair fall out, cause open sores, and make for a very unhappy cat.
Because cats in a multi-cat household usually share water bowls and sometimes food bowls, the bacteria from the affected cat's chin can rub off on the bowls and infect the other cats. Because of this it is important to clean water and food dishes daily when a cat is affected, both to prevent the spread of the infection and to keep the cat from reinfecting itself.
Ringworm is a fungus infection, NOT a disease caused by a worm. Kittens are most usually affected, but they can be carriers, and infect other animals (and people) in the house without showing signs themselves.
I have no idea what to do if a kitten turns out to be a carrier. Whole body treatment is controversial, and there aren't good studies showing it is effective. I'll have to wait and see on that one.
In monstergirl's case, the cat most probably did not have acne, which is almost always confined to the underside of the chin. Ringworm lesions can appear around the eyes, and the kitten could have given ringworm to the cat. But the ringworm would not have cleared up when the kitten disappeared, so that probably wasn't the case either. There's no way of knowing for sure what the problem was there, but kittens play rough and don't always remember to pull their claws in, so the kitten might have inflicted a scratch wound to the cat's face that became slightly infected. Without seeing the cats in question, that's probably the best guess I can muster up at the moment.
Oh, and LisaMarie. The story your uncle told wasn't about ringworm. There is a tropical worm they treat that way though. Can't remember the name off the top of my head, but it has to be pulled out through the skin a millimeter or so each day until it is worked completely out. It's one of those tropical things that make me glad I live way up north where there's a hard frost every winter.

It's 8:42pm. I probably won't have the time or the mental faculties to get back on here to write a full entry, since there's not much to write about today, but I thought I'd quickly test out my new Razer keyboard. I was looking at getting an Alienware keyboard for my computer at work, but I decided against it. I almost didn't get this Razer one, but I saw it at Best Buy and the moment I tested it out on the display model, I knew that I had to buy it. It wasn't a split second decision though. I stood there, writing a full paragraph on it. Fiddling with the backlight. Really taking my time to see if the feel of this keyboard was what I wanted. I decided it was and I bought it. That was around 2:30pm today, and it's been sitting on the passenger seat of my car since then. I decided not to put it in the trunk of my car because I knew it wasn't going to be long before I drove home. I guess I also didn't want to bring it up to my office and deal with that extra hassle either. It wasn't until just over an hour ago when I finally got home, tore it out of the box, and started using it immediately. So far, I'm on the fence. I really like the feel of this keyboard, at least so far, but my fingers are having a difficult time adjusting to the new feel of it. This keyboard, the Razer BlackWidow V4 75% keyboard, feels a lot like my Corsair Strafe keyboard that I have on my work computer, but the keys feel a lot quieter and flatter. I had to change the sound dampening strip that comes in the box. That was no big deal. The keyboard also came with those big wide space bars. I wasn't a huge fan of those. This keyboard looks a whole lot like my Alienware keyboard, but with the bonus and added feature of having a USB-C pass-through, so my phone can stay plugged in while I use my computer. Does it look cool? Hell yeah. Do I think it's going to take some getting used to? Hell yeah. Do I think I made the right decision in buying this keyboard? I'm not sure yet. One more thing, it was cold as hell today. It was 47 degrees Fahrenheit, and I haven't felt that cold of weather in over a year. I'm hoping that this marks an actual change, and that it'll get even colder over the next few weeks. I'm tired of 80-degree weather. That shit can fuck off.

The steering wheel feels colder than I expected tonight, even though it’s already late spring. I can see the glow from the school’s windows reflecting off the hood of my car, and there’s a weird mix of anticipation and exhaustion humming in my chest. I keep replaying my lesson plans for tomorrow in my head, wondering if I’m actually helping my students or if I’m just going through the motions. It’s hard to tell if I’m doing any of this right. I’ve always been organized and tried to keep everything in order, but lately it feels like I’m just barely holding things together—grading papers in the backseat, texting classmates about group projects, making endless lists that never seem to get shorter.

Balancing my own classes with teaching is way harder than I thought it would be. When I was younger, I used to imagine teachers as these put-together adults who had all the answers. Now, sitting here in this parking lot with the faint buzz of the streetlights and the distant sound of someone’s car radio, I feel more lost than ever. I’m restless, constantly thinking about whether I made the right choices or if I’m just settling. There’s this pressure to have some big sense of purpose or identity, but most days I just feel like I’m improvising. I wonder if that’s how everyone feels at this age or if I’m missing something obvious. I’m tired, but I know I’ll still stay up late tonight, worrying about getting everything done. Maybe tomorrow will feel different, but right now, it’s just me and the hum of the engine, trying to find some meaning in all this chaos.

Dearest Diary,
Today was my last shift before my time off. GURL—the amount of nonsense we have to put up with sometimes is beyond me. However, I am grateful for my job and for some of the people I work with. I actually enjoy seeing patients regain their confidence, strut out of the hospital, and leave knowing they're in better shape. Since it's the season of giving, let's talk about that for a minute.
Sometimes, when people bring gifts for nurses or snacks, it's almost always sugary and unhealthy. One of my patient's family members once asked me what I would want. She handed me a packet of Chip Ahoy. I refused and told her I'd rather she brought fruits and smiles. She laughed and asked if Vitamin Water or energy drinks would be better. LOL, gurl, please!
Even when other coworkers bring food, why is it almost always unhealthy? I take fruits to my coworkers, or sometimes dips and veggies. I bake meat buns and all sorts of things.
My second point is when patients give one nurse or worker something as a gift of gratitude because they know we're not paid enough for what we do. Any gift that isn't money—what does one do? When I started here, I was told to outright refuse unless it's snacks or something small, like origami. Today, I had the sweetest patient. The family cooked and saved me a tub of food. My heart melted. I am beyond grateful, especially for homemade meals—they show so much care, in my opinion.
But, like, it's Christmas soon. I have patients trying to give me clothing, cologne, and all sorts. I have to refuse it all. I feel so embarrassed sometimes, especially if they come from a culture where refusing means you'll eventually accept it. Imagine me—holding a pee pan—and the family insisting I take a small basket they made just for me, with compression socks, a warm scarf, and a sweater! Surely they can regift it, but you catch my drift, Diary?
On the other hand, we have those greedy, slimy humans who not only take snacks left for nurses (and other coworkers) but wouldn't even bring a smile when they're around. Just misery and attitude. I'll tell you a comparison story.
I had a patient in one room (on my Halloween-from-hell shift), and the patient next to him—I had to hang IVs for both that night. As I was hanging the nice patient's IV, he kept insisting I take a candy from his Halloween bag that his daughter put together for him to enjoy. I told him I don't eat sweets a lot—especially, offense intended, the ones made in this country! LOL. I eventually took a small candy and came back with an apple for him, joking that an apple a day keeps the doctor away. All this happened while the mean patient was around.
This one didn't even think for a second to offer anything, even though the nice patient gave him a beverage and was being super sweet. I couldn't help myself—when I brought back the apple, I turned to the mean patient and said: "Won't you offer Mr. X something? I see you have loads of snacks." Horrible person replied: "Why should I share?!" Sis, I could have lost all my professionalism and was ready to launch, but Mr. X shyly waved me off and said, "Let it go!"
Anyway, Diary, I am happy I'm going to be off and away. I want to sleep for three days nonstop.
Happy holidays, everyone. Be kind always—first to yourself, then to others.
Much love,
Ross

I keep thinking about how my job is just words on a screen, and yet, those words are supposed to mean something—shape the world, or at least shape an opinion. Sometimes I wonder if I’m losing track of what I actually believe versus what I’m paid to craft, if remote work has made it easier to slip into autopilot. The boundaries between my own thoughts and the assignments are thinner than I’d like to admit.

Still, I can’t deny that I feel good when I finish something challenging, even if it’s at 11:45 pm on a moving bus. There’s a relief in hitting send, even if the work is never really done. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try to unplug for an hour and see what’s left when the notifications stop. Not holding my breath, but maybe.

Info for Abusers
1.Many women say that what they really want is for their abusive partners to take responsibility for their behaviour and go for help.
2.Contact the community services in your area and ask for a referral. Be specific about what you are looking for. Programs may be offered in different languages, or for deaf and hard of hearing men through culturally specific community centres.
3.If you live in an area where there are no services, talk to your family doctor or someone you trust. Look for written information on emotional abuse.
Couples' counselling is not appropriate where abuse is involved. If you are abusive, it is your responsibility to change. Your partner is not responsible for the abuse.
4.Support your partner if she is going for counselling and do not interfere or interrogate her about it.
5.Do it for you! Accept that your partner may leave even if you go for help. Your counselling must not be a way to control your partner or keep her in the relationship. It will still benefit you, your future relationships, and your children

Just finished washing up after dinner, and my mind is still replaying that weirdly nice little conversation I had with the guy from the grocery store earlier. I probably overthought every word I said, but he laughed at my dumb joke about how I only buy tomatoes when I’m feeling optimistic. It felt good to make someone laugh, even if it was just small talk. I’m realizing that meeting new people isn’t always some huge thing, sometimes it’s just these tiny exchanges. Progress, right? Now I keep thinking, maybe this city will start to feel less strange if I let these moments happen.

I felt tired and a little anxious waking up this morning. I spent the first couple hours browsing job boards and sending out applications, but it was hard to focus because my thoughts kept jumping between tasks. The apartment felt quiet, maybe too quiet, and I kept checking my phone hoping for a text or email about an interview. I updated my resume again, rearranged a few lines, then started doubting if I was highlighting the right experiences. I noticed the sunlight on the kitchen counter and realized I hadn’t eaten, so I made some toast and tried to regroup. Most of the day I was distracted, and even writing cover letters, I caught myself rereading sentences over and over. I thought about how much easier it was to network in my old city, but here I don’t really know anyone yet. There’s a job fair next week, so I registered for that, but I’m already worried about how awkward I might feel being in a crowd of strangers. I think I just need to keep putting myself out there, even if it feels uncomfortable. By late afternoon, I decided to take a walk around the neighborhood to clear my head. I noticed a few people chatting outside their buildings but didn’t feel up to introducing myself. Now it’s late and I’m still thinking about what I could have done differently today. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try to set smaller goals so things don’t feel so overwhelming.

I spent most of the afternoon walking around the block, trying to mentally sort out the pile of family logistics that have been building up since the move. The new school registration papers are still sitting on the kitchen table, untouched, and I keep forgetting to call the pediatrician to transfer records. It’s embarrassing how many things are half-finished, like the insurance forms that I start and then lose in the shuffle, or forgetting to update Mom’s contact at the pharmacy. My phone buzzed twice while I was out, both times reminders about appointments I set and then almost instantly forgot about. I keep thinking if I just write everything down in one place I’ll get ahead of it, but I end up with sticky notes everywhere and still feel like I’m missing something important.

I noticed how tense my shoulders were as I walked, probably from sitting at the computer too long and not really getting anywhere with work either. The guilt is there, creeping in every time I catch myself daydreaming or just staring out the window instead of actually calling people back. It’s like I’m juggling all these small but urgent things and not doing any of them well, which is honestly frustrating. I wish I could just pause everything for a day and map out what needs to be done, but I know that’s not how life works. Maybe after dinner I’ll try to organize the paperwork again, or at least set a timer so I don’t get sidetracked. The thought of another week like this makes me feel tired, but I guess I just have to keep chipping away at the list.

The overhead lights on the bus flickered every so often, making the whole aisle feel unsteady, and the constant hum of tires on wet pavement made my head buzz. It was almost midnight and I was just staring out the foggy window, my backpack digging into my shoulder and my phone almost out of battery. I kept replaying the argument with my roommate from earlier—how the kitchen was a mess again and how neither of us could find time to clean it. It’s not even that big of a deal, but every little thing seems bigger when I’m running on five hours of sleep and too many deadlines. My brain felt so full, like there was no room left for kindness, even though I know I want to be understanding. I think maybe we’re both just stretched thin with our schedules; she’s working late shifts, I’m on-call for these never-ending sprints at work, and the apartment feels more like a train station than a home lately. I hate that I snapped at her, but at the same time, I wish she could see how overwhelmed I am too. Sometimes I wonder if we’re just talking past each other, both desperate for the other to notice how hard we’re trying. The bus jerked to a stop and I almost dropped my laptop bag—my hands were shaking, which I didn’t even notice until then. I keep telling myself tomorrow will be better, that maybe if we sit down and talk we’ll figure out a way to make things work. But right now, everything feels so heavy and complicated. The city lights outside blurred into streaks as we sped past, and I just wanted to get home, put on my headphones, and forget about people for a little while. Maybe I’ll text her in the morning. Or maybe I’ll just let things cool off. Either way, I really hope we can find a way to make this place feel lighter again.

The hum of the fridge is louder than I remember, and the early morning light is just barely pushing through the blinds, making odd lines across the kitchen table. I’m standing here in socks, waiting for the kettle to boil, already going over today’s appointments in my head but I keep getting distracted by the pile of pill bottles next to mom’s placemat. It’s funny how routine this has become—crushing her meds into applesauce, checking the mail for bills, layers of care that just sort of attached themselves to my life. My mind is darting between worries about my clients, who bring their own tangled stories, and the nagging feeling that I forgot to reschedule the plumber. I wonder if I even locked the car last night, or did I just imagine doing it while trying to coax mom back to bed at midnight when she thought it was morning. I keep telling myself I’ll start a new exercise routine, or at least carve out ten minutes for stretching, but the day always gets away from me. The kitchen smells faintly of burnt toast even though I haven’t made any in days, maybe it’s just stuck in the toaster tray. I wish I was one of those people who could compartmentalize, but it feels like everything is bleeding into everything else lately, work and home and my own half-formed thoughts. I keep wanting to be more present with my clients, less scattered, but there’s always a part of me running through lists in the background. The bread knife is still out from last night and there are crumbs everywhere, which kind of matches how my head feels. Thinking about dad for a second—he would have made a joke about it being a breadcrumb trail to the coffee pot. I should call my sister but I’m not sure I want to get into another discussion about care plans right now. I keep glancing at the clock, realizing I have less time than I thought, but not moving any faster. Maybe tonight after mom’s asleep I’ll actually just read instead of zoning out to TV. For now, I’ll just stand here a little longer, listening to the fridge and the half-awake world outside, trying to gather myself for another normal, not-so-normal day.

This morning started with my laptop open on the kitchen counter, staring at a calendar full of overlapping meetings that somehow all seem absolutely necessary. The dishwasher was still full and I realized I forgot to defrost anything for dinner, so I had to run through a mental list of what could be thrown together with what’s in the fridge. My phone pinged with a reminder about the team standup, but I was still in pajamas, and the cat kept weaving around my feet, demanding breakfast. I tried to prioritize my tasks for the day, but every time I settled on something, another Slack message popped up or a calendar invite changed. I was supposed to schedule a doctor’s appointment this week, but I keep pushing it off because the idea of finding a slot that doesn’t conflict with work calls is exhausting. Honestly, sometimes the hardest part is just keeping track of who needs what from me, both at work and at home. I wrote out a to-do list on a sticky note and immediately lost it in the shuffle of receipts and grocery lists by the coffee maker. It’s like everything is bleeding into everything else, and I’m not sure when I last had a real break that wasn’t interrupted by someone needing something. I keep telling myself it will get easier if I just organize better, but then a new project lands in my inbox and the whole cycle starts again. This constant juggling act is draining, but I’m holding onto the hope that I’ll figure out some kind of system that actually works for more than a day or two. For now, I’ll just try to get through this list (if I can find it again) and make sure I eat something before my first video call. Maybe I should just set an alarm for every single thing, but even that feels like just another thing to manage.

His tastes are bland -- bread, cheese, meat, potatoes -- he won't eat any fruits or vegetables except potatoes. And I like flavor and spices, and fruit and vegetables, and trying something new. Meat is a side dish, not the main course for me. It took me over a year on my own to realize I don't have to make meals he'll eat anymore. I can have tofu stirfries and Indian curries, African stews and Cajun gumbo, and all the other foods he'd never eat. It's nice to cook for just me, because it used to be I cooked for what my kids would eat and then it was what this middle-aged man-toddler would eat. Now it's just me. Ah, freedom!

Had to clear my head this afternoon, so I took a walk around the block after getting another job rejection. My phone buzzed with a text from Jason, which caught me off guard. We haven’t really talked since that weird argument last week. He said he wanted to talk things out and maybe meet up, but I couldn’t tell if he was actually sorry or just wanted to smooth things over to avoid more awkwardness in the group. Honestly, I’m not sure if I overreacted to what he said, or if I’m right to still be annoyed. It’s been bothering me more than I want to admit, especially since I don’t have a ton of friends here yet.

I kept replaying the conversation in my head as I walked past the same row of empty storefronts. Part of me wants to just move on and forget it, but another part keeps poking at it, wondering if I messed up or if it’s a sign that we’re not really on the same page. I keep thinking about what I should say if we meet up. Should I just be direct and tell him it hurt, or is that making a bigger deal out of things? My anxiety makes me second-guess everything lately, even simple stuff like whether to send a quick reply or wait until I feel less tired. 

By the time I got back to my apartment, I felt a little better, but still unsure. Maybe it’s worth trying to fix things, even if it’s awkward. I do want to feel like I belong here, and keeping things bottled up hasn’t really helped. I’ll probably text him back later tonight. For now, I just needed to write it out and try to get some perspective. Not sure what’s right, but at least I’m thinking about it.
