Today I forgot to log a few small purchases while trying to stick to my budget, which is annoying because every penny counts right now. Spent the afternoon sorting receipts and trying to figure out how to stretch the last bit of my emergency fund through the next two weeks. The desk lamp is the only light on as I write this, and the silence feels heavier than usual. I’m thinking about how uncertain freelancing feels—there’s no steady paycheck, no safety net, and that’s exhausting. Sometimes I wonder if the freedom is worth the stress. I need to fix my tax documents soon but keep putting it off because the numbers make my head spin. I’m tired but can’t sleep yet, maybe because my mind keeps jumping between unpaid invoices and future plans I haven’t made. Honestly, it’s hard not to feel invisible when all your work is remote and the days blur together. At least I have this small space to call mine for now, even if it feels cramped emotionally and financially.

This morning, I was standing in the kitchen, staring at my phone as I checked my email for the third time in twenty minutes. There was nothing new, just the same rejection from yesterday and some spam about online courses. I remember how the countertop felt cool under my hands. Now, a few hours later, I’m walking around the block just trying to shake off this restless energy. The air smells a bit like cut grass, and there’s a kid a few doors down bouncing a basketball against the curb. I keep thinking about the proposal I sent out last week—maybe I should have phrased things differently, or made my portfolio look sharper. My mind keeps circling back to all the places I might have gone wrong, and I can’t help but wonder if I’m missing something obvious that everyone else knows. I keep telling myself that freelancing has always been unpredictable, but lately, the gaps between gigs feel longer and more nerve-wracking. My shoes are rubbing against my heel, and even that small discomfort makes me more irritable. I keep glancing at my phone, half-hoping for some notification—anything, really—but it’s just silent. Every time I try to reassure myself, it doesn’t stick for long. I know I need to keep pushing, but the anxiety feels like it’s always just under the surface, waiting to trip me up. I wish I had a better way to get out of my head on days like this.

The fridge hums in the background while sunlight cuts through the blinds onto the kitchen table. I’m eating leftovers, but not really tasting anything. My mind keeps floating back to the call I had with Mom this morning.

She sounded tired, her voice smaller than usual. When she mentioned Dad’s checkup, there was this pause. I could hear her trying to sound normal but I know her too well. I kept thinking about what I should say, how I could fix it or if I was just making it bigger than it is. It’s hard not being home, especially now. I wonder if I should book a flight or just wait for more news.

Moving here was supposed to be a fresh start, but I feel unsteady, like I’m still waiting for something to settle. I keep checking my phone for updates, even though I know there probably won’t be any. Lunch break is almost over and I haven’t really rested. Everything feels in-between lately.

Last night, I dreamt of her in a strangely vivid way. She had come back from overseas and we met in a place filled with many brown tents. She was wearing exactly what she wore the last time I saw her. I asked her about her life, and she told me she was divorced now and very happy. She also revealed something she had denied before, something that felt chilling but, somehow, I felt a strange sense of relief hearing it. We walked together between the tents, talking about her life. She told me she had met someone after me, but the relationship didn't last because he cheated on her. She said she had always missed me. Then, out of nowhere, she held my face in her hands and kissed me. Suddenly, the scene shifted. We were at a shop with banners and placards outside. She asked me to wait while she went inside. More and more people appeared, and the shop area became crowded. I saw her come out for a moment, but I lost her in the crowd. The scene changed again, this time to the old path we used to walk on together. She told me she was waiting for me. I asked her how I could get to the country she lives in now. And that's when the dream ended.

I felt oddly steady as I rode the bus home late last night, pressed against the cool window, watching streetlights flicker over empty sidewalks. The hum of the engine and the faint scent of rain on the seats gave me a quiet place to think. Lately, I’ve been wondering if I’m still the same person I was before coparenting became my life’s structure, before my calendar was a mess of drop-offs and writing deadlines. Sometimes I miss the me who didn’t have to coordinate everything—who could just disappear into a story for hours and not resurface until I was hungry. Now, it’s all reminders and shared apps, always someone else’s schedule to consider. I do love the warmth of my little family, but I keep asking myself where writing fits, who I am outside the roles I juggle. Maybe I’m just restless, but there’s a kind of comfort in the uncertainty too, like standing at a crossroads and realizing you don’t have to pick a direction yet. Last night, watching my reflection in the dark bus window, I almost recognized myself.

The sky seemed wintry this morning, gray. The temperatures were predicted to be in the high 80s to low 90s. A little warm for this time of the year, but it didn't happen. The sun just couldn't send its blessed heat through the pall of smoke from the forest fires.
Two counties around Sacramento, and one county a little farther east are beset with forest fires. This is the first time in my recollection that fires have come so close to this metropolitan area.
Yes, the sky was gray, overcast with smoke. The sun was an orange ball in the sky with clearly defined border, not usually apparent to the naked eye. I did make the mistake of looking directly at the sun, and clouded as it was, I still had an after-image for several minutes. Dumb thing to do because we're told not to look directly even at a total eclipse because of the chance of retinal damage.
But it was a gorgeous color. Like a brilliantly polished dark golden orb.
For awhile it was only smoke obscuring the sky, then later when I went out to the car, I noticed very fine ash falling all around.
So far about 50,000 acres have burned, but no homes or lives lost. Our firefighters are true heroes. The TV news this evening showed a firefighter standing on the roof of a house and spraying it with water in an effort to save the home.
Another shot showed a woman who had packed some belongings and her children in the family's SUV, and saying how grateful she was that her home had been saved.
The latest report says that the fires are about 10% contained, and firefighters say they hope they'll be fully contained by Saturday. As long as the wind doesn't come up, they probably will be. The weather reporter showed a weather map of the expanse of smoke from these fires. The smoke goes clear to the coast.
Oh, yes, and I probably should be inside with all the windows closed and the fans going. The air quality is very bad for people like me with pulmonary problems, but I'll be going out again tomorrow. Need some groceries. I won't starve if I don't go shopping, but I'd really like to have some more fruit in the house. Tch! I can't make do for a few more days until the air clears???
**********
I know there's a Black Hole in this apartment. Things keep disappearing. And reappearing in the oddest places.
I bought a book a couple weeks ago in anticipation of a class that started this evening. I started reading in it, then decided to put it aside until the class started. To get the full benefit of the text, the Rabbi's input and interpretation are needed.
But now I can't find the book.
I've checked my bookcases, and under the furniture. In my bedroom, although I seldom read there. I've looked everywhere except where the book is. I do hope the Black Hole spits it out before next Thursday.
Have you ever used scissors, put them down near at hand, then couldn't find them when you reached out for the instrument so you could finish the job? Then later, maybe an hour, maybe a day, there they are, right where you put them down????
Let me tell you that if you're afflicted with a Black Hole in your home, you are truly afflicted!
Oh, yes, and the ten pounds of Ghirardelli chocolate. I've managed to foist off some of it on a neighbor. Will hack of great chunks of it and take to my daughter when I return her daughter to her on Sunday. The Black Hole hasn't touched that. Yet. In the meantime, I think my chocoholism has been satisfied for the nonce.
Shalom

One of my absolute favorite poems is this one by Emily Dickinson.
I am Nobody! Who Are You?
by Emily Dickinson
I'm nobody! Who are you?
Are you nobody, too?
Then there's a pair of us--don't tell!
They'd banish us, you know.
How dreary to be somebody!
How public, like a frog
To tell your name the livelong day
To an admiring bog!
What a phrase, "how public like a frog"
And underneath of course is the desire in all of us to be "somebody". I guess the problem comes when one has to decide WHO is going to say you have arrived at the coveted "somebody" stage. There are certain yardsticks I never want to be measured by !
Anyway, in the spirit of the poetical theme of this post, I offer one of my
own, with apologies to Emily for sharing the same page. (Do you think she would think me an upstart, a "toad" ? )
Clouds Without Rain
Heavy clouds tried and succeeded
In obscuring the full moon.
A racing wind blew them about.
And on the edge of this wind rode a nameless desire.
Desire so raw, astonishing in it’s ignorance,
That it could almost masquerade as purity.
But alas, ignorance is no excuse
Even in the face of such a grand illusion.
I stood on such a windy night
Smelling the wildness in the buffeting blows.
That wind, at once warm and cold
Confused my senses and deluded my will.
I thought I would be mistress of its power
And invited it to blow through me
Thinking I might become very wise indeed.
I opened wide a door that I should have guarded well.
That windy night is over now
It’s promise of rain never fulfilled.
And come to think of it
All it’s other mysterious promises broken too.
Oh yes, the door flung open, awaiting enlightenment,
Must now be rebuilt at great expense.
Beware dark windy nights of seeming high adventure
Lest you awaken unprepared in a strange land.

There’s a half-finished mug of chamomile tea next to my laptop, and I keep staring at the golden rim, feeling like I should be winding down but my brain is spinning. Tonight was another argument with Mom about her medications—she insists she doesn’t need the new ones, and I’m trying to be patient, but I snapped. I hate that I lose my cool, especially when I know she’s scared and stubborn because she’s losing control over her own life. The guilt hits hard, like a weight that doesn’t lift no matter how many deep breaths I try to take.

The project at work is dragging, too—every email I open feels like a little landmine. I caught myself zoning out in the middle of a Zoom call, thinking about whether I remembered to lock up her prescriptions. My team expects answers, but honestly I’m barely keeping track of who needs what. I keep wondering if I’m missing something obvious that would make all of this easier, but there’s always another problem to pick apart. It’s exhausting to always be the one who has to figure it out, both at home and at work.

I wish I had someone to talk to who really gets it, but every time I try to open up to friends they just tell me I’m strong and I can handle it. That just makes me feel more alone, honestly. The desk lamp is too bright and I should go to sleep, but I’m just not ready to let go of the day, even if it’s been a mess. Maybe tomorrow I’ll apologize to Mom, or maybe I’ll just do better. I don’t even know what doing better looks like anymore.

Earlier today, when the day was just beginning, I caught a glimpse of the schedule pinned to the bulletin board at work. It looked like a bad joke—double shifts lined up next to classes I still have to cram for this week. I laughed to myself, dry as always, thinking how somehow I signed up for this circus. Now, walking around the block tonight, the cool air barely cuts through the tight knot in my stomach. The streetlights are flickering badly, just like my patience.

I keep reviewing the list in my head, ticking off things that keep piling up: approving time sheets before tomorrow, sorting out that mess with the night crew, and somehow squeezing in reading for the midterm on Friday. It feels like my calendar is a game of Tetris, pieces falling faster than I can place them. The family stuff waits for me too, unchecked emails from the school, text reminders about the dentist appointment for next week that I promised to confirm. At least the walk clears the noise a bit, but by the time I get back, it’s just more papers and screens to stare at. The hope is that all this juggling will look better in hindsight, but the weight of it all keeps me on edge. Maybe tomorrow I’ll laugh about it again, or maybe I’ll just keep pretending I’m not a mess.

A plane down in Queens. I know better, but my mind jumps ahead of events. It's telling how much I (and others) are still affected by September 11. Never before would I have immediately put terrorism at the top of my list of differentials. But I recognize this as a weakness in myself, and am ashamed of it.
The reactions of people around me mystify. Intensify the call to arms, name calling, the need to blame a known enemy. Let it rest, people. Let it be. It doesn't help our case to blindly blame. We have reason enough for war without the need to manufacture or jump to conclusions. Either this was due to foul play or not. No point in calling for justice until we know where the guilt lies. The experts have this in hand. Let them do their job. Let it be.
Regardless. My petty problem pales in comparison. My site meter will tell all in the end anyhow. Future actions will be determined by facts, not fears. May my fellow countrymen follw the same philosophy on matters more grave than my small problems.
I am back.

Hey, just learned something. Thought some of you would like it. Ok, lets say you have a pic on your computer. IF you want to make it a icon on your computer, follow these steps.
1. Download IrfanView *a image viewer program that is less than 1mb* You can find this at download.com* In the search part, type Irfanview
2.open the program
3.Open the picture through file, then open.
4.Then go up to Image, then resize/resample
5.Put the width as 65, the lenght 78 push ok
6. Next, go to save as. In the save as, pick where you want to save, and *important* change the file type to ICO, windows icon. REMEMBER WHERE YOU SAVE IT AT!!!
7. Choose the icon you want to change, like winamp. Right click and pick properties.
8. click on change icon. NOw, search for the file you saved. Push browse to search. Go to the place you saved at. IF you saved it on the desktop, C:\WINDOWS\Desktop. If the icon is in a folder on the desktop. C:\WINDOWS\Desktop\Iconfolder *iconfolder is the name of the folder* IF you named the folder games. IT would be C:\WINDOWS\Desktop\games
Hope this helps you ppl, if you have any trouble, or want to thank me, leave a comment.

Spent too much time today juggling calls about parts and delivery dates. The backlog on the orders list keeps growing, and I can’t shake the feeling that I’m losing control of the shop. It’s weird, though — when I’m under pressure like this, I start questioning if this is really who I want to be at 50. The mechanic who can’t fix his own life. The thought makes me cringe. Maybe I’m just tired, or maybe I need a plan that actually works instead of just hoping for scraps. Either way, I’m stuck sitting here with a dozen half-finished tasks and a brain that won’t stop running in circles. Coffee might help tomorrow, but right now it’s just the same old grind. At least I’m trying, and that has to count for something.

**Around half a million letters a year go to Santa Claus's Main Post Office in Rovaniemi, Finland, along the Arctic Circle.** That might be far away from you, but it's the closest post office to the actual location: The North Pole. Who knows, maybe you'll be one of the lucky few to receive a reply from Santa himself. There's nothing like Christmas morning for many of us, even if we're getting quite old now. There's that sense of anticipation, the aroma of something delicious being cooked, the clamour of excited little voices and perhaps the snow falling outside. But if you can't be with family or don't have family, you can create new memories with other people who are important to you in other places. Whatever you are doing this Christmas, and wherever you are, I hope you feel that sense of anticipation, enjoy something delicious, and feel the warmth of being cared about. If you wake to find some snow in the morning, take a picture and share it, please!

The wind was a little stronger than I expected when I stepped out this afternoon, but I needed the break. My shoes made that familiar sound on the sidewalk, and I tried not to think about emails or the stack of forms waiting on my desk. Instead, I focused on the cold air, the way the sun kept dipping in and out behind the clouds. There’s a neighbor’s garden on the corner—hyacinths just starting to bloom. I paused and smelled them, even though I knew I didn’t have a lot of spare time. 

Work was steady today. I answered more phone calls than I care to count, then squeezed in some reading for my history class at lunch. Sometimes I wonder if going back to school at my age is worth it, but today I felt okay about it. The chapter I read made sense, and I actually remembered most of it. I keep telling myself it’s just one assignment at a time. That helps, mostly. 

On the last stretch of the block, I let myself slow down a little. My mind felt clearer, not racing. The quiet was nice—just the sound of my own steps and some birds in the distance. Tonight I’ll have to get back to the usual routine: dinner, more reading, and a couple of work emails I didn’t finish. But right now, I feel alright. Maybe even a little proud of keeping it all moving, even if it’s not perfect.

Just finished making a piece of toast at the counter, trying not to wake anyone up even though I know someone will come in soon and ask what I’m doing up so early. The kitchen light is so harsh at 5:15, bouncing off the chipped mug I grabbed too fast, and I keep thinking about how I never actually get a moment to myself in this house. I feel like I’m always rushing—between the garage, errands, and random family stuff—never really stopping to ask what I’m even working toward. Sometimes it feels pointless, like I’m just going through the motions, tightening bolts, fixing other people’s mistakes, and still not being seen for who I am. I keep getting these restless thoughts, like I should be somewhere else or someone else, but then I don’t even know what that means. Every day lately I feel this weird pressure in my chest, not exactly anxiety but like something’s missing, and the noise in the house never shuts off enough for me to figure it out. The toast is cold now, and I’m thinking about tonight, how I’ll probably just crash as soon as I get home, but part of me wants to sneak away and just sit in the car, alone, if I can. I wish I could talk to someone about all this, but everyone’s too busy or wouldn’t get it, so I end up rambling here instead. I can’t believe how quickly the days blur together, and I keep wondering if it’s always going to feel like I’m behind, like I’m waiting for something that won’t come. Maybe I’ll try to take a walk later, just for a few minutes, if I can find an excuse to get out of the house without anyone following me.

Feeling neutral this morning, just waiting in the car before heading in. I got here early again, which is starting to feel like a habit. I looked up from my phone and saw two classmates arguing near the entrance. It was about something small, parking spaces I think, but the way their voices carried made it sound bigger. I kept my distance, didn’t want to get pulled in, but part of me wondered if I should’ve said something to cool things down. I’m not really the type to jump into other people’s business though. It’s strange how I can be organized with my own stuff but avoid messy situations like that. I went through my notes for today’s seminar, double-checking the readings. I keep thinking if I’m being too careful, or if it’s just part of how I deal with being around people. Living alone makes it easy to not have to deal with these frictions, but every time I step out, there’s always some tension somewhere. I guess you can’t really avoid it, even if you plan your days down to the minute. The parking lot is quieter now, just a few cars rolling in. I’ll go inside soon, try to keep my head clear and focused. Sometimes I wonder if I’m missing out by not getting involved more, but I also know I like things calm. For now, I’m fine staying in my lane.

My backpack is digging into my shoulder as the bus lurches through another intersection. I can see the city lights flickering past the smudged window, reflecting a bit of how scattered I feel inside. Today was a rush—another round of job applications, a quick sandwich in the park, and a long walk to clear my mind before heading home. I keep replaying the interview call I had earlier; maybe I sounded too eager, or maybe that's a good thing? There's so much I don't know about how people settle in new places, but I'm realizing there are tiny moments—like recognizing the bus driver's face or figuring out which stop is mine—that make things feel a little less foreign. My feet ache and my eyes are burning, but I can't help feeling a small surge of hope every time I check my inbox. Maybe tomorrow I'll hear good news. For now, I just want to take off my shoes and let the quiet of my new apartment wrap around me.

I didn't give her breakfast of course. No point in reloading her with more ammo, if her stomach was still fluttery. She was hungry, though, and screamed at me as I left the apartment. Just finished making a half-hearted attempt at breakfast, staring at the toaster while it hums. The kitchen is colder than usual this morning, and the hum of the fridge is the only background noise. I’m trying to get my head together before my roommate comes in and the day really begins. Juggling the schedules here has been a logistical nightmare lately, especially since my work hours shifted last week. I keep thinking about Dad’s last call—he sounded weaker, and it’s been eating at me. I feel like I should book a trip home, but I’m worried about missing deadlines at work, and the guilt is just… constant. The bread popped up, almost burnt, and I realized I hadn’t even paid attention. It’s like my mind keeps cycling between family worry and engineering projects, without settling on either. I wish I could compartmentalize better, but everything seems to bleed together. Still, I’m trying to stay hopeful; maybe if I organize my tasks more strictly, it’ll help. The sunlight coming through the window made me pause for a second—reminded me there’s still good stuff happening, even if it’s small. I’m not sure how much longer I can keep up this pace, but I’m determined to find a way. If I can just keep moving, maybe things will settle down. There’s a meeting at 9, but all I can think about is calling home again. The sense of responsibility to everyone pulls me in so many directions. I know I need to take care of myself too, but I haven’t figured out how to fit that in. Maybe tomorrow I’ll start a run before breakfast. For now, I’ll just try to focus on the next thing in front of me.

This afternoon, I caught myself smiling when I remembered my mom’s way of telling jokes, always a little awkward but somehow endearing. It’s funny how those small things stick with you, especially when you’re in a new city and your own voice feels lost in the noise around you. Tonight, sitting alone in the dim light of my apartment, I’m suddenly hit by how little I get to hear her laugh or complain about my messy room. It’s strange how grief sneaks up on you unexpectedly during moments you think you're distracted.

My shift was nonstop chaos, the kind where you barely have time to breathe, which honestly helped push thoughts away. But now that it’s quiet, I’m restless, my mind racing from one thing to the next. I wonder if my mom would have thought I’m handling this new job well, or if she’d tell me to slow down a bit and stop trying to prove something to everyone. Sometimes I feel like I’m building this whole new life on shaky ground, trying to make sense of who I am without the family I grew up with standing right behind me. Maybe it’s still too soon to know what I want or who I’m really becoming here.

I guess what’s hardest is the uncertainty of it all. How do you hold onto yourself when everything about your life feels different, when the people you relied on aren’t just a call away? It’s late, but sleep won’t come yet. I keep flipping through memories and conversations, wondering if I missed a chance to say the right thing, or if maybe I’m reading too much into silence. Still, there’s a flicker of hope that with time, this restless feeling will settle, and I’ll find my place—not just in this city, but inside myself too. 🌙

The clock ticks louder than usual during this lunch break, fluorescent lights buzzing overhead. My sandwich sits half-eaten on the desk, and I keep glancing at my planner, trying to make sense of the jumble of notes scribbled in different colors. The parking lot lights flicker a bit tonight, making the asphalt look patchy under the dull glow. I’m here early, hands fumbling with my keys, replaying the morning’s conversation with Jamie. We both spoke over each other, the calendar mix-up for the kids dragging on longer than it should have. It’s frustrating how even with all the reminders and schedules, something always slips through. 

Work’s pressure isn’t helping either. I forgot the special order twice during the morning rush, and there’s a nagging feeling I’m losing my grip. I pride myself on being organized, but today I felt scatterbrained, every detail slipping away. It makes me question if I’m juggling too much, or if I just need to slow down and focus. Maybe a better system could help, but I’m always so restless, jumping ahead before I’ve finished the last task.

I glance at the old coffee shop across the street, the one I sometimes think about opening again someday. For now, I just want to get through tonight without more snafus. The quiet here now won’t last, though. Soon the night crew will arrive, and the rush will begin. I just hope I don’t lose my patience this time.

New Job, New Chapter?
Getting a job can feel a bit like gambling. You can tick all the right boxes only to be told on your interview day that it's going to be difficult for them to choose. There is so much competition for the role, you're one of many who applied and you may be unsuccessful. I'm 38, not 18, so this isn't my first rodeo in the job arena and it all feels slightly patronising to have this explained to you as a grown woman with a wealth of job experience, and qualifications up the wazoo. That little document you sent in trying to "sell" yourself says as much. It takes a great deal of patience to not roll my eyes. Somehow interviews expose you, like a raw, painful, nerve where they like to pick and prod at you to see if you have what it takes to perform to their standards.
So not only do you have to have the skills, explain how they apply to the role and prove you are an upstanding company supporter. You have to market yourself as someone who won't stir the waters too much or speak up too often. They want someone who is pliable, who does the job and doesn't complain, someone they can stick in a position and forget about for the most part. That's exactly the kind of employee my local council is looking for, and that's exactly the person I presented to them during my interview. All for a basic cleaning position at a local primary school. Something to help plug the money gap as I struggle in trying to breathe life back into my art career. A "dream" that never quite took off after college or university as we prioritised the husbands career first. Something for another time.
But yes, whatever I presented at the interview was approved enough that I've landed a new position as "Cleaner" for the local council. Not the most glam of jobs, but at a couple of hours Monday through Friday each week and 24k+ annually, I can hardly complain. In theory I can put some pennies away whilst devoting most of my time figuring out where the hell I go with my art.

I don’t do social media, no Facebook or Insta or X, etc. I don’t believe in forming a clique of people and excluding others. Morning Diary,
Was just staring into the mirrored shelf in my office. Staring at my teeth.
haha
Ive been wanting to get my teeth whitened for years. But its $150 for just the top or bottom. $300 total and insurance doesnt cover that sorta thing.
I was at the gym awhile ago and they have a sign in the bathroom for these Crest Whitening Strips. Im like "Ah why not?" it says you can get a refund if they dont work.
But I couldnt find them in the store each time I looked in the toothpaste isle. Then I found them! Ouch almost $40 for a box.
I debated for several weeks. I didnt want to waste $40 either, just assuming most store or products like this dont really work. But hey its money back guarantee so?
So after weeks of debating thought why not?
So you have to place 2 strips a day on your teeth for 30 min each time. Top teeth first. You can only get the refund if you have used only the TOP strips and no results.
So day after day I have walked around with this little piece of film on my teeth for 30 min twice a day.
I go and look in the mirror and see nothing, ::sigh:: damn store gimmicks!
When the H was here I told him that I was trying this out, he said he could tell, he could? He said yeah its kinda blotchy but you can tell.
THe booklet said it may be blotchy n stuff at first.
So here I am at the final end, maybe about a weeks worth left of upper strips, and a few days ago I looked in the mirror again. Umm I can tell a difference!
FIgures I get to the end of the strips before I notice, most people give up before this point and dont wait.
And the good part about doing the top first is you can compare with your bottom teeth.
Yeah so call me a test case for Crest. HA!
Says results will vary for people.
Only thing that is annoying is a few spots on my teeth where the braces once were, its really white where the brackets were attached. And wonder if there is even a way to blend that.

I still haven't managed to go a twelve hour period without crying. I still see Madelaine in so many things; it hurts, but I also hope I never stop seeing her everywhere? The idea of moving forward or moving on still fills me with dread. I hate the idea of living a long life.
The holiday season is coming up, which means a month of 14-16 hour days and 6 days a week in the box mines. I'm simultaneously looking forward to the lack of time to think about things and dreading the holidays themselves. It had become a tradition at this point to do a giant slow cooker pot of mashed potatoes for Thanksgiving. I got to help Madelaine by doing a some of the more menial tasks (peeling potatoes, grating cheese, dishes, etc) so she could focus on the cooking portions. I miss offering support for the things she enjoyed; usually I would try to focus on related tasks you didn't enjoy so you could focus on what you did enjoy about what you were doing.
I have a new apartment set up for just after the new year which I think is nice. It'll be a fourth floor walk up so at least I'll be getting my steps in. It's a nice space as far as apartments go, but I still don't want to think about a living space without Madelaine included. I keep looking back at the lead ups to us moving in together and how excited we were to be sharing our space. I want to go back to that, please?
I'm trying to keep going forward, and I'm taking the first baby steps even if I'm not happy about it. I keep wishing I could just have our life together back. I miss Madelaine. I miss Merlin and Morgan. I miss my life? I don't want to have to consider who I am now in this worse version of the world that existed a month ago. I know I'm going to have to, but at least I have the next month to be a box mine robot to dissociate through before I have to get there.

Yesterday, I was invited to stop by my boss's house to pick up the Sweet Potato Casserole that she insists on making my son. I can make it, but she loves to do it for both me and my coworker Vicky. Vicky says the recipe is from her mother-in-law and it's amazing. So I stopped by and got the casserole and also got to see her adorable new kitten. Then I stopped by Publix to pick up a few last minute items for Christmas. The store was packed, and parking was almost impossible but I managed. When I got back in the car, I couldn't help but think about how different the Christmas season is now. I remember when I was younger and my mom would take me shopping. We'd go to the mall and she'd let me pick out something special. Those were good times. But now I'm the mom, and my son is grown, and we're all just trying to make the best of the season. When I got home, I started wrapping gifts. I had bought my son a few things - some clothes, a book he'd been wanting, and a gift card to his favorite restaurant. I also got him a framed photo of him and his late father from when he was about 5 years old. I know that will mean more to him than anything else. My son's father passed away several years ago, and the holidays are always bittersweet because of it. But we try to focus on the good memories. Today is Christmas Eve and I'm just relaxing. I've already done all the prep work for tomorrow's dinner. The ham is ready to go in the oven, the sides are prepped, and dessert is in the fridge. All I have to do tomorrow is put it all together. My son will come over around noon and we'll exchange gifts and have a nice meal together. It's simple, but it's perfect for us. I hope everyone has a wonderful Christmas!

Harry sat quietly in his overstuffed armchair. He was watching the birds hopping on the fir tree in the side yard. There was a gentle early winter breeze blowing with just enough cold in it to warn of the gathering storms heading in from Siberia.
He was mulling over a particularly complex philosophical question. But without others at hand to test his thoughts, to try them on for size, he was feeling a bit grumpy. This was the story of his life. Lots of alone time working puzzles in his head, but rarely being able to take them out for a spin amid the possible opposition of real people.
So there was the very annoying suspicion that perhaps after all, it was all drivel. All this stuff rattling about in his own mind. It was like eating sandwiches made of bread alone.
He was a rather dumpy man with a poochy stomach and a caved in chest encased in a brown and yellow plaid shirt. That shirt was at least 15 years old and frayed at collar and cuff. But he kept wearing the thing. Made you want to take him shopping just to look at it. Maybe buy something crisp and starchy new, something periwinkle blue and white with a pair of navy trousers. Then go out and make a fire with the old clothes and toast s’mores over the coals.
Martha came into the room.
“What would you like on your sandwich Harry?”

“Whatever is handy dear.”

She opened the fridge and reached for the peanut butter, pushing aside the package of pepper jack cheese she had bought on a whim that morning at the grocery.

Last night when I was getting ready for a wash-up before going to bed I discovered there was no hot water. Hmmm.
So I went out to the laundry room to see if anyone had meddled with the thermostat again. Nope.
The heater was leaking and the laundry room was half-way flooded. That explained it. So I called the Manager (after hours, of course) and left a message on her phone. For once she was on the ball.
There are plumbers in the laundry room now, as we speak, installing a huge, energy-efficient water heater. The boss plumber assured me that we would have hot water by this evening. But that got me to thinking (a dangerous exercise here).
I remember when Aunt N and Uncle E (on the farm) didn't have indoor plumbing. Can you imagine going out to the privy at night in the middle of December? I don't think so. That's why we had thunder mugs in our bedrooms. And I found out why they were called thunder mugs. (Oh, use your imagination!)
There was a large wood stove in the kitchen with a water reservoir for hot water for dishwashing and the like. Warm water for "spit" baths. But laundry days were a different matter.
I remember a HUGE washtub on the wood stove, scrub boards and lye soap. First the whites were boiled and scrubbed, then the colors, then the work clothes. Then there was the matter of rinse water.
But after everything was clean, I remember laundry being hung on what seems like miles of clothesline. But, oh, how sweet the clothes smelled when they were dry and brought in to be folded, hung up, or otherwise put away.
Later Aunt N got a gas-powered washing machine. She still had to heat water for the machine, but it sure beat the laundry tub! She had a rinse water tub and a hand-cranked wringer. Still the lye soap. I don't remember bleach of any kind, but with lye soap, bleach isn't needed.
Every Saturday night, we bathed in a huge tub set in the middle of the kitchen. Water had to be heated for the tub, of course. The men were elsewhere when the women were bathing. And the women had other things to do when the men bathed. Can you imagine the amount of water that had to be heated for, let's see...6 people while I was living there, and 5 when I was living "in town."
The summers were different. We took towels, soap and shampoo and went to The Dam. The women went first, and then the men went upstream a ways and completed their ablutions. Then when everyone was clean, we all put on our bathing suits and swam until almost dark.
There was a stream up on the mountain, and Uncle E tapped into that and brought cold, clean water into the kitchen. But no faucets. You wanted water, you "primed" the pump and then pumped like crazy until water came flowing out. That also was the water that was put in the stove reservoir, and the water that was heated for bathing, dishwashing and laundry.
So the next time you have to call the plumber, be grateful you have something to call the plumber for.
Shalom

The refrigerator hums louder than usual while I stand here waiting for the kettle to boil. Too early for anyone else to be awake, but already I’m thinking about what needs to be done today—meals to prep, medications to double-check, doctor’s appointments to confirm. There’s a faint smell of toast from yesterday lingering, mixed with the lemon dish soap. I wish I could just sit in the quiet, but my mind’s racing with lists, worries, things I might have forgotten.

Sometimes I wonder if anyone really sees how much I hold together or if the whole thing would just unravel if I took a single day off. No one ever says it out loud, but it feels like I’m just supposed to keep going, whatever happens. I’m tired. Not just this morning, but deep down. I look at my hands wrapped around the mug and they look older than I remember. When did that happen? I used to think I’d have done something else with my life, something that felt more like mine. Now it’s just this routine, taking care of everyone else, always being needed but never really being asked what I need.

Maybe it’s selfish to want something different at this age. I tell myself I’m lucky to have people to care for, a home, even if privacy is a joke. But I can’t help feeling invisible some days. I wonder if it’s too late to change anything or if this is just who I am now—a caregiver before anything else. The kettle whistles and I snap out of it. Time to get on with it, I guess.

Lunch break now, but my mind’s spinning in three directions. Mom’s voice was shaky on the phone this morning. She said she’s still not sleeping well since Dad passed. I tried to sound reassuring, but I don’t know what to say—grief seems to rearrange everything, even the way time moves. The house is too quiet since he died. I catch myself looking for things to fix that just aren’t there. The only thing I could offer was to order her groceries online, which feels pretty thin, all things considered. 

I know there’s a lot I’m supposed to be handling: keeping up with client work, checking on my own health (the back pain’s worse on days like this), and making sure Mom doesn’t slip through the cracks. But if I’m honest, I feel like I’m just patching holes as they come up, not really fixing anything long-term. The logical part of me says to make lists and tackle each issue, but lately even the lists have started to blur together. Maybe I need a stricter schedule, or maybe I just need to accept that things aren’t going to line up neatly for a while. For now, I’ll finish this sandwich and get back to troubleshooting the truck. One thing at a time, even if the rest of it stays messy.

So one night he talked to my girlfriend about being interested in me. And they sat for hours in her car that night at a youth group event. And she came out and said "S, Ive got good news, H is a Christian"

The H and and I held hands to pray. I hadnt really ever done anything like that with him, we just hung out.
So here is where MY mind started the fast path to ASSUMPTION.
I began to feel an attraction from that holding hands during prayer, and in my own mind assumed my H to be a strong Christian man.
I had in my own mind what a boyfriend who was a christian would be like, and imposed my fairytale on my H. In my mind he was what God had sent me. This is what God wanted for me.
The reality of it all was, my H was a new baby christian so hes told me. He been in church for one month, Had dated one of the leaders daughters from the church but once they found out he wasnt a christian, well it lasted about a month. He had told me also had groped her once under her shirt. He started going to church there because he still wanted to see her, but said that he started to go for himself and like it.

I didnt want for much, and I wasnt desiring a physical relationship. I ended all of our dates with prayer, wed sit in his truck and Id pray before hed drop me off at home at my curfew time.
One night he laid on the floor watching tv together at my house in the living room. My parents were home. And we were snuggled under a blanket.
That was the night he touched me for the first time, he reached under my shirt, and I froze. I was confused, and I just froze, I didnt enjoy it at all, yet I wasnt able to say No. I was sort of in shock. This guy is a Christian? He knows my stance? And he says he loves me?

That he said he was sorry. And he wouldnt do it again, and I had been taught to forgive.

From then on there is example after example of behavior like this. Him doing things I find contrary to my beliefs, me feelings guilt and sorrow for partaking in the actions, then after time I start to take part in the same actions.
I did not know how to stand up for myself, to be independent of a guy, I wanted love so bad, I took it how it was.

We read verses like "its better for a man to marry than to burn with lust" thinking that our ultimate goal is marriage here. Finally heard from The Professor, who made a quick pass through cyberspace last night. He found a way to download one of the digital pictures from his camera onto the net (don't ask me how; I didn't think he brought any of the hardware or software for doing that with him on the trip).
He also left me a message that his grandfather is in the hospital, although I suspect it is only temporary. The Prof took him to his chemotherapy treatment yesterday, but when they started administering the drugs his grandfather started having heart fibrillations, so they immediately stopped and admitted him for observation. Colonel Grandfather isn't handling things well, and the upset is spilling over to The Prof, who doesn't know how to deal with his grandfather's emotions nor his own emotions. I don't think that the situation at present is serious, but if The Prof's grandfather continues to be unable to tolerate the chemotherapy, there will be realities that have to be faced.
An emotionally remote grandfather in denial, facing mortality for the last time. An adopted son, who is far more like his grandfather than he'd ever care to admit, in denial, facing mortality for the first time. It's a story older than recorded history. But for all the times it has been played out over the course of human events, I don't think anyone has ever come up with any answers to help the grieving. I hope these two men find a way to make a connection while they still have the time.
And there I am, an outsider privy to the proceedings but not really part of them. It drives home why Colonel Grandfather wants us to move out there and in with them so badly. The Prof said that while he was in the hospital his grandfather kept asking who'd take care of his wife, who would look after Grandmother. I do not doubt that the man is upset, but there remains a component of manipulation in this. Which makes it all the harder for the Professor.
For my own part, I feel caught in the middle. I have tons of good advice to dispense, but this is not a situation where advice is necessarily appropriate. I did not grow up with Colonel Grandfather as my father. My childhood was not the Professor's childhood, and my relationship with my father is not necessarily analogous to The Prof and Colonel Grandfather. My role might be the easiest of anyone's, but it's still hard. Be there, offer a listening ear and compassion, and keep my opinions to myself.
I hate keeping my opinions to myself.

The package for the online customer never showed up in the tracking system this morning, so I spent almost an hour bouncing between the shipping dashboard and the help chat. I get anxious when things slip through, even if it’s not really my fault. The silence in the house at lunchtime feels strange, almost like it’s pressing on my ears. I keep looking at my phone, half-expecting a notification from the warehouse, but it’s just group texts and sale alerts. My sandwich was soggy because I forgot it on the counter while checking if the replacement sweaters actually shipped. Sometimes I wonder if I’m doing enough—like, is all this clicking around and emailing even real work? I miss the old routine of walking the sales floor, talking to people face to face, putting shirts in order by hand. Now I’m always thinking about what I might have missed—a wrong SKU, a forgotten reply, an order sitting in limbo. The boundaries between work and home are so thin now, and I end up answering messages at odd hours. I tried to read a news article while eating, but my mind kept circling back to the lost box and whether I should call the courier again. I wish I could just switch off my thoughts for a while. The sun comes in through the window differently at midday, and sometimes it feels like the only clue about what time it is. I keep promising myself I’ll take a real break, maybe walk outside, but then something else comes up. It’s tiring, but I still hope tomorrow will be smoother. Maybe I’ll leave my phone in another room for lunch and just breathe. For now, though, I need to check the order status one more time before my next shift starts.

Just finished a long conversation with Alex about how we've been missing each other’s signals lately, and now I’m sprawled out on the couch, feeling the late evening chill even with the blanket pulled up. I know I have a tendency to react quickly, sometimes to fill the silence or just because I want to keep things moving. Today, I tried to hold back and listen, but I caught myself zoning out halfway through his explanation, probably because I’m so tired. It’s weird how being hopeful for us sometimes feels at odds with being honest—like I’m afraid to admit things still feel a little off. I’m trying to remind myself that progress isn’t always obvious, and small steps still count. For now, I’m going to let the noise of the TV wash over me and hope tomorrow feels a bit lighter.

Dialysis Day
Today for dialysis day, I got here and on before 11:45 AM. Today, being H & H
(Hemoglobin and Hematocrit
). The doctor has his patients checked twice a month with the labs of everything else done once a month. Anyway, my first hematocrit number was 7.3, so a nurse took another vial to have it tested, and the result was 12.8. The head nurse came to me and asked me I was feeling okay, and told me what the symptoms of a low hemoglobin are, and I did not have any said symptoms. She then told me that I was not having any of the said symptoms and the reason my hemoglobin can read low, and she did not believe the number was exact, but she wanted me to have it rechecked. So, for a few minutes, I was getting panicky. The results came in lickity split, and it was in the green—normal at 12.8. See what can happen in a few seconds to get upset? It does not take much with my disorder.

Crickets were so loud last night as I walked around the block that I almost forgot where I was for a minute, just the chirping and my shoes on the uneven sidewalk, the sodium glow of the streetlights making everything a little more surreal. I needed to get out of the house after that tense conversation, not even angry exactly but both of us sort of stuck, talking in circles and trying to say what we mean without hitting the old landmines. I had this restless energy, couldn't sit still, so I just grabbed my jacket and started walking, not really thinking about where I was going. The air had that dampness that sticks to your skin, and I realized I'd forgotten to eat dinner again, stomach growling but somehow food just felt like another chore. I passed the neighbor's yard where their dog always barks at me, but tonight it just stared, silent, like even it knew I needed some peace. My mind was racing with all these half-finished thoughts about Dad, about how grief sneaks up even when you don't expect it, and how sometimes I want to call him and tell him something dumb, like what I cooked for lunch or a weird dream I had, and then remember that I can't. Then I circled back to the fight earlier, or really, the argument about nothing and everything, about how much we both want to get it right but end up talking past each other. I keep telling myself it's normal, that long-term relationships are messy and real communication takes work, but in the moment it feels like I should have the answers, or at least better questions. I started mentally drafting a new story idea, something about a couple who can't talk but who also can't let go, and then I wondered if that's too close to home, if writing about it will help or just make me dwell. By the time I got back to our porch, I felt a little calmer, heart not pounding so hard, and I could hear laughter from a few houses down, which made me oddly hopeful. Sometimes just moving helps, just walking until my thoughts slow down enough to catch up with me. I still don't know how we'll fix the stuck places, but I do believe we want to, which has to count for something. Maybe tomorrow I'll try again, maybe say less and listen more. I wish I could tell Dad about all of this. I wish he could see how much I'm trying not to give up on the things that matter. For now, at least, I just needed that walk.

I checked my phone and, as expected, there was a message from my best friend.

“Adik na ata ako sa APEX. Kasi paggising ko, laro iniisip ko.”

I huffed a laugh.

Because… yeah. Same.

It’s funny too, considering we both started out reluctant when my siblings invited us to try APEX. Dee’s always been more of a gamer than me—mobile games, battle royales, FPS games, all other games. But she retired from competitive gaming because, let’s be honest, competitive spaces can get toxic as hell.

Probably because she’s playing with us, honestly. And she did say, she mostly played multiplayer games with me and my siblings.

Last night’s session started around 9 p.m.

Then suddenly it was 6 a.m.

My sister and I stared at the clock like it personally offended us.

“That’s… that’s a whole work shift,” one of us said.

We both laughed.

What makes it even funnier is that before we started, we explicitly agreed:

“We’re feeling lethargic.”
“Yeah, let’s not play too much.”
“Just a few rounds.”

Famous last words.

We’re always “fixing” our sleep schedule, failing spectacularly, and somehow ending up lethargic even on the days we supposedly fixed it. So yes, we agreed—just a few rounds.

Then we won one.

Then another.

Blood started pumping.
Dee joined in.
And suddenly it was morning.

Lethargic who?

So when Dee said she thinks she’s getting addicted to APEX, I had to admit—I probably am too.

Especially last night, when I noticed I was actually… getting kills.

“These are bots,” I told my sister.
“They’re not,” she said. “Their movement’s different. And look, Asian names.”
“Nah,” I insisted. “I’m racking up kills and damage. That never happens. These are bots.”
“Come on,” she said, “give yourself some credit. You've been getting kills.”

I scoffed. Internally, mostly.

I still feel like I’m shit at it. But... I might actually be getting better.

Jesus Christ, I write so much about this game.
And why am I defending myself to my own writing?

Cue the voices:

You should be improving skills relevant for work, not gaming.
You’re wasting time.
How is this helping you?
You’re pathetic in life, even in games. You suck ass.

Okay. Enough. Shut up!

I think I write about APEX so much because—well. Because it matters to me that my siblings intentionally invite me to play. And I say intentionally because I can feel it. They always loop me in, no matter how noob I am.

I don’t want to be a burden.
I want to pull my weight.

Why am I always this defensive, even in my own writing?

Future Xu, this is how your mind worked at 33.
Yikes.

Alright. Let me try to land this plane.

It is funny that Dee feels addicted, because I do too—especially now that I can see some improvement. Even though I still don’t love FPS games, I’ve been enjoying this with my siblings and with her.

And I’ve been enjoying playing Lifeline.

She’s the kind of legend opponents hate—keeps the team alive, revives fast, refuses to let people stay down. And somehow, that fits. I’ve been focusing on improving supporting my siblings long enough for us to win rounds. Or at least place high.

Top two.
More wins.
Better runs.

I’m still shit at shooting. But I can support. And sometimes, that’s enough.

And there it is.
The crux of it all.

Support.

The voices are extra loud today, sure. But at the end of it, I’m just happy to be useful—to keep people standing. Whether that’s in a game… or in real life.

Today felt like a nonstop scramble just trying to keep everything balanced, work tasks piling up while also trying to not screw up communicating properly with her. The bus was packed and kind of loud, which only made my brain race faster instead of giving me space to unwind. I kept flipping through my phone, half-reading emails and messages, but nothing really stuck because my mind kept wandering back to what I needed to say later tonight. I really want to get better at explaining what I’m feeling without jumping straight to overthinking every reaction. It’s like a weird loop that doesn’t stop until I force myself to pause, which is hard on a crowded bus when there’s so much noise and motion around. I still haven’t figured out how to just be spontaneous without panicking internally about the logistics of timing or phrasing.

By the time I got off, my legs were stiff and my head was buzzing from trying to juggle work, relationship stuff, and just getting home without wandering into anxious territory. I’m pretty sure she noticed I was off today, but I didn’t want to bring it up until I could gather my thoughts properly. It’s frustrating to want to be open but feel like you’re behind on your own emotional cues sometimes. I’m hoping that if I start small, like just saying one simple thing honestly, it might help break this cycle. For now, I’m just glad to be in my room, quiet except for the hum of the fan, and letting my brain slow down a bit. Maybe tomorrow won’t feel as overloaded or restless—it has to, right? 🚌

There are three appointments showing for tomorrow, not counting the orthodontist, and I’m pretty sure I forgot to RSVP to the school event for next week. I need to talk to my partner tonight about who’s handling pickup since my work meeting might run late, but last night we got sidetracked by an argument about the dishwasher (ridiculous, but it just spiraled). I try to remind myself that most of these things will get sorted out, and there’s no real disaster looming, but my mind keeps spinning anyway. Maybe I’ll make a list after lunch or just try to breathe for a minute before diving back in. The quiet in the break room is nice at least, just the hum of the refrigerator and nobody else around. Now, I’m eating leftover rice at the kitchen table. The apartment is quiet except for the sound of the fridge humming. My phone keeps buzzing with emails about freelance gigs, but I can’t focus on any of them. I keep replaying that memory of her in my mind, wondering if it’ll ever stop feeling so sharp.

I told myself I’d get some reading done during this break, but all I’ve managed is staring at the wall. I feel restless and tired at the same time. Missing her comes in waves, and today feels heavier. I wish I could tell her about my projects, or just complain about being broke. I’m not sure what to do with all this, so I’m just writing it down and hoping it makes it feel a little less big. Maybe it will, maybe not.

I’m frustrated with myself for not handling the conversation better. Was I too pushy? Maybe I should have just agreed, but I can’t help wanting to know every detail to make sure nothing gets missed. A part of me wonders if the way I ask things makes people defensive. I want to help, but I end up feeling like I’m the problem. Nobody in my group really talks unless it’s to correct someone, and I keep wondering if I’m just too quiet or if I’m missing some secret code for fitting in. The thing is, I like coding and I don’t mind the work, but the people part is draining. I keep thinking about how everyone else seems to slip into conversation so easily, while I’m busy overanalyzing if I’m interrupting. I can hear the hum from the supermarket delivery trucks around the corner, and I keep tapping my fingers on my thigh, almost unconsciously, like I’m trying to keep pace with a song I don’t remember. The sun’s nearly down—orange light bouncing off the building across the lot, and I keep wondering if I’ll ever get used to these fragmented days, where I’m squeezing art between work shifts and roommate schedules and meal planning. My paints are still out back at the apartment, but I’ve got my pencil and a scrap of paper, and I keep scribbling ideas for that mural I’ve been obsessing over, even though I know I won’t touch it again until late tonight, maybe after midnight.

There’s something energizing about being this busy, even if my thoughts feel like they’re darting in every direction at once. I keep thinking about how I’ll probably forget to grab groceries again, because by the time I get home, my mind will already be on the next thing—did I remember to text back about that show next week? Did I leave my brushes soaking? The repetition of juggling my roommate’s calendar with my own, swapping nights for dishes, splitting fridge space, it’s a mess sometimes but I can’t imagine living totally alone. The chaos is weirdly comforting. I glance at the time—ten minutes before I have to go in. I wish I could freeze these little moments, just hang out in the quiet before everything picks up speed again. Maybe tonight I’ll finally finish that background layer, or maybe I’ll just end up doodling in the kitchen while my roommate reheats leftovers. Either way, it’s okay.

I spent a chunk of today just trying to get my calendar under control. The lab meeting ran late, so I had to push back the time I was supposed to finish prepping samples, and now I’ve got a backlog that’s going to bleed into tomorrow. I’m still not sure if my supervisor noticed, but it feels like there’s always something slipping through the cracks. I kept glancing at my phone all afternoon, half-hoping someone from the group chat would suggest getting together, but nothing. It’s just me in this apartment, surrounded by sticky notes and half-packed moving boxes I never finished unpacking.

I keep telling myself to be patient, that eventually I’ll get a grip on both the research schedule and maybe even a social life. But it’s hard when every to-do list seems to get longer by the end of the day. Dinner was microwaved leftovers (again), and I’m pretty sure I forgot to email the data set to Dr. K. I’ll set a reminder for tomorrow, but I know I’ll wake up already feeling like I’m behind. I wonder if anyone else here ever feels this scattered, or if that’s just a me thing.

Feeling heavy and a little numb tonight. The kitchen clock says 5:14 am and the fridge is humming louder than usual. I haven’t really slept, just drifted in and out, mind replaying yesterday’s phone call with my sister. She’s still upset about how I missed Mom’s appointment last week. I keep telling myself it wasn’t intentional—I just lost track, but I know she’s tired of hearing my excuses. I keep replaying her voice, sharp but tired, and I can’t stop wondering if I’m just letting everyone down lately.

I made toast but let it go cold, too busy staring at the steam from the kettle and overthinking everything. The empty chair at the kitchen table makes the place feel even quieter, and sometimes I feel like I’m rattling around in this apartment, echoing off the walls. I know I should reach out more, but something holds me back—maybe it’s guilt, maybe it’s fear of another argument or just not knowing what to say anymore.

My body feels worn out, shoulders tight and eyelids heavy, but my brain won’t shut up. Thoughts swirling about Mom’s health, my unemployment, and how distant I feel from everyone lately. It’s exhausting trying to be strong when every little thing seems to hit harder these days. I wish I knew how to fix things with my sister, or at least stop beating myself up over every mistake. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try calling her again, or maybe I’ll just let another day pass—sometimes it’s hard to tell which is worse.

We spent the last few days at Disneyland. It's been a while since I've gone and it was definitely a different experience this time. I wasn't really looking forward to it, and I was dreading being around all of the crowds and whatnot, but I will admit that once we were there I did have a good time. We got to ride a lot of rides, I'm talking probably two dozen over three days. We also got to watch one of the nighttime spectaculars. And we walked from one side of the park to the other probably a hundred times, because that's what you do at Disneyland and it's exhausting as hell. I will say, I'm glad we went when we did. We got to spend some quality time all together as a family, including with my parents, siblings, in-laws, and even my grandma. We got to see the Christmas decorations before they took them down for the year. And most importantly, we got to take my daughter for the first time and she absolutely loved it. She may have even enjoyed it more than us haha. I will also say that I am getting way too old for this, and I am very much glad to be home and resting. On a random note, my mind is on the future and is starting to think about the things I want to accomplish in my life. Disneyland is definitely a place for dreams, maybe that has something to do with it.

I didn’t plan on being so distracted this afternoon, but the conversation with Mark caught me off guard. We were sitting on the living room couch, and I thought I was clear about needing space to finish the report, but he kept trying to jump in with ideas, and it felt like he wasn’t hearing me. I ended up shutting down instead of explaining better, which probably made things worse. I want to believe he just didn’t realize how overwhelmed I was in the moment, but I keep wondering if I was too cold or impatient. Maybe if I’d been more patient or taken a breath before responding, it wouldn’t have spiraled. Now the tension lingers in the air, and I’m not sure how to bring it back to a good place without sounding like I’m blaming him. It’s frustrating because I want us to understand each other without all this back and forth. Hopefully, I can find a way to talk again tonight that feels calm and clear.

Feeling a bit on edge tonight, not exactly anxious but my mind keeps hopping from one thing to the next and not settling anywhere useful. I finished dinner about an hour ago—leftover chicken and some slightly overcooked green beans, which is better than what I managed last week. The kitchen is still a mess, but I just don’t have the energy to deal with it right now. Work was relentless today, too many emails about things that probably don’t matter and too many people who think I know more than I actually do. Sometimes I wish I could just tell them that the secret to the universe isn’t hiding in my filing cabinet, but I guess that’s not the best career move.

I keep thinking about where things are going with Lisa (well, not her real name, but that’s what I call her in my head now), and I can’t tell if I’m excited or just nervous. She texted me this afternoon about her mother’s health, which brought up that old ache about Dad again. Funny how family stuff never really leaves you alone, even after years. I know I’m supposed to be present and supportive, but part of me is worried I’ll say the wrong thing or just not be enough. I keep telling myself to relax, to just see what happens, but my brain is stubbornly refusing to cooperate tonight. Maybe I’ll make some tea and try to read, but knowing me, I’ll just end up scrolling through my phone until it’s way past bedtime. So it goes.

I woke up to the sound of the fridge humming louder than usual, reminding me that I need to figure out if it’s about to die or just being dramatic. My roommate was already in the kitchen, making coffee and moving with this hurried energy that made me feel like I was in the way even though I was just trying to get a glass of water. We keep tiptoeing around each other lately, schedules overlapping at the worst times, and I feel guilty for thinking I wish I had the kitchen to myself, just for once. Today is packed with deadlines and meetings, and even though I’m kind of proud of how much I’ve managed to keep up, I can feel the tiredness settling behind my eyes. When I sat down at the little table by the window this afternoon, trying to outline a new story idea, I ended up just staring outside for a long time, watching the neighbor’s dog chase its tail. It hit me, how much I miss writing just for the fun of it and not always worrying about if it’ll be good enough or if it fits into someone else’s expectations. I’m self-critical to the point where I sometimes talk myself out of even starting, and today that voice felt especially loud. Still, I managed to jot down a couple paragraphs before my roommate came back in to microwave leftovers, the smell of curry filling the whole place. I wish I was better at not letting the little daily frictions get under my skin. I know I’m lucky to have a roof over my head and someone to split rent with, but sometimes I crave quiet more than company. Maybe tomorrow I’ll try working at the library instead, just for a change of pace. For now, I’m just going to let myself be tired and not fight it. It’s enough to have shown up and tried.

The old radiator is clicking again, keeping me company while I stare at the ceiling. I left the kitchen light on by accident, and it’s casting this weird, sharp rectangle on the living room floor. I keep thinking about the conversation I had today with a regular who asked if I was settling in. I gave my usual answer, the upbeat one, but the truth is it’s still mostly guesswork. I haven’t found a rhythm yet, and every time I think I’m getting closer, something feels off. Maybe it’s just the way everything is unfamiliar: the street names, the bus lines, even the way people pause in conversation. 

Tonight I caught myself wondering what would make this place feel like mine. Back home, I always knew what to expect, even when I didn’t like it. Here, it’s all possibility, which sounds nice until you realize it’s also a lot of uncertainty. I keep overanalyzing every small interaction, like maybe if I say the right thing or laugh at the right moment, I’ll suddenly fit in. Sometimes I feel optimistic that it’ll click eventually, but right now I’m restless, turning things over in my mind when I should be sleeping. Maybe tomorrow I’ll join that trivia night after my shift. Or maybe I’ll just go for a walk and see where I end up. Either way, I hope I start to feel a little more like myself, wherever that self is supposed to fit here.

My shoes made that squeaky noise again as I stepped off the curb, which is apparently how I announce myself to the neighborhood at 9:40pm. The air was that kind of crisp that makes your nose sting a little, but at least the streetlights were cooperating for once, not flickering like some horror movie. I ended up counting the mailboxes just to keep my mind from drifting too far—there are twelve in the block, which makes sense, but I’d have bet on thirteen for some reason. Walking after dinner has become a habit, mostly because I can’t stand staring at my phone, waiting for a client to confirm or cancel another gig. The freelance chef life: glamorous in theory, endlessly waiting in practice. At least the sidewalks don’t judge if I mumble about how much I miss steady paychecks. Saw that tabby cat again slinking under the same dented sedan, looking like it knows more about surviving on scraps than I do. The smell of someone’s barbecue drifted by, and I’ll admit, I critiqued it out loud—too much lighter fluid, not enough patience, story of most home cooks. I caught my reflection in a shop window and realized my hat’s crooked, which is probably why the only people who talk to me tonight are dogs. Got back to my building and just stood under the awning for a minute, letting the cool air settle in. Thoughts about invoices and ingredient lists started to bubble up, but I figured they could wait till morning. For now, I’ll just be grateful my feet still work and the city hasn’t run out of surprises—or at least, things to grumble about.

The fridge hums steadily and there’s a faint clatter from the kitchen next door. Sunlight comes in through the blinds at a sharp angle, cutting across the table where I’ve spread out my lunch—just a salad and some crackers. I keep glancing at my phone, double-checking the calendar. Tonight is going to be tight, and I feel the clock ticking already.

My roommate has her shift ending late, so I’ll need to make sure dinner is something easy to reheat. There’s laundry in the dryer I have to fold before she gets back, and I promised I’d water the plants this time. Work calls were nonstop this morning, and my notepad is covered with scribbled reminders. I’m trying to decide if I have time to run to the store for groceries before my next meeting. It’s always a puzzle, fitting in the errands and chores between calls and messages. I feel focused, but I’m already making lists for tonight: prep lunches, set up coffee for the morning, check emails one last time before bed. The quiet right now feels like a pause before everything starts up again. I know I’ll get it all done, somehow, but I wish it didn’t always come down to the wire. Maybe I’ll sneak in a quick walk after dinner if there’s a gap. Just a bit of fresh air would help. For now, I’m going to finish my lunch and review my to-do list once more.

It makes sense that we might quite enjoy reading a diary of a
pioneer woman who braved the elements every day just to take care
of the most basic of human needs. We might find it interesting
to see how she managed to survive a long cold winter cooped up
in a sod hut.
But what will it be like to read about a woman of 2002, 100
years from today ? I wonder if the pioneer woman thought her
life extraordinary? But we are grateful that she wrote about her
life, because in so many ways it is very different from our own.
This is a difficult thing for me at least, to see my life in
any way as extraordinary. But what if I am wrong ?
I saw a program last night about Thomas Jefferson. The last
entry in his personal journal was a caluclation of how much
lamp oil had cost him for a month and how many hours of light
he had gotten from that quanity. Amazing.
But then, he was not constantly distracted by television,
radio, music at the push of a button... I often wonder what
American society would be like without the teletube....
So as an excersize I give you some mundane details of my day.
A homemaker in California (NOT Los Angeles, thank you very
much).
This morning at 7:30 my neighbor Diane and I went for our
daily walk. We were gone for an hour. Talked a blue streak and
felt refreshed. We had planned to go to the library today so
after breakfast we headed out in Diane's car. Stopped at the
bank where I deposited a $350. check from the sale
of a Jack Russel Terrier pup that we could not civilize to
accept our older dog and a passive cat that the pup mauled
unmercifully. Along with the 350.00 was a check for $10.00
that I got from my father because we bet on the World Series
and my Angels won :-) And another 228.00 that was my "mad money"
from selling hand crafted gourds that I make and some baby
sitting I had done for my daughter in law.
Diane and I went to Wal-Mart to buy yarn (2.09) a skein
because her aunt from Maine is here visiting and is going to
teach Diane to crochet. We then went to the library where we
both picked out some more cookbooks. Diane has a web site where
she posts recipies once a week. I also got a book about
menopause because I think I am starting to have hot flashes !
Eeek ! We then headed over to Wal-Mart where I bought Black Cohosh, Evening Primrose Oil and
Ginko Biloba tablets that are supposed to help with the onset
of menopause. I am starting with the Black Cohosh first I have
decided. These were all priced reasonably at about
4 dollars a bottle.
Then we headed over to Mervyn's and I bought another down
lap blanket like one we already have because they were on sale
for 20.00 and my husband wanted another one.(He is wrapped up
in it right now on the couch.) I bought a country blue one.
We got home just after lunch time and I spent a quiet
afternoon. When my husband got home (we only have one car)
I drove over to yoga class and spent a lovely hour practicing
yoga. I even did some research today about what would be
involved in getting a yoga instructor's certificate. I found
very mixed results. If I am serious about it, I will need to
talk to some people who have done it and get some advise.
I thought it might be very nice to conduct yoga classes in
my home, just to make a little extra money.
I don't know, it does seem pretty ordinary doesn't it ?
But what do you think the average person's life will be like
in 2102 ? Maybe all this running around will sound funny to
them. Maybe they will do everything from home. Shopping,
virtual classes, banking. Actually, all those things ARE
available now, but not everyone does them ALL the time.
Oh, I am rambling .... excuse me. I better go to bed.
Thomas Jefferson I am not......
